questions.good_to_know: Spread placement groups put instances on distinct hardware to reduce correlated failure. Partition placement groups fit large distributed stores such as Hadoop or Kafka. Dedicated Hosts are the socket-license answer.

questions.q: A company has run the same 40 Amazon EC2 web instances, 24 hours a day, for 18 months and expects that baseline to continue for at least another year. Traffic above the baseline is small and already handled by Auto Scaling. The finance team wants a lower unit price for the steady 40 instances and will accept a one-year commitment. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Cover the 40-instance baseline with a Savings Plan or Reserved Instances.
B. Replace the 40 instances with Spot Instances in a diversified Auto Scaling group.
C. Move the 40 instances onto Dedicated Hosts to receive a hardware discount.
D. Change the 40 instances to a larger On-Demand type so fewer of them run.

questions.explain: A measured, long-lived baseline is what Savings Plans and Reserved Instances discount. Which Savings Plan type is more flexible across families and Regions is a Lesson 16 decision.
questions.good_to_know: Spot would cut the unit price further but can be reclaimed, which a customer-facing web baseline usually cannot accept. Dedicated Hosts are for socket-level licenses, not a generic discount. A larger On-Demand type is not a purchase-model saving.

questions.q: A company is launching a new customer-facing web application on Amazon EC2 in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Traffic volume is unknown and may stay low for months. The application cannot tolerate instance interruption: in-flight checkout requests must not be dropped because AWS reclaimed capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the Auto Scaling group on Spot Instances with a diversified mixed instances policy.
B. Run the Auto Scaling group on On-Demand instances.
C. Run the Auto Scaling group on Dedicated Hosts to avoid shared hardware.
D. Cover an estimated peak with a three-year all-upfront Reserved Instance purchase.

questions.explain: On-Demand has no interruption and no commitment, which matches an uninterruptible workload whose size is still unknown. Spot's discount comes with a two-minute reclamation warning the checkout path cannot accept.
questions.good_to_know: Spot is correct when the stem says the work can checkpoint or retry. A long Reserved Instance term is the answer after the baseline is measured. Dedicated Hosts solve licensing, not interruption.

questions.q: A company must present one HTTPS hostname to the internet for a website and a REST API that run on Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets. Requests to api.example.com must reach one target group, and requests whose path starts with /static must reach another. TLS must terminate at the load balancer with a certificate already in ACM. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Application Load Balancer with host-based and path-based listener rules.
B. Create a Network Load Balancer and route TLS connections by URL path.
C. Attach the ACM certificate to an HTTPS listener on that load balancer.
D. Create a Gateway Load Balancer and terminate HTTPS on the appliance fleet.
E. Create a Route 53 weighted policy that splits api.example.com from /static.

questions.explain: Layer 7 host and path rules select an Application Load Balancer, and TLS termination with an ACM certificate is an HTTPS listener on that same balancer. Both pieces are required; neither NLB nor DNS can split on URL path.
questions.good_to_know: Weighted routing can split two hostnames, not a hostname versus a URL path. A Network Load Balancer does not inspect HTTP. Gateway Load Balancer is the appliance answer.

questions.q: A ticket vendor runs Amazon EC2 web instances in an Auto Scaling group. On-sale events start at published clock times, and new instances need several minutes to become healthy. Between events, traffic is low and variable. The architecture must have spare capacity ready when an on-sale begins and must still follow demand after the doors open. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Add a simple scaling policy that launches instances only after CPU has already reached 90 percent.
B. Add a scheduled scaling action that raises desired capacity before each on-sale time.
C. Change the launch template to the largest available instance type and freeze desired capacity.
D. Add a target tracking policy that keeps a load metric near a chosen value after the event starts.
E. Replace the group with Spot Instances so extra capacity is always cheap enough to over-provision.

questions.explain: Scheduled scaling warms the group before a known clock time. Target tracking then follows live demand. The two policies solve different parts of the same day.
questions.good_to_know: A simple policy that waits for 90 percent CPU is reactive and starts too late when bootstrap takes minutes. Vertical scaling and Spot do not address the schedule.

questions.q: A company wants one Auto Scaling group to keep four On-Demand web instances as a base and to fill additional capacity with Spot Instances. Spot launches must spread across several instance types in the same generation so a shortage in one pool does not halt scaling. The group today uses a launch configuration. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Keep the launch configuration and enable Spot allocation on that configuration.
B. Place the group in a cluster placement group so Spot and On-Demand share a rack.
C. Create a launch template that specifies the AMI, security groups, and a baseline instance type.
D. Migrate the web tier to AWS Fargate so purchase options are no longer required.
E. Attach a mixed instances policy with instance-type overrides for the Spot portion of the group.

questions.explain: Mixing On-Demand with Spot and naming more than one instance type requires a launch template plus a mixed instances policy. Launch configurations cannot express either requirement.
questions.good_to_know: A cluster placement group is the HPC-latency answer. Fargate is a Lesson 09 compute model; it does not satisfy a stem that keeps an EC2 Auto Scaling group.

questions.q: Partners send a custom TCP protocol to a market-data service on Amazon EC2 in two Availability Zones. Each partner firewall allowlists destination IPv4 addresses and cannot follow DNS changes. The service is not HTTP. The company needs a regional load balancer whose address in each enabled zone never changes. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an internet-facing Network Load Balancer and enable both Availability Zones.
B. Create an internet-facing Application Load Balancer and attach Elastic IP addresses to it.
C. Create a CloudFront distribution with a TCP origin that points at the instances.
D. Create a Gateway Load Balancer and register the market-data instances as targets.
E. Allocate an Elastic IP address for each enabled zone and associate it with the load balancer.

questions.explain: A Network Load Balancer is the Layer 4 regional balancer, and it is the one that accepts an Elastic IP address per enabled Availability Zone. Those two steps give partners a stable TCP destination in each zone.
questions.good_to_know: Application Load Balancers cannot be assigned Elastic IP addresses and do not serve arbitrary TCP. CloudFront is HTTP at the edge. Gateway Load Balancer inserts appliances; it is not the partner-facing TCP listener.

questions.q: A web fleet in an Auto Scaling group sits behind an Application Load Balancer. Operators see HTTP 502 errors while CloudWatch still reports every instance as passing EC2 status checks. On several instances the web process has exited. The group must stop sending traffic to those instances and must replace them without a manual terminate. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Increase the group's maximum capacity so extra instances hide the 502 errors.
B. Configure the target group health check to a path the application actually serves.
C. Set the Auto Scaling group's health check type to ELB.
D. Switch the group from a launch template to a launch configuration.
E. Move the instances into a spread placement group so a dead process is isolated.

questions.explain: The target group must detect that the application is dead, and the Auto Scaling group must treat that target-group failure as instance failure. Default EC2 status checks watch the virtual machine, not the web process.
questions.good_to_know: Raising maximum capacity, changing to a launch configuration, or picking a different placement group leaves the dead processes in service. Health-check grace period matters at boot, not after a running process has already exited.

questions.q: A company runs third-party intrusion-detection appliances on Amazon EC2. Every packet to and from application subnets must pass through those appliances. The security team must scale the appliance fleet independently of the applications, and the applications must keep their existing TCP and UDP protocols. The appliances already accept GENEVE. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Application Load Balancer and register the appliances as HTTP targets.
B. Create a Network Load Balancer and register the appliances as TLS targets on port 443.
C. Replace the appliances with an internet-facing Classic Load Balancer.
D. Create a Gateway Load Balancer in the appliance VPC.
E. Register the intrusion-detection appliances as targets of that load balancer.

questions.explain: Gateway Load Balancer plus an appliance target group is the pattern that inspects all IP traffic and scales the fleet over GENEVE. ALB and NLB sit in front of applications; they are not an inspection fabric for a third-party appliance.
questions.good_to_know: Choose an Application Load Balancer for host and path routing, or a Network Load Balancer for a static IP in front of a TCP service. Classic Load Balancer is not an IDS scaler.

questions.q: A company is building a new stateless web tier on Amazon EC2. Golden AMIs already contain the application. The tier must launch consistent instances, replace them automatically, and remain available if one Availability Zone fails. The team does not want to keep using launch configurations. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create a launch template that points at the golden AMI and the web instance type.
B. Create an Auto Scaling group that uses that template and spans at least two Availability Zones.
C. Create a launch configuration that points at the golden AMI and pin the group to one zone.
D. Place every instance in a cluster placement group that stretches both Availability Zones.
E. Store the application binaries only on instance store so new launches stay fast.

questions.explain: A launch template is the current way to start Auto Scaling instances from an AMI, and the group must span two Availability Zones so one zone outage does not take the tier down. Those two steps are the replaceable-compute baseline.
questions.good_to_know: Launch configurations cannot mix instance types or purchase options and are the legacy path the stem already rejects. Cluster placement groups do not span Availability Zones. Instance store is ephemeral and is not where unique data belongs.

questions.q: A media company runs transcoding workers on Amazon EC2 instances in three Availability Zones. Every worker must read and write the same project files at the same time using POSIX file semantics. The dataset grows without a planned size, and the company does not want to manage file-server instances. The workers stay in private subnets. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it from each instance.
B. Attach one gp3 Amazon EBS volume to a lead instance and share it over NFS.
C. Store the project files in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval.
D. Place the files on instance store volumes and rsync them between instances.

questions.explain: Concurrent multi-AZ POSIX access and elastic capacity select Amazon EFS. A single EBS volume stays in one AZ and is not a shared regional file system.
questions.good_to_know: FSx for Lustre would be the answer if the stem demanded a parallel HPC file system integrated with S3. Glacier is archive object storage, not a POSIX mount.

questions.q: A research lab runs tightly coupled high-performance computing jobs on Amazon EC2 in one VPC. The jobs need a parallel file system with very high throughput and must read training datasets that already live in Amazon S3. Operators want a managed file service rather than building Lustre on instances. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon EFS One Zone file system in the same Availability Zone as the cluster.
B. Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server and expose an SMB share to the cluster.
C. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 dataset.
D. Attach Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) Amazon EBS volumes to each compute node.

questions.explain: Parallel HPC I/O plus S3 integration is the FSx for Lustre pattern. EFS is elastic NFS for Linux, not a Lustre-style parallel file system.
questions.good_to_know: FSx for Windows File Server is the SMB and Active Directory answer. EBS HDD classes fit sequential block workloads on a single instance, not a shared HPC namespace.

questions.q: A company hosts a latency-sensitive relational database on a single Amazon EC2 instance. The database needs durable block storage with consistent low-latency IOPS. The instance and its data will remain in one Availability Zone. Other instances must not mount the same volume as shared storage. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store database files in Amazon S3 Standard and mount the bucket with a file gateway.
B. Attach a provisioned IOPS SSD Amazon EBS volume to the instance.
C. Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it on the database instance.
D. Create Amazon FSx for OpenZFS and present the share to the instance.

questions.explain: A single-AZ database that needs attached block semantics and predictable IOPS is an EBS io-class (or similarly provisioned SSD) volume. S3 and EFS are not local block devices for that engine.
questions.good_to_know: gp3 is the usual general-purpose SSD when capacity and performance can be set independently. Choose io-class when the stem stresses demanding IOPS or latency.

questions.q: A software vendor stores user-uploaded objects in Amazon S3. Access frequency varies by customer and changes over time, so the team cannot pick a fixed lifecycle day. Objects must stay immediately available over HTTP. Operations wants Amazon S3 to move objects between access tiers automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access for every object.
B. Use S3 Glacier Deep Archive and restore objects when a user downloads them.
C. Store the objects on Cold HDD (sc1) Amazon EBS volumes.
D. Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for the objects.

questions.explain: Unknown or changing access plus immediate availability is Intelligent-Tiering. Deep Archive requires a restore and is not immediately readable.
questions.good_to_know: One Zone-IA would be cheaper infrequent access only if the stem accepted a single-AZ durability trade-off. EBS is block storage for an instance, not an object store for user downloads.

questions.q: A company is retiring an on-premises Windows file cluster used by desktop applications in one office. Those applications need managed SMB shares, Microsoft Active Directory authentication, and Windows access-control lists. Linux NFS is not in use. The company wants AWS to operate the file servers rather than EC2 file VMs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server joined to the directory.
B. Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it with the NFS client on Windows.
C. Store files in Amazon S3 and map a drive with the AWS CLI sync command.
D. Attach Amazon EBS volumes with Multi-Attach to a fleet of Windows instances.

questions.explain: SMB, Active Directory, and Windows ACLs are the FSx for Windows File Server constraints. EFS is NFS for Linux, not a Windows-native SMB service.
questions.good_to_know: S3 File Gateway (Lesson 14) would appear if the stem wanted a hybrid local NFS or SMB cache in front of S3. EBS Multi-Attach is not a Windows file namespace and is not taught as the SMB answer.

questions.q: A marketing site stores millions of product images as objects. The images are read many times per day from a public website and a mobile app. The company needs eleven nines of durability and does not want retrieval delays or restore jobs. Which Amazon S3 storage class should a solutions architect choose?

options.text: A. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
B. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
C. S3 Standard
D. S3 Glacier Deep Archive

questions.explain: Frequent object access with immediate reads is S3 Standard. Glacier classes are archive economics for rarely retrieved data.
questions.good_to_know: Intelligent-Tiering would win if access were unknown or changing. Instant Retrieval fits archive objects that are rarely read but must still open in milliseconds when they are.

questions.q: A hospital must keep medical images for seven years to meet a retention rule. Staff retrieve an object only a few times per year and can wait hours for a restore. The hospital wants the lowest storage cost among Amazon S3 archive classes and does not need millisecond access. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store the objects in S3 Standard-Infrequent Access.
B. Store the objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
C. Store the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering Immediate Access.
D. Store the objects on Throughput Optimized HDD Amazon EBS volumes.

questions.explain: Years of retention, rare retrieval, and hours of restore time select Glacier Deep Archive. Standard-IA and Intelligent-Tiering keep objects immediately available at a higher storage price.
questions.good_to_know: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is the middle archive class when restore in minutes to hours is acceptable but Deep Archive’s longer restore is not. Instant Retrieval is the millisecond archive class.

questions.q: An Amazon EC2 database uses a 2 TB Amazon EBS volume in Availability Zone A. The company needs point-in-time backups and must be able to create a new volume in Availability Zone B in the same Region if Zone A fails. Operators will attach the new volume to a replacement instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon S3 versioning on the volume and copy the object to Zone B.
B. Configure Amazon EFS replication from Zone A to Zone B.
C. Copy the instance store of the database instance into Zone B nightly.
D. Create EBS snapshots of the volume and restore a snapshot in Zone B.

questions.explain: EBS snapshots are the point-in-time backup for volumes and can restore a volume in another AZ in the Region after the snapshot exists.
questions.good_to_know: Cross-Region copy of snapshots is the next step if the stem required a second Region. Instance store is ephemeral and is not a backup. S3 versioning does not apply to EBS volumes.

questions.q: A partner application must download a private report object from Amazon S3 for 15 minutes after a user clicks a link in a portal. The bucket must stay private. The company does not want to create IAM users for partners, does not want to make the object public, and will not change the partner application beyond the download URL. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Generate an S3 presigned URL that expires after 15 minutes.
B. Attach a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject from 0.0.0.0/0.
C. Move the object to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval and share the key.
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and send the object name.

questions.explain: Presigned URLs grant time-limited object access without making the bucket public. A public bucket policy would violate the private-bucket constraint.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront signed URLs (Lesson 12) would appear if the stem required a global CDN in front of private S3. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances; it is not an authorization mechanism.

questions.q: Analysts overwrite objects in an Amazon S3 data lake with the same key when they republish a dataset. Last month a bad publish replaced a week of results and the previous object was gone. The company must be able to recover the prior object after an overwrite or delete. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Change the storage class to S3 One Zone-IA.
B. Create an Amazon EFS file system and copy objects there nightly.
C. Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket.
D. Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration.

questions.explain: Versioning keeps prior object versions after overwrite or delete so they can be restored. Storage class and Transfer Acceleration do not retain old keys.
questions.good_to_know: Replication can copy versions to another bucket or Region once versioning is on. Lifecycle rules then expire old versions when retention allows.

questions.q: A company stores application logs as objects in Amazon S3 Standard in one bucket. After 90 days the logs are almost never read, and legal still requires them for four years. Restores may take hours. Operations wants Amazon S3 to move objects automatically based on age and does not want a nightly copy job. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Change the bucket to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and disable lifecycle rules.
B. Add a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days.
C. Copy objects to Amazon EBS snapshots every 90 days and delete the originals.
D. Enable S3 Replication Time Control to a second bucket in the same Region.

questions.explain: Known age plus rare access and long retention is a lifecycle transition into a Glacier archive class. Intelligent-Tiering is for unknown access, not a fixed 90-day archive handoff.
questions.good_to_know: If the stem said access patterns were unknown, Intelligent-Tiering would be the better automatic-tiering answer. Replication copies objects; it does not change storage class by age.

questions.q: A backup application writes large objects to Amazon S3. Objects are read only a few times a month but must remain immediately available. The company can accept storing them in a single Availability Zone to reduce cost. A zone failure may require rebuilding the backups from the source. Which storage class will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. S3 Standard
B. S3 Glacier Deep Archive
C. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
D. S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access

questions.explain: Infrequent access, immediate reads, and an explicit single-AZ cost trade-off select One Zone-IA. Standard-IA still stores across AZs; Deep Archive is not immediately available.
questions.good_to_know: Standard-IA is the answer when infrequent access must still survive an Availability Zone failure. Standard is the frequent-access default.

questions.q: An Amazon EC2 application uses a 1 TB general-purpose SSD volume as its only data disk. Sequential throughput is already fine, but the application now needs more random IOPS. The team does not want to grow the volume solely to get more performance. Capacity must stay 1 TB. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Migrate the volume to gp3 and provision additional IOPS independently.
B. Change the volume to Cold HDD (sc1) to raise IOPS.
C. Move the data to Amazon S3 Standard-IA.
D. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the volume.

questions.explain: gp3 lets capacity and performance be provisioned independently, which is the constraint against oversizing the disk just for IOPS.
questions.good_to_know: io-class SSD is the next step if even gp3 cannot meet the IOPS or latency target. HDD classes are for large sequential I/O, not higher random IOPS.

questions.q: A video archive sits in Amazon S3 in a single bucket. Producers sometimes need an object within milliseconds, but each object is retrieved only a few times per quarter. The company wants archive storage pricing rather than S3 Standard. Multi-hour restore jobs are not acceptable for the production workflow. Which storage class will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
B. S3 Glacier Deep Archive
C. S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
D. S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access

questions.explain: Rare retrieval that must still open in milliseconds is Glacier Instant Retrieval. Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive require a restore job.
questions.good_to_know: One Zone-IA is infrequent access in a single AZ, not an archive class with Glacier pricing. Flexible Retrieval fits when minutes-to-hours restore is fine.

questions.q: A company uses Amazon EBS volumes on EC2, Amazon EFS file systems, and Amazon RDS instances in one AWS account. Compliance wants one backup plan, one retention schedule, and centralized restore history across those services. Teams must not keep separate snapshot scripts per service. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable S3 Versioning on each resource and expire versions with lifecycle rules.
B. Use AWS Backup to define a backup plan that covers the supported resources.
C. Copy every volume to instance store nightly.
D. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system as the backup target.

questions.explain: AWS Backup centralizes backup plans and retention across supported services. S3 Versioning does not protect EBS, EFS, or RDS as a unified plan.
questions.good_to_know: Cross-Region or cross-account copies in AWS Backup are the follow-on when the stem adds a regional or account-isolation recovery requirement.

questions.q: An Amazon EC2 worker writes unique results to local disk during a 12-hour batch job in a private subnet. If the instance is stopped or the underlying host fails, those results must still exist so a replacement instance can continue. The job is not a tightly coupled HPC cluster and does not need a shared file system. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Write the results only to the instance store volume.
B. Write the results to Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive at the end of each minute.
C. Write the results to a cluster placement group scratch disk.
D. Write the results to an Amazon EBS volume attached to the instance.

questions.explain: Unique durable data belongs on EBS, which persists independently of the instance unless delete-on-termination is set. Instance store is wiped on stop, terminate, or host failure.
questions.good_to_know: Lesson 03 already established that instance store is ephemeral. This item tests the storage choice: EBS for durable block data on a single instance.

questions.q: A company stores objects in a versioned Amazon S3 bucket in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. A regulator requires a second copy in the Europe (Ireland) Region that updates as objects are written. Operations must not run a nightly sync job on EC2 and must not download the objects to EBS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Configure S3 Replication from the source bucket to a bucket in eu-west-1.
B. Create an Amazon EFS file system in eu-west-1 and mount it from US East instances.
C. Take Amazon EBS snapshots of an EC2 instance that downloads the bucket.
D. Change the storage class to S3 One Zone-IA in the source Region.

questions.explain: S3 Replication copies objects within or across Regions according to the rule. Versioning on the source is the usual prerequisite for replication.
questions.good_to_know: AWS Backup is the cross-service backup answer. EFS does not replicate an S3 object namespace to another Region by mounting it.

questions.q: A genomics pipeline writes multi-terabyte sequential files from a single Amazon EC2 instance in one Availability Zone. The instance needs a large block volume optimized for throughput rather than random IOPS. The data must persist if the instance is stopped. No other instance will mount the volume. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an io2 Block Express volume provisioned for maximum IOPS.
B. Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it from that instance only.
C. Attach a Throughput Optimized HDD (st1) Amazon EBS volume.
D. Store the files in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

questions.explain: Large sequential block I/O on one instance is the HDD EBS class (st1). io-class SSD is for demanding random IOPS and latency, which this stem does not ask for.
questions.good_to_know: EFS would be correct if multiple Linux instances needed a shared NFS namespace. Glacier Instant Retrieval is object archive, not an attached block device.

questions.q: Linux application servers in three Availability Zones must share a POSIX file system that grows automatically. Each AZ must keep working if another AZ fails. The company will not manage NFS servers on Amazon EC2 and will not use Windows SMB. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create a Regional Amazon EFS file system.
B. Create one gp3 Amazon EBS volume and enable Multi-Attach from all three AZs.
C. Create EFS mount targets in each Availability Zone the servers use.
D. Store the files in S3 Standard and mount the bucket with s3fs on each instance.
E. Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server and mount it with the NFS client.

questions.explain: EFS is the elastic multi-AZ NFS service, and mount targets in each AZ give zonal access without a self-managed NFS farm. Those two steps are jointly required.
questions.good_to_know: EBS Multi-Attach does not span three AZs as a POSIX file service. FSx for Windows is SMB. A fuse S3 mount is not the managed POSIX answer the lesson teaches.

questions.q: A data lake in Amazon S3 is overwritten in place when pipelines republish partitions. The company must recover a previous object after a bad publish and must also keep a copy of new objects in a second Region for disaster recovery. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Change every object to S3 Glacier Deep Archive immediately on upload.
B. Enable S3 Versioning on the source bucket.
C. Attach an Amazon EBS volume to a sync instance in the second Region.
D. Configure S3 Replication to a bucket in the second Region.
E. Disable bucket versioning so replication can use a single key.

questions.explain: Versioning retains prior objects after overwrite. Replication then copies those objects (and typically requires versioning) to the second Region.
questions.good_to_know: Lifecycle rules would transition old versions to archive after recovery windows expire. Deep Archive on upload would fight immediate lake queries.

questions.q: A database on Amazon EC2 in one Availability Zone needs durable SSD block storage and nightly point-in-time backups. If the zone fails, operators will launch a replacement instance in a second AZ and attach a restored volume. The engine cannot use a shared NFS data directory. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Store the database files on instance store and snapshot the instance store.
B. Create an Amazon EFS file system and mount it as the database data directory.
C. Attach a gp3 or provisioned IOPS Amazon EBS volume to the instance.
D. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the EBS volume.
E. Create EBS snapshots on a schedule and restore them in the second AZ when needed.

questions.explain: Durable low-latency block storage is EBS, and snapshots are how you restore that volume in another AZ. Instance store cannot be snapshotted as durable database storage.
questions.good_to_know: EFS is shared NFS, not a typical database data directory. Intelligent-Tiering is an S3 storage class, not an EBS setting.

questions.q: A company is moving a Windows department share to AWS. Desktop applications in the office require SMB, NTFS-style access-control lists, and authentication against the existing Microsoft Active Directory. The company wants a managed file system in AWS and will not operate file-server instances. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server.
B. Create Amazon EFS and enable Windows ACLs on the file system.
C. Create an io2 Amazon EBS volume and share it with Microsoft iSCSI from one instance.
D. Store the share in Amazon S3 Standard and map it as a network drive with the AWS CLI.
E. Join the file system to the Active Directory domain the desktops already use.

questions.explain: FSx for Windows File Server is the managed SMB service, and directory join supplies the AD authentication the desktops already depend on.
questions.good_to_know: EFS is Linux NFS. A self-managed iSCSI EBS share is not the managed Windows file service the stem asks for.

questions.q: Compliance requires a single backup policy for Amazon EBS volumes and Amazon EFS file systems, with 35-day retention. Recovery must still work if the workload account is compromised, so copies must land in a separate AWS account in a second Region. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable S3 Versioning on each EBS volume.
B. Create an AWS Backup plan that includes the EBS and EFS resources.
C. Configure the plan to copy recovery points to a vault in the second account and Region.
D. Store backups only on instance store in the source account.
E. Replace EFS with S3 Glacier Deep Archive so AWS Backup is unnecessary.

questions.explain: AWS Backup is the centralized plan across supported services, and cross-account plus cross-Region copies reduce blast radius from a compromised workload account.
questions.good_to_know: S3 Versioning does not back up EBS or EFS. Moving data to Glacier changes the storage type; it does not implement the backup policy the stem described.

questions.q: A simulation cluster on Amazon EC2 needs a high-throughput parallel file system. Input datasets already reside in Amazon S3 and must be readable from the file system without a manual copy farm. The team will not operate Lustre on self-managed instances. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create Amazon FSx for Windows File Server and enable Lustre mode.
B. Create an Amazon EFS One Zone file system in the cluster’s Availability Zone.
C. Place the datasets on Cold HDD Amazon EBS volumes attached to a NAT instance.
D. Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system.
E. Link the file system to the S3 bucket that holds the datasets.

questions.explain: FSx for Lustre is the managed parallel file system, and the S3 link is how those datasets are presented without a home-grown copy fleet.
questions.good_to_know: EFS is the general Linux NFS answer. FSx for Windows does not have a Lustre mode. EBS HDD is single-instance sequential block storage.

questions.q: A partner portal stores private PDF objects in Amazon S3. Each download link must work for 10 minutes and must not require an IAM user for the partner. The bucket must remain private, and objects must not be readable with a guessable key. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Keep the bucket private with no public-read bucket policy.
B. Issue an S3 presigned URL that expires after 10 minutes for each download.
C. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and email the object key to the partner.
D. Move the objects to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval and share restore credentials.
E. Turn on S3 website hosting and list the objects in an index document.

questions.explain: A private bucket plus a short-lived presigned URL is the lesson’s time-limited access pattern. Website hosting or a public policy would make objects world-readable.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront signed cookies (Lesson 12) would appear if the stem required a CDN in front of private content. Transfer Acceleration is a transfer-speed feature, not an access-control feature.

questions.q: A retailer runs an order-entry application on Amazon EC2 that writes to a single-AZ Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance in private subnets. The application needs SQL transactions and automatic failover if the primary Availability Zone fails. Reporting queries can wait, and the team does not need extra read capacity. The company will not rewrite the schema. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Convert the instance to an RDS Multi-AZ deployment.
B. Add an in-Region RDS read replica and fail over to it for writes.
C. Replace RDS with Amazon DynamoDB global tables.
D. Place Amazon ElastiCache in front of the writer as the ledger.

questions.explain: In-Region relational high availability with automatic failover is RDS Multi-AZ. A read replica is asynchronous read scaling and is not the synchronous standby pattern.
questions.good_to_know: A read replica would be the answer if the stem demanded extra read capacity and accepted replica lag. DynamoDB global tables fit active-active key-value, not this SQL writer.

questions.q: A media site uses Amazon RDS for MySQL as the system of record. Editors write infrequently, but the public website issues many identical SELECT queries. The application can tolerate a few seconds of replica lag. Failover to a standby is already configured and is not the gap. Operators must not rewrite the application onto a NoSQL store. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable another Multi-AZ standby and query it for reads.
B. Migrate the catalog to Amazon Redshift for each page view.
C. Add RDS read replicas and send read queries to them.
D. Replace the database with Amazon Neptune for the website.

questions.explain: Read scaling with tolerated lag selects RDS read replicas. Multi-AZ is already present for failover and does not offload application reads.
questions.good_to_know: Another Multi-AZ standby would matter if the gap were availability rather than read throughput. Redshift is a warehouse, not the OLTP read scaler.

questions.q: A company invokes thousands of AWS Lambda functions that open short-lived connections to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. During traffic spikes the database exhausts its connection limit and new functions fail. The team must keep the relational schema and must not replace RDS with a NoSQL store. Connection pooling should sit between Lambda and the database. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable RDS Multi-AZ so the standby pools connections.
B. Place Amazon RDS Proxy between the functions and RDS.
C. Add Amazon ElastiCache and write every transaction only there.
D. Convert the database to Amazon DynamoDB on-demand mode.

questions.explain: Lambda connection storms against a relational engine are the RDS Proxy pooling pattern. Multi-AZ failover does not multiplex application connections.
questions.good_to_know: Multi-AZ would be the answer if the stem asked for in-Region writer failover. DynamoDB would fit if the team were willing to abandon SQL.

questions.q: A SaaS vendor wants a MySQL-compatible relational database whose storage automatically replicates across Availability Zones and is decoupled from database compute. The application needs a managed writer with fast failover in one Region. The team does not want to operate shared storage on Amazon EC2. An analytics warehouse is out of scope. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create a Single-AZ RDS instance that uses instance store.
B. Load the data into Amazon Redshift and run OLTP there.
C. Store rows in Amazon ElastiCache as the system of record.
D. Create an Amazon Aurora cluster with storage across AZs.

questions.explain: Aurora separates compute from distributed storage that spans Availability Zones. That is the managed relational cluster the stem describes.
questions.good_to_know: Redshift would be correct for warehouse analytics SQL, not OLTP. ElastiCache is an in-memory cache, not durable relational storage.

questions.q: An Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL cluster has a single writer that is CPU-bound from reporting SELECTs. The application can send reads to other endpoints and can tolerate brief replica lag. The company also wants those readers to be eligible for failover if the writer fails. The workload must stay relational and in one Region. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add Aurora Replicas and send read traffic to them.
B. Enable RDS Multi-AZ on a separate MySQL instance only.
C. Cache every write in Amazon ElastiCache as durable storage.
D. Move reporting to Amazon DynamoDB global tables.

questions.explain: Aurora Replicas offload reads and can participate in failover. That pair of constraints is the Aurora reader pattern, not a second unrelated RDS instance.
questions.good_to_know: ElastiCache would be the answer if the stem allowed cache-aside staleness in front of the writer without extra Aurora readers. Global tables are key-value active-active, not SQL reporting replicas.

questions.q: A department runs a MySQL-compatible reporting database that is idle most nights and then spikes for a few hours when analysts connect. The team wants elastic relational capacity without resizing instance classes by hand. The data model stays SQL. The workload is not a key-value store and is not a data warehouse. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon DynamoDB on-demand for the SQL reports.
B. Use Amazon Redshift as the OLTP writer for analysts.
C. Use Amazon Aurora Serverless for database capacity.
D. Use a fixed Single-AZ RDS instance sized for peak hours.

questions.explain: Variable or intermittent relational load is the Aurora Serverless fit. DynamoDB on-demand is elastic, but it is not a SQL reporting engine.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB on-demand would be correct if the access pattern were key-value with unknown traffic. A peak-sized RDS instance would work if idle-time elasticity were not required.

questions.q: A ticketing platform uses Amazon Aurora in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. Customers in Europe need local low-latency reads of the same relational data, and operators want a managed way to promote a second Region for disaster recovery. Writes remain in one primary Region. The team will not rewrite the application onto key-value APIs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create DynamoDB global tables and dual-write from Aurora.
B. Create an Aurora Global Database with a secondary Region.
C. Enable RDS Multi-AZ in the primary Region only.
D. Put Amazon ElastiCache in Europe as the system of record.

questions.explain: Cross-Region relational reads, locality, and managed DR promotion are Aurora Global Database. Multi-AZ stays in one Region and does not place readers in Europe.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB global tables would be the answer for active-active key-value writes in both Regions. Multi-AZ would win if the only need were in-Region failover.

questions.q: A mobile game stores player inventories as items accessed by a known user identifier. Traffic is expected to reach very large request rates with single-digit millisecond reads and writes. The team does not want to manage database servers and does not need SQL joins. Graph traversal is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store the items in Amazon RDS for MySQL.
B. Store the items in Amazon Redshift.
C. Store the items in Amazon Neptune.
D. Store the items in Amazon DynamoDB.

questions.explain: Key-based access at huge scale with no server management is DynamoDB. RDS and Redshift are SQL engines; Neptune is a graph store.
questions.good_to_know: RDS would be correct if the stem required SQL transactions and joins. Neptune would win if the queries were multi-hop relationship traversals.

questions.q: A company stores session records in Amazon DynamoDB. The partition key is a status flag with only three values, so almost all traffic hits a few partitions and requests throttle. Access remains by key rather than SQL joins. The team must spread traffic across partitions and will not migrate the table to Amazon RDS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Choose a partition key that distributes traffic.
B. Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode only.
C. Replace DynamoDB with a Multi-AZ Amazon RDS instance.
D. Put Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the DynamoDB table.

questions.explain: Hot partitions come from a poorly distributed partition key. Changing capacity mode does not fix a key that concentrates traffic.
questions.good_to_know: On-demand capacity would be the answer if traffic volume were unknown but keys already spread evenly. RDS Proxy pools relational connections, not DynamoDB partitions.

questions.q: A new social feature writes to Amazon DynamoDB. Traffic is spiky and unknown for the first quarter, so the team cannot forecast read and write capacity units. Operators want AWS to handle capacity without a provisioning plan. After traffic becomes steady they may revisit cost. The access pattern stays key-value. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use provisioned capacity locked to a tiny fixed WCU.
B. Use Amazon RDS provisioned IOPS as the session store.
C. Use DynamoDB on-demand capacity mode.
D. Use Amazon ElastiCache as the only durable store.

questions.explain: Unpredictable key-value traffic is on-demand capacity. A tiny provisioned ceiling will throttle spikes the team cannot forecast.
questions.good_to_know: Provisioned capacity (often with autoscaling) would be the economical answer if traffic were already predictable. ElastiCache is not the durable system of record.

questions.q: Users in two AWS Regions must read and write the same player profiles with locally low latency. The data is key-value, and the application can tolerate last-writer conflict handling. The company wants managed multi-Region replication rather than application-managed dual writes. Cross-Region RDS replicas are considered too write-constrained. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an RDS cross-Region read replica and write to it.
B. Enable DynamoDB global tables in both Regions.
C. Create an Aurora Global Database and write in both Regions.
D. Use Amazon ElastiCache in each Region as the source of truth.

questions.explain: Managed multi-Region active-active key-value writes are DynamoDB global tables. An RDS replica is not an active-active writer.
questions.good_to_know: Aurora Global Database would be the answer for relational reads and DR in a second Region with one primary writer. RDS replicas scale reads, including cross-Region, with lag.

questions.q: An ecommerce API reads the same Amazon DynamoDB product items thousands of times per second and needs microsecond in-memory latency. The team wants a cache purpose-built for DynamoDB rather than a generic Redis client. Brief staleness is acceptable. The table must remain the durable system of record. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Place Amazon ElastiCache for Redis in front of the DynamoDB table.
B. Create Amazon RDS read replicas of the DynamoDB table.
C. Migrate the items to Amazon Redshift and query with SQL.
D. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the table.

questions.explain: Microsecond caching that is purpose-built for DynamoDB is DAX. The table stays the system of record; DAX is not a warehouse or an RDS replica.
questions.good_to_know: ElastiCache cache-aside would be the answer for hot RDS (or generic) queries with tolerated staleness. DAX is the DynamoDB-specific cache.

questions.q: A catalog service on Amazon EC2 queries Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL for product pages. The same rows are requested repeatedly, the database CPU is high, and the application can tolerate a few seconds of stale data. The team will keep RDS as the source of truth and will not replace it with DynamoDB. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add Amazon ElastiCache with cache-aside and a TTL.
B. Add a second RDS Multi-AZ standby and query it for pages.
C. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator on the RDS instance.
D. Convert the catalog to Amazon Redshift for each page view.

questions.explain: Repeated RDS reads with accepted staleness are ElastiCache cache-aside plus TTL. Extra Multi-AZ standbys do not serve those application reads.
questions.good_to_know: Read replicas would be correct if the stem wanted SQL read offload with lag instead of an in-memory cache. DAX is the DynamoDB cache, not an RDS feature.

questions.q: A gaming platform needs an in-memory cache for leaderboards and session state. The cache must support replication, optional persistence, and rich structures such as sorted sets. The team will use Amazon ElastiCache rather than a self-managed cluster on Amazon EC2. Amazon RDS remains the durable store for purchases. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an ElastiCache cluster for Memcached only.
B. Create Amazon RDS Multi-AZ and use it only as a cache.
C. Create an ElastiCache cluster for Redis or Valkey.
D. Create Amazon Redshift and store sessions in a warehouse.

questions.explain: Redis/Valkey-style ElastiCache provides richer structures, replication, and persistence options. Memcached is the simpler distributed cache.
questions.good_to_know: Memcached would be the answer if the stem wanted a simple distributed cache without those richer features. RDS is the durable OLTP store, not the in-memory leaderboard cache.

questions.q: A fraud team must query how accounts, devices, and payments are connected through many hops. The application issues graph traversals, not SQL joins or key-value GetItem calls. The team wants a managed graph database and will not force the model into Amazon RDS or Amazon DynamoDB. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon DynamoDB with a single partition key only.
B. Use Amazon Neptune for the relationship graph.
C. Use Amazon Redshift as an OLTP graph store.
D. Use Amazon ElastiCache Memcached as the graph database.

questions.explain: Graph relationship traversals select Amazon Neptune. DynamoDB and RDS are the wrong data models for multi-hop graph queries.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB would be correct for key-value lookups by a known partition key. Redshift would win for warehouse analytics SQL, not graph hops.

questions.q: A product team already uses MongoDB APIs and drivers for a document catalog. They want a managed AWS database that remains MongoDB-compatible rather than rewriting queries to SQL or to the DynamoDB API. The workload is operational documents, not analytics SQL and not a graph of hops. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Migrate the catalog to Amazon RDS for MySQL.
B. Migrate the catalog to Amazon Redshift.
C. Migrate the catalog to Amazon Neptune.
D. Migrate the catalog to Amazon DocumentDB.

questions.explain: MongoDB-compatible document workloads map to Amazon DocumentDB. RDS and Redshift are SQL; Neptune is graph.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB would appear if the team were willing to adopt that API and key design. RDS would be correct if they were ready to rewrite to relational SQL.

questions.q: Developers run a wide-column application that speaks Apache Cassandra Query Language. They want a managed AWS service that stays Cassandra-compatible so they do not rewrite the data model for SQL or for DynamoDB. The access pattern is wide-column, not graph traversal and not a warehouse. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Keyspaces for the application tables.
B. Use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL as the CQL endpoint.
C. Use Amazon Neptune for the wide-column rows.
D. Use Amazon Redshift as the Cassandra-compatible store.

questions.explain: Cassandra-compatible wide-column access is Amazon Keyspaces. RDS is SQL, Neptune is graph, and Redshift is a warehouse.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB would be the answer if the team could redesign around partition and sort keys instead of CQL. DocumentDB would win for MongoDB APIs.

questions.q: Analysts need to run complex SQL aggregations over years of order history for dashboards. The current Amazon RDS instance slows down when those queries run. The company wants a columnar data warehouse, not another OLTP writer, and will not use a graph database. Nightly loads from RDS are acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Move the OLTP writer onto Amazon ElastiCache for Redis.
B. Replace RDS with Amazon Neptune for the dashboard SQL.
C. Load the history into Amazon Redshift and query there.
D. Use Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator as the analytics warehouse.

questions.explain: Analytics SQL over large history is Amazon Redshift, not another OLTP system. ElastiCache and DAX are caches, not warehouses.
questions.good_to_know: Keeping the queries on RDS (or Aurora) with replicas would be the answer if the stem still wanted OLTP reporting rather than a warehouse. Neptune is for graph traversals.

questions.q: A payments API uses Amazon RDS for MySQL in one Region. The company needs automatic failover if the writer Availability Zone fails, and a reporting fleet must offload SELECTs. Reporting can tolerate replica lag. The application must keep SQL transactions and must not use the Multi-AZ standby as a read replica. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable Multi-AZ for synchronous standby failover.
B. Direct reporting queries to the Multi-AZ standby endpoint.
C. Add RDS read replicas and point reporting at them.
D. Replace RDS with Amazon ElastiCache as the payments ledger.
E. Convert the database to Amazon Neptune for card authorizations.

questions.explain: In-Region HA and read offload are different controls: Multi-AZ for failover, read replicas for lag-tolerant SELECTs. The standby is not the read scaler.
questions.good_to_know: Querying the Multi-AZ standby would look right if Multi-AZ were taught as read scaling. ElastiCache is a cache, not the transactional ledger.

questions.q: AWS Lambda functions open a new database connection on every invoke against Amazon RDS for MySQL. During campaigns the instance hits its connection limit. The schema must stay relational. The team will not cache writes in Amazon ElastiCache as the source of truth. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable a second Multi-AZ standby to absorb connections.
B. Deploy Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the RDS instance.
C. Rewrite the functions to write only to Amazon DynamoDB.
D. Point the Lambda functions at the RDS Proxy endpoint.
E. Store each transaction exclusively in Amazon ElastiCache.

questions.explain: RDS Proxy must exist and the functions must connect through it so connections are pooled. Multi-AZ does not provide that pooling layer.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB would be correct if the team dropped SQL. Multi-AZ would be correct if the stem were about writer failover rather than connection storms.

questions.q: A retailer uses Amazon Aurora in one Region and must serve read-heavy storefront traffic from a second Region with a managed relational replica. Operators also need a documented path to promote the second Region during a regional event. The application stays SQL. Active-active key-value writes are not required. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable DynamoDB global tables and dual-write every row.
B. Use RDS Multi-AZ in the primary Region as the only change.
C. Create an Aurora Global Database from the cluster.
D. Make Amazon ElastiCache in the second Region the database.
E. Add a secondary Region to that global database.

questions.explain: Aurora Global Database plus a secondary Region supplies cross-Region reads, locality, and a promotion path for DR. Those two steps are jointly required.
questions.good_to_know: DynamoDB global tables would be the answer for active-active key-value. Primary-Region Multi-AZ alone does not place relational readers in the second Region.

questions.q: A social app needs active-active key-value reads and writes in two Regions with managed replication. Poor key design already caused throttling in one Region. The team will not use Aurora Global Database as an active-active writer pair and will not store profiles only in ElastiCache. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable DynamoDB global tables in both Regions.
B. Create an RDS cross-Region replica and write to both sides.
C. Use Amazon ElastiCache as the multi-Region system of record.
D. Place Amazon RDS Proxy in front of DynamoDB in each Region.
E. Choose partition keys that distribute writes evenly.

questions.explain: Global tables provide the managed active-active key-value fabric; even key design is still required so partitions do not overheat.
questions.good_to_know: An RDS cross-Region replica would be the answer for lag-tolerant SQL reads in a second Region, not active-active writes. RDS Proxy does not sit in front of DynamoDB.

questions.q: A news site on Amazon EC2 reads the same Amazon RDS rows for every homepage request. Database CPU is high. Editors accept that headlines may be up to 30 seconds stale. RDS must remain the durable store. The team will not enable DAX against RDS. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Add another Multi-AZ standby and point the homepage at it.
B. Add Amazon ElastiCache and use cache-aside in the app.
C. Set a TTL so cached entries expire after about 30 seconds.
D. Enable DynamoDB Accelerator in front of the RDS instance.
E. Replace RDS with Amazon Redshift for each page render.

questions.explain: Cache-aside plus TTL is how ElastiCache absorbs repeated RDS reads while keeping staleness within the allowed window.
questions.good_to_know: DAX would be the answer if the hot keys lived in DynamoDB. Extra Multi-AZ standbys still do not serve homepage reads.

questions.q: A high-traffic API uses Amazon DynamoDB as the only database. Repeated GetItem calls for the same keys dominate read capacity. The team wants a DynamoDB-specific in-memory cache and must keep the table as the system of record. Generic Redis in front of RDS is out of scope. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Replace the table with Amazon ElastiCache as the database.
B. Create RDS read replicas of the DynamoDB table.
C. Move the items to Amazon Redshift and disable DynamoDB.
D. Enable Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the table.
E. Point the application DynamoDB reads at the DAX cluster.

questions.explain: DAX must be enabled and the application must send DynamoDB reads through it. The table remains durable storage behind the cache.
questions.good_to_know: ElastiCache as the database would violate the system-of-record constraint. ElastiCache cache-aside would be correct for hot RDS queries.

questions.q: A company stores device telemetry in Amazon DynamoDB. Items should disappear after 90 days without a cleanup fleet, and a downstream AWS Lambda function must react to new inserts. The team will not run a nightly Amazon RDS copy job. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable DynamoDB TTL on the time-to-live attribute.
B. Enable DynamoDB Streams and invoke Lambda on new items.
C. Create Amazon RDS read replicas of the DynamoDB table.
D. Use Amazon ElastiCache as the only store for telemetry.
E. Load every item into Amazon Redshift on each write path.

questions.explain: TTL expires items without a sweeper fleet. Streams deliver change events so Lambda can react to inserts. Those features are independent and both required here.
questions.good_to_know: A scheduled copy into RDS would be a different, heavier lifecycle design. ElastiCache alone is not durable telemetry storage.

questions.q: An application on Amazon EC2 in private subnets must read objects from Amazon S3. Security forbids long-lived access keys on the instance, in user data, or in the AMI. The company will not use the root user. Temporary credentials must be issued to the workload automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an IAM role with an instance profile.
B. Embed a long-lived IAM user access key in the AMI.
C. Put root access keys in the instance user data.
D. Create an SCP that grants s3:GetObject to the instance.

questions.explain: EC2 workloads use a service role (instance profile) so STS can issue temporary credentials. SCPs do not grant permissions to the instance.
questions.good_to_know: An IAM user key in the AMI would be the (insecure) answer only if the stem allowed long-lived secrets on disk. An SCP is a permission ceiling, not a grant.

questions.q: AWS Lambda functions process files and must write results to Amazon DynamoDB. The team must not store IAM user access keys in environment variables or in the function package. Credentials should be temporary and rotated by AWS. The functions already run in one account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Save an IAM user access key in the Lambda environment.
B. Use the AWS account root access keys in the function.
C. Attach an IAM execution role to the Lambda functions.
D. Share one long-lived IAM user among all functions.

questions.explain: Lambda uses an execution role for temporary STS credentials. User or root access keys are long-lived secrets the stem forbids.
questions.good_to_know: An IAM user key in the environment would be the anti-pattern if the stem had allowed packaged secrets. Identity Center is for workforce SSO, not the function’s AWS API calls.

questions.q: A company still creates an IAM user with access keys for every employee who uses the AWS Management Console. Security wants to stop minting long-lived user credentials for people and to federate staff instead. Customer sign-in to a mobile app is a separate project and must not drive this choice. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Adopt Amazon Cognito user pools for employee console access.
B. Adopt IAM Identity Center for workforce sign-in.
C. Issue root credentials to each employee.
D. Embed IAM user keys in every Amazon EC2 instance.

questions.explain: Workforce SSO across accounts is IAM Identity Center. Cognito is the customer and application identity service, not the staff console path the lesson teaches.
questions.good_to_know: Cognito would be the answer if the stem were customer sign-up and sign-in for an app. IAM users remain a legacy option when federation is not yet available.

questions.q: Administrators in Account A must perform limited actions in Account B for one hour at a time. The companies refuse to copy IAM user access keys between accounts. Account B should issue temporary credentials after a successful assume. An SCP must not be used as the way to grant the administrators permissions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy IAM user access keys from Account B into Account A.
B. Attach an SCP to Account A that grants AdministratorAccess in B.
C. Use Amazon Cognito user pools as the only control in Account B.
D. Create an IAM role in Account B that Account A assumes with STS.

questions.explain: Cross-account temporary access is AssumeRole through STS. SCPs do not grant permissions in the target account.
questions.good_to_know: A bucket or table resource policy would appear if the stem kept the principal in Account A without assuming a role in B. Cognito is customer identity, not this admin path.

questions.q: A company found that an IAM allow policy let operators delete production objects. Security wants those deletes blocked for that identity even if other allow statements remain. The block must win during policy evaluation. The team will not rely on hunting down every allow by hand. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add an identity-based explicit deny for s3:DeleteObject.
B. Add a second allow policy for s3:* on the same operator.
C. Attach an SCP that allows s3:DeleteObject as a grant.
D. Disable IAM and rely on resource tags only.

questions.explain: An applicable explicit deny wins over allows. A second allow cannot override that deny, and an SCP allow does not grant the delete.
questions.good_to_know: A second allow would have been enough if the gap were a missing grant and no deny existed. SCPs cap member accounts; they do not grant.

questions.q: Security must prevent member accounts from creating most resources outside a list of approved Regions, even when those accounts’ administrators try. IAM policies in the member accounts can be edited by those administrators. The control must be an organization guardrail and must not be the mechanism that grants day-to-day permissions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an IAM allow policy in each account for those Regions.
B. Create an IAM group in each account named SecurityAdmins.
C. Attach an SCP with the Region deny to the relevant OU.
D. Use Amazon Cognito to lock the AWS Management Console.

questions.explain: An SCP on the OU is the guardrail that even member administrators cannot remove. IAM policies in those accounts are easier to alter.
questions.good_to_know: An identity allow in each account would be part of granting work inside approved Regions, but it cannot stop an administrator from widening IAM. Cognito is not the org Region lock.

questions.q: An application role in Account A must read objects from a bucket in Account B without assuming a role in B. The role already has an identity policy that allows s3:GetObject on that bucket ARN. Access still fails. The bucket must state who may read it. The teams will not copy access keys. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an SCP in Account A that grants s3:GetObject.
B. Add a bucket policy in B that allows the Account A role.
C. Put IAM user keys from Account B on the application servers.
D. Enable IAM Identity Center in Account B with no bucket policy.

questions.explain: When the principal stays in Account A, a resource policy on the bucket must allow that principal. Identity policy alone is not enough cross-account, and an SCP does not grant.
questions.good_to_know: A role in Account B that Account A assumes would be the other cross-account pattern and would not require this bucket policy shape. Identity Center is workforce SSO, not the bucket allow.

questions.q: Developers may create IAM roles for their applications, but security requires that no created role can ever exceed an approved permission ceiling. A normal allow policy on the developer would be too easy to widen later. An SCP on the whole OU is too coarse for this per-role cap. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an SCP that grants AdministratorAccess to developers.
B. Issue IAM user access keys instead of application roles.
C. Use Amazon Cognito user pools as the permissions ceiling.
D. Require a permissions boundary on every role they create.

questions.explain: A permissions boundary sets the maximum identity-based permissions a delegated role can receive. An SCP is an OU-wide cap, not a per-role delegation ceiling.
questions.good_to_know: An SCP would be the answer if the stem needed one guardrail on every account in an OU. Access keys would increase long-lived secret risk.

questions.q: A company runs production, development, and a security logging archive in one AWS account. A compromised developer key could reach production data. Leadership wants separate blast radius so that development identities cannot reach production resources by default. Central billing should remain, and the company already uses AWS Organizations. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Place production, development, and logging in separate accounts.
B. Create IAM users in the same account with similar admin policies.
C. Keep one account and rely only on resource tags for isolation.
D. Share the account root password with developers for isolation.

questions.explain: Multiple Organization accounts shrink blast radius and separate production from development and logging. IAM users in one account still share that account’s blast radius.
questions.good_to_know: IAM policies and tags still matter inside an account, but they are not a substitute for account isolation when the stem demands blast-radius separation. RAM can later share selected resources across those accounts.

questions.q: A network account holds VPC subnets that application accounts must use for Amazon EC2. Duplicating the VPC in every account would break the central network design. The company already uses AWS Organizations and wants a managed share of supported resources rather than copied credentials. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy IAM user keys from the network account into each app.
B. Attach an SCP that grants VPC ownership to every account.
C. Share the subnets with member accounts using AWS RAM.
D. Recreate the same CIDR independently in each member account.

questions.explain: AWS RAM shares supported resources such as subnets across accounts without duplicating them. An SCP cannot grant VPC ownership.
questions.good_to_know: Recreating CIDRs would be the answer only if each account needed an independent network. Access keys would share identity secrets, not the subnet resource.

questions.q: Employees in one corporate directory must sign in once and assume permissions in many member accounts. The company wants permission sets mapped to groups rather than an IAM user in each account. Amazon Cognito is reserved for the consumer mobile app, not for staff. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Cognito user pools for AWS console staff access.
B. Use IAM Identity Center permission sets on the accounts.
C. Create IAM users in every member account for each employee.
D. Distribute the management account root password to staff.

questions.explain: Workforce SSO plus permission sets is IAM Identity Center. Cognito is customer identity; per-account IAM users recreate long-lived humans.
questions.good_to_know: Cognito would be correct for application customer sign-up and sign-in. IAM users would appear if the stem still required long-lived console users and forbade Identity Center.

questions.q: A consumer mobile application needs sign-up, sign-in, and user profiles for millions of customers who are not employees. Staff will continue to use workforce federation for the AWS Management Console. The identity service must be application identity, not IAM users for each customer. Permission sets stay reserved for employees. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use IAM Identity Center permission sets for each mobile user.
B. Create an IAM user and access key for every customer.
C. Use SCPs to grant customers s3:* in the production account.
D. Use Amazon Cognito for customer authentication.

questions.explain: Customer and application identity is Amazon Cognito. Identity Center is workforce SSO; IAM users and SCPs are not a customer directory.
questions.good_to_know: IAM Identity Center would be the answer for employees assuming roles in AWS accounts. This item does not ask for an API Gateway authorizer.

questions.q: A new AWS account’s root user still has an access key from a proof of concept. Finance uses root for daily billing clicks. Security wants root used only for the few tasks that require it, with no standing access keys. Workforce users should have their own identities for routine work. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Delete root access keys and stop using root for daily work.
B. Issue additional root access keys to each administrator.
C. Store the root password in a shared operations chat channel.
D. Attach AdministratorAccess to root through an SCP grant.

questions.explain: Protect root by removing standing keys and keeping it off routine tasks. Daily work belongs on IAM or Identity Center identities.
questions.good_to_know: Enabling MFA on root is the usual companion control and would be required if the stem stressed a second factor. SCPs do not grant root extra power in that way.

questions.q: Privileged humans sign in to the AWS Management Console with IAM users that still have only a password. Security requires a second factor before those users can perform administration. Workloads on Amazon EC2 must keep using roles, not human passwords. The company will not share the account root user. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Bake IAM user access keys into the EC2 AMIs instead.
B. Share a single root user among all administrators.
C. Require MFA for the privileged IAM users.
D. Use Amazon Cognito user pools as the staff console identity.

questions.explain: MFA is the second factor for privileged human console access. EC2 should keep instance roles; Cognito is not the workforce console path taught here.
questions.good_to_know: Identity Center can also enforce MFA for workforce SSO. Access keys in AMIs would violate the workload-role rule. Root sharing increases blast radius.

questions.q: An application role currently has AdministratorAccess so developers can move quickly. The role only needs s3:GetObject on one bucket and dynamodb:PutItem on one table. Security wants the identity policy narrowed to those actions. An SCP already allows those services in the OU and must not be treated as the grant. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach a second AdministratorAccess policy for defense in depth.
B. Replace AdministratorAccess with a narrow identity policy.
C. Grant the role the account root user permissions.
D. Remove the identity policy and rely on the SCP to grant access.

questions.explain: Least privilege is an identity policy that allows only the needed actions. The SCP already leaves room; it does not grant those actions by itself.
questions.good_to_know: Relying on the SCP alone would be correct only if SCPs granted access, which they do not. A second admin policy would widen, not narrow, the role.

questions.q: Developers in a member account cannot read a logging bucket even though an SCP on their OU allows s3:GetObject. The SCP must remain a guardrail and must not be treated as the grant. Shared access keys are forbidden. The bucket is in the same account as the developers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach a second SCP that grants the bucket read by itself.
B. Use the account root to copy access keys into AWS Lambda.
C. Enable Amazon Cognito so SCPs start granting S3 reads.
D. Attach an IAM policy that allows s3:GetObject.

questions.explain: The SCP already leaves room for S3 reads; an identity (or resource) allow is still required. A second SCP cannot grant the permission.
questions.good_to_know: If the SCP denied S3, you would first open room in the SCP and then add the identity allow. Cognito does not change SCP evaluation.

questions.q: Security must attach one guardrail that covers all production member accounts but not sandbox accounts. The company already uses AWS Organizations. Sandbox teams must keep experimenting in a separate OU from production. Workload IAM policies in production should still grant only what each role needs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Place production accounts in an OU and attach the SCP.
B. Attach the SCP only to individual IAM users in production accounts.
C. Attach the same SCP to the sandbox OU and the production OU.
D. Recreate IAM users in the management account for every workload.

questions.explain: OUs group accounts so an SCP can cap production without constraining sandbox. SCPs attach to the organization tree, not to individual IAM users as the primary pattern.
questions.good_to_know: Attaching the SCP to sandbox as well would freeze experiments. IAM users in the management account would mix blast radius rather than apply an OU guardrail.

questions.q: A CI pipeline currently uses a 90-day IAM user access key stored in a vault. Security wants the pipeline to obtain short-lived credentials by assuming a role instead. The pipeline is not a customer-facing mobile app. The company will not put root keys in the pipeline. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Lengthen the access key rotation period so it never expires.
B. Use Amazon Cognito user pools for the pipeline AWS API calls.
C. Replace the user key with an IAM role assumed through STS.
D. Embed the management account root key in the pipeline.

questions.explain: Pipelines should assume a role for temporary STS credentials instead of long-lived user keys. Cognito is customer identity, not this machine path.
questions.good_to_know: An IAM user key would remain only if the stem still required a long-lived principal and forbade roles. Identity Center is for workforce users, not typical CI machine identity.

questions.q: An Amazon EC2 fleet must read from Amazon S3. Security forbids access keys in AMIs, user data, or local disk. Temporary credentials must come from the instance. An SCP already allows S3 in the OU and must not be treated as the grant. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an IAM role with the required S3 permissions.
B. Bake a long-lived IAM user access key into every instance AMI.
C. Attach the role to the instances as an instance profile.
D. Place root access keys in instance user data scripts.
E. Use the SCP alone to grant S3 to the instances.

questions.explain: The role holds the identity allow and the instance profile delivers it to EC2. The SCP only leaves room; it does not grant.
questions.good_to_know: Keys in the AMI would be the anti-pattern if long-lived secrets were allowed. A resource policy on the bucket could add who may access, but the instances still need a role.

questions.q: An application in Account A needs GetObject on a bucket in Account B. Long-lived keys must not be shared. Account B will host the credentials the application uses. The teams will not make the bucket public, and an SCP must not be used as the grant. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Copy Account B access keys into Account A’s application servers.
B. Create a role in Account B with s3:GetObject on the bucket.
C. Attach an SCP in Account A that grants the bucket in B.
D. Add a trust policy so Account A can assume that role with STS.
E. Make the bucket public instead of using a cross-account role.
