questions.explain: Cross-account temporary access is a role in the resource account plus a trust policy that lets Account A assume it. SCPs and public buckets are the wrong grants.
questions.good_to_know: A bucket policy that allows a principal still in Account A is the resource-policy alternative when the app does not assume a role in B.

questions.q: Developers in a member account must read objects in that account’s S3 bucket. An SCP on their OU currently denies all S3 actions. Security will not use the SCP as a grant and will not share access keys. The bucket remains private. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Rely on the SCP alone to grant s3:GetObject to the developers.
B. Create IAM users in the management account and share their keys.
C. Update the SCP so it no longer denies the required S3 reads.
D. Disable MFA so the organization deny no longer applies.
E. Attach an IAM policy allowing the developers those S3 reads.

questions.explain: Effective access needs SCP room and an identity allow. Opening the SCP without an IAM allow still fails; an IAM allow under a deny SCP still fails.
questions.good_to_know: If the SCP already allowed S3, only the identity policy would still be missing. MFA does not override an SCP deny.

questions.q: A company wants employees to use one workforce sign-in to reach multiple member accounts. Each department needs different AWS permissions. Customer mobile sign-in is out of scope. The company will not create an IAM user in every account for each employee. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable IAM Identity Center for the organization.
B. Create Amazon Cognito user pools for each employee console user.
C. Create duplicate IAM users in every member account for staff.
D. Distribute the root password to each department lead.
E. Assign permission sets to groups on the target accounts.

questions.explain: Identity Center provides the workforce SSO plane; permission sets map groups onto account roles. Cognito is the customer-identity choice.
questions.good_to_know: Cognito would be correct for app customer sign-up. Per-account IAM users would be the long-lived alternative the stem rejected.

questions.q: Developers may create application roles but must not attach policies beyond a security-approved ceiling, and they must not pass arbitrary roles to Amazon EC2. An OU-wide SCP is considered too coarse for this per-role limit. Long-lived access keys are not an acceptable substitute. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Attach AdministratorAccess to every developer-created role.
B. Require a permissions boundary on roles the developers create.
C. Restrict iam:PassRole to only approved roles.
D. Use an SCP as the only per-role ceiling in the member account.
E. Issue long-lived access keys instead of application roles.

questions.explain: The permissions boundary caps what a delegated role can become. Scoped PassRole stops developers from attaching other roles to EC2.
questions.good_to_know: An SCP would be the answer for an OU-wide service or Region guardrail. AdministratorAccess on created roles would ignore the ceiling.

questions.q: A new production account still uses the root user for daily console work and has no MFA on root. Security wants root reserved for rare account-recovery tasks and a second factor on that user. Workforce identities should handle daily administration. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create additional root access keys for the operations team.
B. Share the root password in a team wiki for faster logins.
C. Disable MFA on privileged IAM users to simplify console logins.
D. Enable MFA on the root user.
E. Stop daily root use; give staff IAM or Identity Center access.

questions.explain: Root protection is MFA plus not using root for routine work. Daily administration belongs on least-privilege workforce identities.
questions.good_to_know: More root access keys would increase standing secret risk. MFA on privileged IAM users is also good practice but is a different control than protecting root.

questions.q: A company wants production compute in one account and a shared networking resource in a network account to reduce blast radius. The compute account must use the shared resource without duplicating it. The company already uses AWS Organizations. Customer identity services are out of scope. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use separate Organization accounts for production and networking.
B. Share the network resource with production using AWS RAM.
C. Merge everything into one account and use a single IAM user.
D. Copy the network account root keys onto production instances.
E. Use Amazon Cognito identity pools to share VPCs between accounts.

questions.explain: Separate accounts cut blast radius; RAM shares supported resources such as networking constructs without copying them. Cognito does not share VPCs.
questions.good_to_know: A single account with IAM users would be simpler operations but would not meet the blast-radius constraint. SCPs would cap those accounts; they would not share the subnet.

questions.q: A retail company serves a public website through an Application Load Balancer. Security logs show SQL injection payloads in HTTP POST bodies and thousands of requests per minute from individual client IPs. Packet filters on the instances cannot inspect query strings. The company needs Layer 7 blocking and per-IP throttling at the load balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with SQLi and rate-based rules.
B. Rely on AWS Shield Standard to inspect HTTP bodies and drop SQL payloads.
C. Enable Amazon GuardDuty and block each finding in a security group.
D. Create a network ACL that denies TCP 443 from every client CIDR.

questions.explain: HTTP payload inspection plus per-client rate limits is AWS WAF. Shield is DDoS protection, and GuardDuty detects threats without filtering requests.
questions.good_to_know: Shield Advanced would be correct if the stem asked for DDoS response, DRT access, or attack cost protection. Network Firewall would be correct for VPC network traffic rather than ALB HTTP rules.

questions.q: A company runs Amazon RDS that application servers query from private subnets. Database credentials sit in deployment artifacts and change only when operators rebuild the fleet. Compliance requires the password to rotate on a schedule without a new deployment. Applications must retrieve the current secret at runtime using IAM. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS KMS key and treat Decrypt output as the password.
B. Store the password in Parameter Store standard parameters.
C. Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and enable rotation.
D. Put the password in instance user data and reboot nightly.

questions.explain: Managed secret rotation and runtime retrieval select Secrets Manager. KMS protects encryption keys; it is not a rotating database-password store.
questions.good_to_know: Parameter Store standard parameters would be closer if the stem only needed a plaintext parameter without native managed rotation. KMS is the answer when the requirement is encryption keys, not secret values.

questions.q: A security team must detect unusual AWS API calls and traffic to known malicious IP addresses across several accounts. They will not deploy agents on Amazon EC2. The service must analyze CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS data and emit findings for automated response. HTTP filtering at the load balancer is already in place. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach additional AWS WAF SQL injection rules to the Application Load Balancer.
B. Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the accounts and Regions that need coverage.
C. Enable Amazon Macie on every VPC Flow Log group.
D. Replace CloudTrail with AWS Artifact for API threat analysis.

questions.explain: Agentless threat detection from CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS is GuardDuty. WAF already covers HTTP; it does not analyze those account telemetry sources.
questions.good_to_know: WAF would be correct for SQL injection or rate-based HTTP blocking. Macie would be correct for discovering sensitive data in Amazon S3, not Flow Logs.

questions.q: A company encrypts Amazon S3 objects with a customer managed AWS KMS key. An IAM role identity policy allows kms:Encrypt and kms:Decrypt, but the calls still fail with access denied. Service control policies do not deny KMS. The team must allow that role to use the key without making the key usable by every principal. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Attach an AWS WAF web ACL to the KMS API endpoint.
B. Enable Amazon GuardDuty malware protection on the KMS key.
C. Store the KMS key material in AWS Secrets Manager.
D. Add the IAM role to the KMS key policy.

questions.explain: A KMS key policy is the foundational authorization document. An IAM allow fails when the key policy does not permit the principal or IAM delegation.
questions.good_to_know: If the key policy already enabled IAM policies for the account, adding the KMS actions on the role would have been enough. WAF and GuardDuty do not grant cryptographic permissions on a key.

questions.q: A media company already has Shield Standard on Amazon CloudFront. Large volumetric DDoS attacks caused extra scaling charges last quarter. Leadership wants 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team and cost protection for those attacks. SQL injection rules already run on AWS WAF and must remain. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the CloudFront distributions.
B. Add more AWS WAF rate-based rules and disable Shield Standard.
C. Enable Amazon Inspector on the CloudFront edge locations.
D. Move the origin behind AWS Network Firewall in a public subnet.

questions.explain: DRT access and DDoS cost protection are Shield Advanced capabilities beyond Shield Standard. WAF remains the Layer 7 SQL injection control.
questions.good_to_know: Additional WAF rules would be correct if the remaining problem were HTTP floods or injection, not volumetric DDoS insurance and DRT. Inspector assesses workload vulnerabilities, not CloudFront DDoS.

questions.q: A media company stores large video objects in Amazon S3. Applications must use envelope encryption so AWS KMS protects short data keys while the service encrypts object bytes. Operators must create the key, set its key policy, and manage rotation. Using a key they cannot view or administer is not acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store plaintext data keys in AWS Secrets Manager for each object.
B. Enable Amazon Macie to encrypt objects that contain personal data.
C. Use a customer managed AWS KMS key for S3 encryption.
D. Import a TLS certificate into ACM and attach it to the S3 bucket.

questions.explain: Envelope encryption with a key policy and rotation that the customer sets is a customer managed KMS key. AWS-owned keys cannot be viewed or administered.
questions.good_to_know: An AWS managed key (for example aws/s3) would fit if the stem only needed KMS with AWS-operated policy and rotation. Secrets Manager stores secret values, not S3 data-key envelopes.

questions.q: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances and stores container images in Amazon ECR. Security wants a managed service that continuously assesses those workloads for software vulnerabilities and network exposure. The team already has threat detection for CloudTrail anomalies and does not need PII discovery in Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon GuardDuty for CloudTrail and VPC Flow Logs only.
B. Enable Amazon Inspector on the EC2 and ECR resources.
C. Enable Amazon Macie on the application S3 buckets.
D. Enable AWS Shield Advanced on each EC2 instance.

questions.explain: Vulnerability and exposure assessment for supported compute and container workloads is Inspector. GuardDuty is threat detection, not a CVE scanner.
questions.good_to_know: GuardDuty would be correct for suspicious API or network behavior. Macie would be correct for sensitive data discovery in S3.

questions.q: A data lake in Amazon S3 holds objects from many business units. Compliance suspects some prefixes contain personal data and needs a managed service that discovers sensitive information in those objects. The team already uses GuardDuty for threat detection and does not need a web ACL on an Application Load Balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon Inspector to scan the S3 lake buckets.
B. Attach an AWS WAF web ACL directly to the S3 REST API.
C. Create an AWS KMS grant for every object key prefix.
D. Enable Amazon Macie on the S3 lake buckets.

questions.explain: PII and sensitive-data discovery in Amazon S3 is Macie. Inspector assesses compute and images; WAF does not attach to the S3 REST API.
questions.good_to_know: GuardDuty would be correct if the stem asked for threat detection from logs. WAF would be correct for SQL injection on CloudFront, ALB, or API Gateway.

questions.q: A company must inspect east-west and egress traffic inside a VPC using a managed firewall that applies stateful network rules. AWS WAF already protects the public Application Load Balancer. The new control must sit on VPC traffic, not only on HTTP to the load balancer. Operators will not run third-party appliances on Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Deploy AWS Network Firewall and route VPC traffic through it.
B. Add AWS WAF IP match statements to the existing web ACL.
C. Enable AWS Shield Standard on the NAT gateway.
D. Turn on Amazon GuardDuty and rely on findings to drop packets.

questions.explain: Central VPC network filtering is Network Firewall. WAF inspects HTTP at supported web fronts; GuardDuty detects and does not filter packets.
questions.good_to_know: WAF would be correct if the remaining gap were SQL injection or HTTP rate limits. Firewall Manager would appear if the stem required the same firewall policy across many accounts.

questions.q: An AWS Organizations administrator must apply the same AWS WAF web ACL policy to Application Load Balancers in dozens of member accounts. Teams must not attach ad-hoc ACLs that drift from the standard. The company already uses Organizations and wants AWS to enforce the policy centrally. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon Detective in the management account only.
B. Create one customer managed KMS key in each member account.
C. Use Firewall Manager to apply the WAF policy to ALBs.
D. Subscribe each account to AWS Artifact independently.

questions.explain: Firewall Manager centrally applies supported security policies, including WAF, across Organizations accounts and resources.
questions.good_to_know: A single-account WAF association would be enough if only one ALB needed rules. Detective investigates events; Artifact provides compliance reports.

questions.q: A company uses several AWS accounts. Security already receives findings from Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector, and Amazon Macie in separate consoles. Leadership wants one place that aggregates and normalizes those findings across accounts so analysts do not hop between products. Building investigation graphs is a later project. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon Macie as the only findings aggregator.
B. Enable AWS Security Hub to aggregate the findings.
C. Store all findings as objects in S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
D. Replace GuardDuty with AWS Certificate Manager.

questions.explain: Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and other providers. Macie itself is a PII discovery source, not the multi-service aggregator.
questions.good_to_know: Amazon Detective would be correct if the stem asked to investigate related activity around a finding. Macie remains the S3 sensitive-data scanner.

questions.q: After Amazon GuardDuty reports a compromised IAM credential, analysts must investigate related CloudTrail activity, VPC flows, and resource relationships without building their own graph database. They already aggregate findings in AWS Security Hub. They need a managed investigation service, not another web ACL, and will not query raw log buckets by hand. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS WAF Bot Control on every public API.
B. Enable AWS Secrets Manager rotation on the IAM user password.
C. Enable Amazon Inspector ECR scanning only.
D. Enable Amazon Detective to investigate the finding.

questions.explain: Detective is the managed investigation service for security events and related resource activity. Security Hub aggregates; it does not replace investigation.
questions.good_to_know: Security Hub would be the answer if the gap were a single findings console. WAF would be correct for malicious HTTP at a supported web front.

questions.q: A company terminates TLS on an Application Load Balancer and on an Amazon CloudFront distribution. It wants AWS to provision and automatically renew public certificates for those integrated services. The team will not install certificates on Amazon EC2 instances and will not export a public certificate to disk. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Request ACM public certificates for the ALB and CloudFront.
B. Store PEM files in Secrets Manager and copy them onto each instance.
C. Use AWS CloudHSM to issue public certificates for CloudFront.
D. Enable Amazon GuardDuty certificate protection on the ALB.

questions.explain: ACM provisions and renews public TLS certificates for supported AWS integrations such as ALB and CloudFront. Public ACM certificates are not installed on EC2 as exported PEM files.
questions.good_to_know: Secrets Manager plus a self-managed web server would appear if the stem required TLS on EC2 with a certificate the team can export. CloudHSM is the dedicated HSM answer, not public ACM issuance for CloudFront.

questions.q: A payments processor must run cryptographic operations on dedicated hardware security modules that the company controls, including key material that must not live only in AWS KMS. FIPS-validated HSMs are required. Customer managed KMS keys already encrypt Amazon S3 objects and are not sufficient for this isolated requirement. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store private keys in Amazon Macie findings.
B. Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the KMS API.
C. Deploy AWS CloudHSM clusters for the dedicated HSM workload.
D. Use ACM public certificates as the hardware security module.

questions.explain: Dedicated HSM appliances under customer control are CloudHSM. KMS customer managed keys are the usual encryption-key service, not dedicated HSMs.
questions.good_to_know: KMS would remain correct for envelope encryption and key policies without a dedicated-HSM mandate. ACM would be correct for TLS certificates on supported AWS integrations.

questions.q: Employees must sign in to the AWS access portal with corporate credentials. The company already uses Amazon Cognito user pools for a public mobile game and must not reuse that pool as the employee directory for AWS accounts. Game players are not AWS operators. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an IAM user for every employee and share long-lived access keys.
B. Configure IAM Identity Center for workforce access to AWS accounts.
C. Attach AWS WAF to the AWS Management Console login page.
D. Enable Amazon Macie on employee laptops to gate AWS sign-in.

questions.explain: IAM Identity Center is workforce identity into AWS accounts. Cognito user pools are application customer identity, not the employee AWS directory.
questions.good_to_know: Cognito would be correct if the stem asked for mobile-app sign-up and JWT tokens for customers. Directory Service would appear if Windows workloads needed a managed Microsoft AD domain.

questions.q: A company is migrating an on-premises Active Directory-aware application to Amazon EC2. The servers must domain-join a managed Microsoft Active Directory in AWS for group policy. Amazon Cognito user pools already serve a separate mobile app and must not replace AD. Operators will not run domain controllers on Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Cognito user pool for the Windows servers.
B. Enable IAM Identity Center and domain-join the instances to it.
C. Store NTLM hashes in AWS Secrets Manager as the directory.
D. Create an AWS Directory Service managed Microsoft AD directory.

questions.explain: Directory Service managed Microsoft AD is the managed directory for domain-joined Windows workloads. Identity Center is workforce AWS access, not an AD domain for EC2.
questions.good_to_know: Cognito would be correct for application customer sign-in. Identity Center would be correct for employee SSO into AWS accounts rather than domain join.

questions.q: A compliance rule requires CloudTrail records when someone uses an encryption key, plus the ability to set a key policy and a customer-controlled rotation schedule. Objects live in Amazon S3. An AWS-owned key that the company cannot view would fail the audit. The security team must administer the key in the account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use a customer managed KMS key for S3 encryption.
B. Use an AWS-owned key that S3 selects and that cannot be viewed.
C. Disable encryption and rely on Amazon Macie to hide objects.
D. Put the S3 encryption key in a Lambda environment variable.

questions.explain: Customer managed KMS keys provide a viewable key, a key policy, and customer-controlled rotation. AWS-owned keys are not visible or administrable in the account.
questions.good_to_know: An AWS managed key such as aws/s3 would fit if CloudTrail on key use were enough and the team did not need to edit the key policy. Macie discovers sensitive data; it does not replace encryption.

questions.q: A global site uses Amazon CloudFront in front of an Application Load Balancer. Attackers send SQL injection to the CloudFront URL. A WAF web ACL exists only on the ALB, and malicious requests still appear in CloudFront logs before they reach the origin. The company wants to block injection at the edge. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Rely on AWS Shield Standard to inspect HTTP bodies at edge locations.
B. Add a deny rule to the origin security group for 0.0.0.0/0.
C. Associate the AWS WAF web ACL with the CloudFront distribution.
D. Enable Amazon Inspector on the CloudFront distribution.

questions.explain: WAF inspects HTTP at CloudFront or ALB. A web ACL only on the origin never sees requests that the edge should have blocked. Shield does not replace WAF SQL rules.
questions.good_to_know: Keeping WAF only on the ALB would be enough if clients hit the load balancer directly. Shield Advanced would be correct for DDoS DRT and cost protection.

questions.q: A public Application Load Balancer receives SQL injection attempts and excessive requests from individual clients. The website runs on Amazon EC2 targets behind the load balancer in a VPC. Security groups cannot inspect HTTP payloads. Shield will remain in place for DDoS only and must not be the Layer 7 control. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Associate an AWS WAF web ACL with the Application Load Balancer.
B. Replace the ALB with AWS Shield Advanced as the only HTTP filter.
C. Add SQLi managed rules and a rate-based rule to the ACL.
D. Enable Amazon Macie on the ALB access logs as the injection control.
E. Store WAF rule statements in AWS Secrets Manager.

questions.explain: WAF must be associated with the ALB, and the ACL needs SQLi plus rate-based rules. Those two steps are jointly required. Shield does not parse SQL.
questions.good_to_know: Shield Advanced would join the design if volumetric DDoS cost protection or DRT access were also required. Macie is S3 sensitive-data discovery.

questions.q: A Lambda function in a VPC needs Amazon RDS credentials that must rotate without redeployment. The password currently sits in an environment variable baked into the deployment artifact. A teammate proposed putting the password in a KMS key alias. The function must retrieve the current value at runtime with least privilege. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Put the password in a Lambda layer and publish a new version daily.
B. Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager and enable rotation.
C. Create a KMS key whose plaintext is the database password.
D. Grant the Lambda execution role permission to read the secret.
E. Enable AWS WAF on the RDS listener to rotate credentials.

questions.explain: Secrets Manager stores and rotates the credential; the execution role must be allowed to retrieve it. KMS is for keys, not a rotating password value.
questions.good_to_know: Parameter Store standard parameters would not supply native managed rotation. A KMS grant would appear if the function only needed to decrypt data keys.

questions.q: Security needs managed detection of unusual API calls and known malicious network activity without deploying agents. CloudTrail is already enabled. Findings must fan out to an automated response workflow. HTTP filtering at the ALB is already handled by AWS WAF. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Deploy Amazon Inspector agents only on NAT instances.
B. Disable CloudTrail so GuardDuty uses VPC Flow Logs exclusively.
C. Enable Amazon GuardDuty in the required accounts and Regions.
D. Attach AWS WAF to CloudTrail as the threat detector.
E. Send GuardDuty findings to Amazon EventBridge for response.

questions.explain: GuardDuty provides agentless threat analytics on CloudTrail and related logs. EventBridge is how those findings drive automated response.
questions.good_to_know: Inspector would be correct for vulnerability assessment of compute. WAF would be correct if the remaining gap were SQL injection or HTTP rate limits.

questions.q: An application on Amazon EC2 uses an IAM role to encrypt and decrypt Amazon S3 objects. The team must administer the key, including its key policy. An AWS-owned key cannot receive a custom key policy. Calls must succeed for that role only. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create a customer managed KMS key for the objects.
B. Use an AWS-owned key so no key policy is required.
C. Store the KMS plaintext key in AWS Secrets Manager.
D. Enable AWS Shield Advanced on the KMS key.
E. Allow the application role in the KMS key policy.

questions.explain: Only a customer managed key lets the team set a key policy, and that policy must allow the application role. IAM alone is not sufficient without it.
questions.good_to_know: An AWS managed key would fit encryption without customer key-policy control. Secrets Manager would be correct for a rotating database password.

questions.q: Critical applications behind Amazon CloudFront suffered DDoS-related scaling charges. The company still sees SQL injection in access logs and must keep Layer 7 rules. Leadership wants DDoS Response Team access and cost protection. The applications must remain on CloudFront. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Disable WAF because Shield Advanced inspects SQL query syntax.
B. Subscribe to AWS Shield Advanced for CloudFront.
C. Keep an AWS WAF web ACL with SQLi and rate-based rules.
D. Enable Amazon Macie on CloudFront cache behaviors.
E. Replace CloudFront with Amazon Inspector.

questions.explain: Shield Advanced adds DRT and cost protection. WAF remains required for SQL injection and HTTP rate limits; Shield does not replace those rules.
questions.good_to_know: Shield Standard would already cover baseline DDoS on supported services but not DRT or cost protection. Macie discovers sensitive data in S3.

questions.q: Compliance must discover personal data in Amazon S3 and view those findings next to Amazon GuardDuty findings in one console. The data lake already holds objects from several business units in one Region. Analysts must not open a separate Macie-only workflow as the long-term operating model. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Attach an AWS WAF web ACL with SQLi rules to the S3 REST API.
B. Use AWS CloudHSM to scan object contents for personal data.
C. Delete GuardDuty so only Macie findings remain.
D. Enable Amazon Macie on buckets that may hold personal data.
E. Enable AWS Security Hub to aggregate those findings.

questions.explain: Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. Security Hub is the aggregator that places those findings beside GuardDuty in one console.
questions.good_to_know: Detective would be the next step if the stem asked to investigate a finding's related activity. WAF does not attach to the S3 REST API.

questions.q: An Organizations administrator must inspect VPC traffic with a managed network firewall and apply that policy across many member accounts. AWS WAF already covers HTTP at the Application Load Balancer. Teams must not deploy one-off firewall appliances per account. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Deploy AWS Network Firewall to inspect VPC traffic.
B. Use AWS Firewall Manager to apply the firewall policy.
C. Attach Amazon Cognito to each VPC route table.
D. Enable ACM on firewall endpoints to replace network rules.
E. Rely on Shield Standard to filter east-west VPC flows.

questions.explain: Network Firewall filters VPC traffic; Firewall Manager applies that supported policy centrally across Organizations. WAF does not replace VPC packet inspection.
questions.good_to_know: A single-VPC Network Firewall deployment would suffice without Organizations scope. WAF would remain the answer for SQL injection at the ALB.

questions.q: A startup receives spiky HTTP traffic for a photo-upload API. Traffic is idle most of the night and can jump many times during a campaign. The team wants the LEAST operational overhead and will not manage Amazon EC2 capacity. Each request runs for under a second and is stateless. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the handler on AWS Lambda behind Amazon API Gateway.
B. Run a fixed fleet of Amazon EC2 instances at peak size all day.
C. Run a long-lived process on a single Amazon EC2 instance.
D. Process uploads only with AWS Glue crawlers on a nightly schedule.

questions.explain: Short, variable, stateless requests with low operational overhead select Lambda behind API Gateway. A fixed EC2 fleet is the capacity-management path the stem forbids.
questions.good_to_know: Amazon EC2 or containers would be correct if the work were long-running or highly stateful. AppSync would be correct if the API had to be GraphQL with subscriptions.

questions.q: A Lambda function writes to a relational database that supports only 40 concurrent connections. Event bursts cause the function to scale to hundreds of concurrent executions and exhaust the database. The team must cap concurrent executions of this function. Predictable cold starts are not the requirement. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable provisioned concurrency only, without a concurrency ceiling.
B. Increase Lambda memory to the maximum so fewer executions run.
C. Set reserved concurrency on the Lambda function.
D. Replace the function with Amazon API Gateway caching.

questions.explain: Reserved concurrency places a hard ceiling on concurrent executions and protects the downstream database. Provisioned concurrency warms environments; it does not cap database pressure.
questions.good_to_know: Provisioned concurrency would be correct if the stem asked to reduce cold starts for predictable traffic. An SQS buffer would appear if producers needed burst absorption in front of the worker.

questions.q: A latency-sensitive Lambda function serves a morning traffic spike that is predictable from week to week. Amazon API Gateway invokes the function. Users report delays on the first requests after idle periods. Operations must keep execution environments initialized ahead of those requests. The database is not being overwhelmed. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Set reserved concurrency to 1 to serialize all requests.
B. Configure provisioned concurrency on the Lambda function.
C. Enable Amazon SQS long polling on the function URL.
D. Turn on API Gateway throttling and drop the morning traffic.

questions.explain: Provisioned concurrency keeps initialized execution environments ready and addresses predictable cold starts. Reserved concurrency guarantees and limits capacity but does not pre-initialize environments.
questions.good_to_know: Reserved concurrency would be correct if the problem were protecting a downstream system from unbounded scale. Throttling at API Gateway would be correct if the API itself were being overwhelmed.

questions.q: A company runs a public mobile checkout API. The app needs customer sign-up, sign-in, password recovery, and JWT tokens. The REST API must validate those tokens before invoking AWS Lambda. The team must not build a custom user directory and must not mint long-lived AWS access keys for each player. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool only, with no user directory.
B. Create IAM users for every mobile player and embed access keys.
C. Host sign-in forms on Amazon EC2 and store passwords in DynamoDB.
D. Create a Cognito user pool and validate JWTs at API Gateway.

questions.explain: A user pool is the customer directory and JWT issuer. API Gateway validates those tokens before Lambda. An identity pool alone does not provide sign-up.
questions.good_to_know: An identity pool would be correct if the app needed temporary AWS credentials to call AWS APIs directly. IAM Identity Center would be correct for workforce access to AWS accounts.

questions.q: A mobile game authenticates players with a social identity provider. After sign-in, the app must upload photos directly to Amazon S3 using temporary AWS credentials. The team does not want to embed IAM user keys in the app and does not need Amazon API Gateway for this upload path. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool to issue temporary AWS credentials.
B. Use an Amazon Cognito user pool as the only component, without AWS credentials.
C. Ship an IAM access key in the mobile application binary.
D. Open the S3 bucket as public-read and public-write.

questions.explain: Identity pools exchange authenticated identities for temporary AWS credentials. A user pool issues JWTs for app sign-in; it does not by itself mint AWS keys.
questions.good_to_know: A user pool would be correct for sign-up, sign-in, and JWT validation at API Gateway. Together, a user pool can be an identity provider to an identity pool.

questions.q: A company needs a managed HTTPS front door for a REST API that Lambda and an existing HTTP backend will serve. The API must support usage plans and per-client throttling. The team will not manage reverse proxies on Amazon EC2. Clients need REST, not GraphQL. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS AppSync API and expose only REST-looking resolvers.
B. Expose Lambda function URLs and rely on IP allow lists only.
C. Create an API Gateway REST API with Lambda and HTTP integrations.
D. Put Amazon SQS in front of browsers as the HTTPS API.

questions.explain: API Gateway is the managed REST front door with throttling, usage plans, and integrations to Lambda or HTTP backends. AppSync is the GraphQL path.
questions.good_to_know: AppSync would be correct if the stem required GraphQL and subscriptions. An Application Load Balancer with a Lambda target would appear without usage plans and API-stage throttling.

questions.q: Thousands of browsers use a live dashboard. Web clients need GraphQL queries and near-real-time updates when Amazon DynamoDB items change. The team wants a managed GraphQL service with subscriptions and does not want to build WebSocket fan-out on Amazon API Gateway. Polling is not acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API and poll every second.
B. Create an AWS AppSync API with subscriptions to DynamoDB.
C. Create an Application Load Balancer with sticky sessions only.
D. Host a WebSocket server on a single Amazon EC2 instance.

questions.explain: AppSync provides managed GraphQL, resolvers, and subscriptions. Clients reach AppSync directly rather than through API Gateway REST fan-out.
questions.good_to_know: API Gateway WebSocket would be closer if the stem required a custom WebSocket API without GraphQL. REST plus polling is the high-overhead alternative the scenario rejects.

questions.q: A team must host a static single-page application with a managed front-end workflow, including builds from a Git repository. They want AWS to operate the hosting rather than Amazon EC2 web servers. The REST API will remain a separate backend. Customer authentication is out of scope for this hosting choice. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Serve the single-page app from an Amazon RDS instance.
B. Run Apache on a single Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet.
C. Store HTML in AWS Secrets Manager and return it from Lambda.
D. Use AWS Amplify Hosting for the front-end application.

questions.explain: Amplify Hosting is the managed front-end hosting and Git-based deploy path. EC2 web servers are the operational model the stem rejects.
questions.good_to_know: Amazon S3 with CloudFront would also host a static SPA if the stem did not require Amplify's front-end toolchain. AppSync would be the GraphQL API, not the static host.

questions.q: Producers on Amazon EC2 in private subnets can emit tens of thousands of events in a few seconds. A Lambda worker would overwhelm a downstream database if it scaled with every event. The team must absorb bursts between producer and worker. Message ordering guarantees are not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Place an Amazon SQS queue between the producer and the Lambda worker.
B. Invoke the Lambda function synchronously from every producer.
C. Enable provisioned concurrency so the database receives more parallel writes.
D. Replace Lambda with a single-threaded Amazon EC2 cron job that drops events.

questions.explain: SQS between producer and worker is the lesson's burst-absorption pattern. Direct invoke removes the buffer; provisioned concurrency increases readiness, not decoupling.
questions.good_to_know: Reserved concurrency would still be needed if the worker itself must be capped. Provisioned concurrency would be correct for predictable cold starts, not burst absorption.

questions.q: An application invokes AWS Lambda asynchronously. When a third-party endpoint is down, the function fails repeatedly. After retries are exhausted, the team must retain the original event payload for later analysis. The function is not an Amazon SQS event-source mapping and is not behind Amazon API Gateway. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable Amazon API Gateway stage cache for failed events.
B. Store failures in an Amazon Cognito identity pool.
C. Configure a Lambda on-failure destination or DLQ.
D. Increase provisioned concurrency so failures cannot occur.

questions.explain: After asynchronous retries, Lambda can send exhausted events to an on-failure destination or a supported DLQ. Caching and identity pools are not failure stores.
questions.good_to_know: For an SQS event-source mapping, a redrive policy on the queue is the usual DLQ. Provisioned concurrency does not prevent third-party outages.

questions.q: A CPU-bound Lambda function finishes just inside the timeout. Amazon API Gateway invokes the function synchronously. Metrics show the function uses little of its allocated memory. The team must speed up the function without rewriting the algorithm. They know memory size also controls available CPU. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Decrease memory to the minimum to force more CPU onto the host.
B. Increase the function memory allocation and remeasure duration.
C. Enable API Gateway throttling to give the function more CPU.
D. Attach an Amazon EBS volume to the Lambda execution environment.

questions.explain: Lambda CPU scales with the memory setting. Raising memory is how you give a CPU-bound function more compute without a code rewrite.
questions.good_to_know: Reserved concurrency would be correct to protect a downstream system. EBS is not an attachable volume for the Lambda runtime.

questions.q: A Lambda function invoked by Amazon API Gateway must write items to Amazon DynamoDB. Developers must not put AWS access keys in environment variables or in the deployment package. The function already has an execution role attached. The table is private to the account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Embed an IAM user access key in the function code.
B. Make the DynamoDB table publicly writable with a wildcard policy.
C. Store AWS root credentials in Parameter Store for the runtime.
D. Grant the Lambda execution role DynamoDB write permissions.

questions.explain: Lambda reaches AWS services through its execution role. Embedded access keys violate the constraint against long-lived credentials in the package.
questions.good_to_know: A Cognito identity pool would be correct if end-user apps needed temporary AWS credentials. Secrets Manager would be correct for rotating a database password.

questions.q: A Lambda function currently writes session files to /tmp and expects the next invocation to read them. Amazon API Gateway invokes the function on every HTTP request. Under load, users lose sessions because another execution environment handles the request. The function must remain serverless and store durable session state outside the runtime. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store session state in Amazon DynamoDB, not in /tmp.
B. Increase /tmp size and pin one execution environment forever.
C. Enable provisioned concurrency so /tmp becomes a shared disk.
D. Use Amazon EC2 instance store as the Lambda home directory.

questions.explain: Lambda must stay stateless; durable state belongs in an external store such as DynamoDB. /tmp is per environment and is not shared across invocations.
questions.good_to_know: Amazon EC2 or containers would be correct if the stem required long-lived local disk and in-memory state that serverless cannot hold. Provisioned concurrency warms environments; it does not share /tmp.

questions.q: A public REST API on Amazon API Gateway is overwhelmed by a traffic spike from a partner integration. The backend Lambda is healthy at normal load. The company must limit request rates at the API front door without using Lambda reserved concurrency as the first control. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Disable the API and serve clients from Amazon Amplify only.
B. Turn on Amazon Cognito identity pools to drop HTTP requests.
C. Configure throttling and usage plans on Amazon API Gateway.
D. Set Lambda reserved concurrency to the account unreserved maximum.

questions.explain: API Gateway throttling (and usage plans) rate-limits at the managed API front door. Reserved concurrency caps the function, which the stem says not to use first.
questions.good_to_know: Reserved concurrency would be correct if the Lambda worker were overwhelming a database. Cognito authenticates users; it is not an HTTP rate limiter.

questions.q: A chat application needs a managed WebSocket API so browsers can hold persistent connections. The team does not need GraphQL, and message fan-out must not require a GraphQL schema. AWS Lambda should handle connect, message, and disconnect events. They will not run a WebSocket fleet on Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS AppSync GraphQL API even though clients are not GraphQL.
B. Create an Amazon API Gateway WebSocket API integrated with Lambda.
C. Create an Amazon API Gateway REST API and have clients poll.
D. Terminate WebSockets on an Amazon SQS queue.

questions.explain: API Gateway WebSocket APIs are the managed persistent-connection front door with Lambda integrations. AppSync subscriptions assume a GraphQL API.
questions.good_to_know: AppSync would be correct if clients needed GraphQL queries plus subscriptions. REST polling is the alternative the live-dashboard scenario rejects.

questions.q: A video encoder must run for 45 minutes, keep a large in-memory working set, and write checkpoints to local disk during the job. The job is a batch encoder, not an HTTP request handler. The team tried AWS Lambda and hit timeout and ephemeral-storage limits. They want compute without a Lambda-style duration cap. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Raise the Lambda timeout to 45 minutes and attach instance store.
B. Use Amazon API Gateway HTTP APIs to encode video in the integration.
C. Enable provisioned concurrency so Lambda can run for hours.
D. Run the encoder on Amazon EC2 instances sized for the working set.

questions.explain: Long-running, highly stateful work fits Amazon EC2 (or containers) rather than Lambda. Lambda has a maximum duration well below 45 minutes.
questions.good_to_know: Lambda would be correct for short event-driven handlers. Provisioned concurrency reduces cold starts; it does not extend the maximum runtime.

questions.q: A SaaS product needs a managed customer directory with sign-up, sign-in, and JWT tokens for a REST API. Temporary AWS credentials for S3 uploads are not required in this release. IAM Identity Center is already used for employees and must not be the customer directory. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Cognito user pool for customer sign-in.
B. Create an Amazon Cognito identity pool only, without a user pool.
C. Register each customer as a user in IAM Identity Center.
D. Issue IAM user access keys during customer sign-up.

questions.explain: Cognito user pools are application customer identity and JWT issuance. Identity Center is workforce access; an identity pool is for temporary AWS credentials.
questions.good_to_know: An identity pool would be correct if the app needed temporary AWS credentials after sign-in. Identity Center remains the employee AWS access portal.

questions.q: A REST API on Amazon API Gateway serves mostly identical GET responses. Lambda origin load is high because every client hits the integration. Operations wants method-level cache TTLs inside API Gateway, not a separate CDN distribution, and will not rewrite the API as GraphQL. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Convert the REST API to AWS AppSync to obtain a cache.
B. Enable Lambda provisioned concurrency as the response cache.
C. Enable API Gateway caching on the GET methods.
D. Store GET responses in an Amazon SQS queue for clients to poll.

questions.explain: API Gateway caching is the method-level TTL control on a REST stage. Provisioned concurrency warms Lambda; it does not cache GET bodies.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront would be correct if the stem required a global CDN in front of the API. AppSync would be correct for GraphQL, not a REST cache retrofit.

questions.q: A company runs a mobile checkout API on Amazon API Gateway and AWS Lambda. The API has sharp bursts and must authenticate customers. The team wants the LEAST custom identity code. An identity pool alone is not a user directory. Lambda must run only after tokens are validated. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Cognito user pool to issue JWT tokens.
B. Create an identity pool only and skip user sign-in.
C. Configure API Gateway to validate the JWTs before Lambda.
D. Embed the Lambda execution role in the mobile application.
E. Replace the API with Amazon SQS as the client-facing HTTPS endpoint.

questions.explain: A user pool supplies the directory and JWTs; API Gateway validates them before Lambda. Those two steps are the bursting-checkout pattern.
questions.good_to_know: An identity pool would be added if the app also needed temporary AWS credentials. SQS is the burst buffer between producers and workers, not the HTTPS customer API.

questions.q: A company ingests asynchronous jobs with AWS Lambda. Producers are Amazon EC2 applications in one Region. Those jobs spike beyond what a downstream database can accept. Direct Lambda invoke removes buffering. Provisioned concurrency is already on for latency and did not cap database pressure. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable provisioned concurrency as the only database protection.
B. Buffer work in an Amazon SQS queue between producers and the worker.
C. Invoke Lambda synchronously from each producer with retries in a loop.
D. Set reserved concurrency on the Lambda worker to cap scale.
E. Keep unbounded Lambda scale and change only the database engine family.

questions.explain: SQS absorbs bursts; reserved concurrency caps how many workers hit the database. Provisioned concurrency does not provide that ceiling.
questions.good_to_know: Provisioned concurrency remains the cold-start control. A connection pooler taught in the databases lesson would help sessions, not replace the queue or the concurrency cap.

questions.q: The product is a live collaborative dashboard in the browser. Web clients need GraphQL queries and server-pushed updates when data changes. They must not poll a REST API, and they must not place Amazon API Gateway in front of the GraphQL service. Resolvers may read Amazon DynamoDB. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Put Amazon API Gateway REST in front of AppSync.
B. Use Amazon Amplify Hosting as the GraphQL engine.
C. Create an AWS AppSync GraphQL API.
D. Run a WebSocket fan-out service on Amazon EC2.
E. Enable AppSync subscriptions for live updates.

questions.explain: AppSync is the managed GraphQL front door, and subscriptions provide the push path. Clients call AppSync directly, not through API Gateway.
questions.good_to_know: API Gateway WebSocket would be correct for a custom non-GraphQL persistent API. Amplify Hosting is the static front end, not the GraphQL engine.

questions.q: A company exposes a latency-sensitive Lambda function through Amazon API Gateway. The function has predictable morning traffic and also writes to a database with a connection limit. Cold starts are unacceptable in the morning, and unbounded scale would exhaust the database. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Configure provisioned concurrency for the morning traffic.
B. Remove reserved concurrency so provisioned concurrency can scale without a cap.
C. Use Amazon SQS as the client-facing HTTPS API.
D. Increase memory only, without concurrency controls.
E. Set reserved concurrency so executions cannot exceed the database limit.

questions.explain: Provisioned concurrency warms environments for predictable load. Reserved concurrency caps concurrent executions so the database is not overwhelmed.
questions.good_to_know: Provisioned concurrency counts toward reserved concurrency, so the reserved value must be at least the provisioned value. SQS would buffer async work, not replace an HTTPS API.

questions.q: A team needs a hosted static front end and customer sign-in for that app. They do not want Amazon EC2 web servers or IAM users for customers. The API will be added later. Workforce IAM Identity Center must not be the customer directory. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create IAM users for each browser session.
B. Host the static application with AWS Amplify Hosting.
C. Use Amazon Cognito user pools for sign-up and sign-in.
D. Serve the application from AWS Lambda /tmp storage.
E. Use IAM Identity Center as the customer player directory.

questions.explain: Amplify Hosting is the managed front-end host; Cognito user pools are customer identity. Identity Center remains workforce AWS access.
questions.good_to_know: S3 with CloudFront would also host a static SPA without the Amplify toolchain. An identity pool would be added if the browser needed temporary AWS credentials.

questions.q: An application invokes AWS Lambda asynchronously. After retries fail, events must land in Amazon SQS for operators. The execution role must be able to deliver those failed events. The team must not use API Gateway cache as the failure store. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool as the async failure store.
B. Enable API Gateway caching of 500 responses.
C. Delete the execution role so failures skip retries.
D. Configure a Lambda on-failure destination or DLQ.
E. Grant the execution role permission to write to that queue.

questions.explain: Async failures go to an on-failure destination or DLQ, and the execution role must be allowed to send to that queue. Those two steps are jointly required.
questions.good_to_know: For SQS event-source mappings, configure a redrive policy on the source queue. Cognito identity pools issue temporary AWS credentials, not failure events.

questions.q: A Lambda function must persist order records and must not keep them in /tmp across invocations. Orders must survive a cold start on a new execution environment. It must call Amazon DynamoDB without embedded access keys. The function already exists and is invoked by Amazon API Gateway. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Write durable order records to Amazon DynamoDB.
B. Grant the execution role permission to access the table.
C. Store AWS access keys in the function environment for DynamoDB.
D. Depend on /tmp surviving across all future invocations.
E. Use Amazon API Gateway usage plans as the database.

questions.explain: Durable state belongs outside the execution environment, and the execution role is how Lambda is authorized to write to DynamoDB.
questions.good_to_know: Embedded keys would be the anti-pattern the execution-role model replaces. API Gateway usage plans throttle callers; they do not store orders.

questions.q: A startup hosts a request/response HTTP API as containers in one AWS Region. A two-person team has no Kubernetes experience and must not patch worker nodes or pay for idle cluster instances between traffic spikes. Images must remain private. Tasks must run in private subnets, and users must reach the API through a public Application Load Balancer. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate and pull images from Amazon ECR.
B. Run self-managed Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 and store images in Amazon S3.
C. Run Amazon EKS with self-managed node groups so the team can learn Helm later.
D. Place each container on its own Amazon EC2 instance with no orchestrator.

questions.explain: No Kubernetes API requirement plus no worker-node management selects ECS on Fargate. ECR holds private images; ECS keeps the desired task count behind the ALB.
questions.good_to_know: EKS would be correct if Helm, operators, or the Kubernetes API were required. Plain EC2 has no service scheduler to replace unhealthy copies.

questions.q: A company already operates Helm charts and Kubernetes operators in another cloud. After moving to AWS it must keep those APIs and the same ecosystem tooling. AWS should run the Kubernetes control plane. The team will choose worker compute separately and does not want to operate etcd itself. Existing charts must deploy without a rewrite to Amazon ECS task definitions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon ECS cluster and rewrite each chart as an ECS task definition.
B. Submit the Helm releases as AWS Batch jobs on a nightly schedule.
C. Create an Amazon EKS cluster and deploy the existing Helm charts.
D. Use Elastic Beanstalk to expose a Kubernetes-compatible API.

questions.explain: Helm, operators, and Kubernetes API compatibility select EKS. AWS manages the control plane; ECS does not expose those APIs.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on Fargate would be the lower-operations answer if Kubernetes were not required. Batch schedules finite jobs, not a long-running Kubernetes platform.

questions.q: An Amazon ECS service already runs a containerized HTTP API on Amazon EC2 container instances. Operators spend too much time patching those instances and still pay for idle cluster capacity between spikes. The team must keep ECS as the orchestrator and must stop managing worker AMIs and capacity providers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Move the tasks onto Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts.
B. Change the service to the AWS Fargate launch type.
C. Rebuild the API on Amazon EKS self-managed node groups.
D. Run Docker Engine on a single Amazon EC2 instance.

questions.explain: Fargate is the serverless compute engine for ECS tasks, so operators no longer provision or patch worker nodes and they pay for task resources rather than idle instances.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on EC2 would remain correct if the stem required custom AMIs or instance types that the team must manage. Dedicated Hosts increase host control, not reduce it.

questions.q: A platform team must store versioned, private container images next to AWS compute in the same Region. Orchestrators will pull those images at deploy time. The store must integrate with IAM and must not be the runtime that executes containers. A public registry is not acceptable for these images. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Upload image layers to Amazon S3 Standard and start tasks from the bucket.
B. Use Amazon ECR lifecycle rules as the compute engine for the tasks.
C. Host the images on an S3 static website and pull them over HTTP.
D. Push immutable tags to Amazon ECR and grant the task execution role pull access.

questions.explain: ECR is the managed registry. Orchestrators pull and run images; ECR itself does not execute containers. S3 is object storage, not an OCI registry.
questions.good_to_know: A public registry would fit only if images were allowed to be world-readable. Lifecycle rules expire old tags; they are not a task runtime.

questions.q: A genomics lab submits thousands of finite analysis jobs that wait until compute is free. The jobs are not a long-running HTTP service. Researchers may outpace capacity, so work must queue. The lab wants AWS to schedule jobs onto Fargate or Amazon EC2 and does not need Kubernetes APIs. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Submit the jobs to AWS Batch.
B. Keep an Amazon ECS service at a desired count equal to peak jobs.
C. Store each job payload in Amazon S3 Glacier and restore it by hand.
D. Run Elastic Beanstalk environments at full capacity all day.

questions.explain: Queued finite jobs select AWS Batch, which schedules onto Fargate or EC2. An always-on ECS service is for long-running request/response capacity, not a job queue.
questions.good_to_know: ECS would be correct for a steady HTTP API with a desired task count. EKS would appear if Kubernetes Job APIs were the constraint.

questions.q: A product team needs to deploy a conventional web application with the LEAST operational overhead for environment provisioning. The application is not containerized and does not need Kubernetes. The team still wants AWS to create the underlying load balancer and compute rather than assembling every resource by hand. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon EKS cluster and install the uncontainerized app with Helm.
B. Create an AWS Batch job queue for each inbound HTTP request.
C. Create an Elastic Beanstalk environment for the application.
D. Place AWS Outposts in the office to host the public website.

questions.explain: Elastic Beanstalk abstracts application environment provisioning while still using underlying AWS resources. EKS and Batch do not match an uncontainerized web environment.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on Fargate would be the answer after the app is packaged as containers and Kubernetes is still not required. Outposts is for on-premises latency or residency, not simpler Region provisioning.

questions.q: A factory must run an AWS-based control application beside the production line. Round-trip latency to the nearest AWS Region is too high for the control loop, and some process data must remain on the factory floor. The company wants AWS-designed infrastructure on premises rather than a fully custom private cloud. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate in the distant Region and add more vCPU.
B. Deploy AWS Outposts at the factory and run the application there.
C. Use Elastic Beanstalk in the Region with a larger instance type.
D. Store the process data in Amazon ECR instead of running compute locally.

questions.explain: Outposts extends AWS infrastructure on premises for latency and data-residency constraints. More Regional Fargate or Beanstalk capacity does not move the control loop onto the factory floor.
questions.good_to_know: ECS Anywhere would be the recognition-level answer if the stem required the ECS task model on customer-owned servers rather than AWS-owned Outposts hardware.

questions.q: A retailer already owns on-premises servers in each store and wants to run Amazon ECS tasks on that hardware. Kubernetes is not required. The company will not install AWS Outposts racks. It needs AWS container tooling on customer-managed infrastructure rather than a new Regional-only cluster or a Batch queue in the closest Region. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Install AWS Outposts in every store and retire the owned servers.
B. Use AWS Batch in the closest Region for in-store interactive latency.
C. Use Elastic Beanstalk to provision the on-premises hypervisors.
D. Use Amazon ECS Anywhere on the existing servers.

questions.explain: ECS Anywhere is the recognition-level option for ECS on customer-managed or on-premises hosts. Outposts is AWS infrastructure placed on site, which this stem rejects.
questions.good_to_know: EKS Anywhere would appear if the constraint were Kubernetes on customer-managed hardware. Batch in the Region cannot meet store-floor latency on existing boxes.

questions.q: A checkout path must run a short function whenever an order event arrives. Each invocation finishes in seconds, needs no container orchestrator, and should incur no idle instance cost. The team does not need Kubernetes APIs and is not packaging a long-running HTTP service. AWS Batch on an hourly schedule is too slow for checkout. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Invoke AWS Lambda for each order event.
B. Keep an Amazon EKS node group sized for peak checkout all day.
C. Run AWS Batch on a schedule once per hour.
D. Place the function on AWS Outposts to avoid using Lambda.

questions.explain: Short event-driven functions select Lambda. EKS nodes and hourly Batch jobs add idle capacity or delay that the stem does not ask for.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on Fargate would be correct for a long-running containerized API. Lesson 08 owns Lambda concurrency and API Gateway details; this item only picks the function compute model.

questions.q: A vendor ships a network appliance as an Amazon Machine Image that needs custom kernel modules, a specific Linux distribution, and full operating-system access. The workload is not packaged as a container and is not a short function. The company will run it in AWS and must retain maximum OS control. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the appliance as an AWS Fargate task.
B. Deploy the appliance as an Amazon ECS service with desired count 1.
C. Launch Amazon EC2 instances from the appliance AMI.
D. Package the kernel modules as an Amazon ECR image and let ECR execute them.

questions.explain: Maximum OS control, custom kernels, and an AMI select EC2. Fargate and ECS hide or replace the guest OS the appliance requires. ECR does not run images.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on EC2 would be in play if the appliance were containerized but still needed managed instances. Lambda is the short-function model, which this stem excludes.

questions.q: A media company wants AWS-native container orchestration for a long-running video transcoder in one Region. Operators must use a custom AMI, apply their own host patches, and binpack tasks onto Reserved Instances they already purchased. Kubernetes APIs are not required. Hiding the instance layer is not acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the tasks only on AWS Fargate.
B. Run an Amazon ECS service on Amazon EC2 capacity.
C. Run Amazon EKS solely because containers are involved.
D. Submit each transcode as an AWS Lambda invocation.

questions.explain: ECS can run tasks on EC2 when the team must manage AMIs, patches, and instance purchases. Fargate removes that instance layer, which the stem forbids.
questions.good_to_know: Fargate is the answer when the constraint is no worker-node management. EKS is for Kubernetes portability, not a default for every container.

questions.q: An enterprise is moving a platform that already uses Kubernetes APIs and Helm charts. After the move to AWS it must keep that tooling. It also refuses to provision or patch worker nodes. Supported pods can run on serverless container compute. AWS must still operate the Kubernetes control plane. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon ECS cluster on Amazon EC2 Dedicated Hosts.
B. Install self-managed Kubernetes on Amazon EC2 and operate etcd.
C. Use Elastic Beanstalk Docker and expose the Kubernetes API.
D. Create an Amazon EKS cluster that runs pods on AWS Fargate.

questions.explain: Kubernetes APIs select EKS; no worker-node management selects Fargate for supported pods. ECS does not provide the Kubernetes API.
questions.good_to_know: EKS managed node groups would be correct if the stem required EC2 worker capacity the team is willing to patch. ECS on Fargate would win without Helm.

questions.q: A payments API is packaged as containers in one AWS Region. The service must keep six healthy copies in private subnets, replace failed copies automatically, and receive HTTPS traffic from a public Application Load Balancer. Kubernetes is not required, and the team does not want to manage worker nodes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use an Amazon ECS Fargate service with desired count 6 behind the ALB.
B. Store six image tags in Amazon ECR and rely on ECR to listen on port 443.
C. Set AWS Batch job concurrency to 6 and attach the ALB to the job queue.
D. Run six AWS Lambda functions as the only HTTPS targets.

questions.explain: An ECS service maintains desired task count and integrates with a load balancer. Fargate removes node work. ECR is a registry, not a listener.
questions.good_to_know: Host and path listener rules are a Lesson 03 ALB topic; this item only tests ECS desired count plus ALB integration. Batch is for queued jobs, not six always-on API copies.

questions.q: A hospital runs Amazon ECS tasks in private subnets in one Region. It must keep container images private, scan them for vulnerabilities, and tag them immutably so deploys are repeatable. Tasks will pull images at launch using IAM rather than a shared password. Developers must not embed registry credentials in task definitions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Push images to a public registry and hard-code a token in the task definition.
B. Copy images into Amazon EFS and mount the file system as the Docker root.
C. Use Amazon ECR with image scanning and grant the task execution role pull permission.
D. Use Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration as the container registry.

questions.explain: ECR provides private, scannable, versioned images. The task execution role pulls at launch without embedding secrets in the definition.
questions.good_to_know: S3 is not an OCI registry. A public registry would violate the private-image constraint even if scanning existed elsewhere.

questions.q: A two-person team is launching a containerized internal API on AWS in a single account. They have no Helm charts, no operators, and no requirement for the Kubernetes API. They want AWS-native orchestration and will not add Kubernetes operational concepts for fashion. Worker-node patching should be avoided. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run Amazon EKS because Kubernetes is the default for all containers.
B. Run Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate.
C. Run AWS Batch as a long-running HTTPS service.
D. Run docker on Amazon EC2 at boot with no scheduler.

questions.explain: When Kubernetes APIs are not required, ECS is the AWS-native orchestrator. Fargate removes node patching. EKS is not the default merely because workloads are containers.
questions.good_to_know: EKS is correct when Helm, operators, or portability of the Kubernetes API are real constraints. Batch remains the queued-job answer.

questions.q: A company currently runs Kubernetes itself on Amazon EC2, including etcd and control-plane nodes. It must keep Helm and the Kubernetes API but wants AWS to operate the control plane. Worker nodes can remain EC2 managed node groups. The team will not switch to Amazon ECS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Migrate the workloads to Amazon ECS and drop the Kubernetes API.
B. Move control-plane nodes to AWS Lambda.
C. Replace Kubernetes with Elastic Beanstalk platforms.
D. Migrate the cluster to Amazon EKS with managed node groups.

questions.explain: EKS is the managed Kubernetes control plane. Managed node groups keep EC2 workers without self-managed etcd. ECS would abandon the Kubernetes API the stem requires.
questions.good_to_know: EKS on Fargate would fit if the stem also forbade worker-node management. Self-managed Kubernetes on EC2 is what the company is leaving.

questions.q: A video processor runs for 45 minutes per file, needs a custom runtime inside a container, and must scale copies from a queue of work. The team does not want to manage Kubernetes. A short function model is too brief for each file, and Amazon ECR must not be treated as the compute engine. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate as queue workers.
B. Invoke AWS Lambda once per file as the only compute.
C. Use Amazon ECR alone to transcode each object.
D. Use Elastic Beanstalk to schedule Kubernetes Jobs.

questions.explain: Long-running container work without Kubernetes selects ECS. Fargate avoids node management. Lambda is the short-function model; ECR does not execute containers.
questions.good_to_know: AWS Batch would be equally reasonable if the stem stressed a managed job scheduler rather than an ECS task worker. Lambda remains Lesson 08's short-event path.

questions.q: A university runs nightly simulation jobs that each last two hours and then stop. Between runs, no compute should sit idle. Jobs must queue when researchers submit more work than capacity. The team will not operate a Kubernetes control plane and does not need a 24-hour HTTP service. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Keep an Amazon ECS service at desired count 50 all day.
B. Use Amazon EKS with a Deployment that never scales to zero.
C. Use AWS Batch to queue the jobs onto Fargate or Amazon EC2.
D. Use Amazon ECR lifecycle policies to execute the simulations.

questions.explain: Finite queued jobs that should not leave idle service capacity select Batch. A high desired count on ECS or EKS keeps compute running between nights.
questions.good_to_know: An ECS service is the right shape for a continuously listening API. Fargate under Batch still pays for job compute rather than an always-on service.

questions.q: A catalog API is packaged as containers. The team has no Helm charts and no Kubernetes requirement. It must not patch worker nodes. Private images will live in a registry, and a public Application Load Balancer will send HTTPS to the service in private subnets. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon ECS service for the API.
B. Create an Amazon EKS control plane so Helm can be added later.
C. Run the service on AWS Fargate.
D. Store running containers only in Amazon ECR with no orchestrator.
E. Use AWS Batch as the HTTPS front door.

questions.explain: ECS is the AWS-native orchestrator; Fargate removes the node layer. Both are required for this constraint set. ECR stores images but does not run them.
questions.good_to_know: EKS plus Fargate would be the pair if Kubernetes APIs were mandatory. Batch would pair with a job queue, not a public HTTP API.

questions.q: An organization is moving platform tooling that depends on Helm charts, custom operators, and the Kubernetes API. AWS must run the control plane. The team will keep those manifests rather than rewriting them as Amazon ECS task definitions. Worker compute can be chosen after the cluster exists. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Convert every chart into an Amazon ECS task definition.
B. Create an Amazon EKS cluster.
C. Use Elastic Beanstalk as the Kubernetes API.
D. Deploy the existing Helm charts and operators onto that cluster.
E. Use Amazon ECR as the only runtime with no cluster.

questions.explain: EKS supplies the managed Kubernetes API; deploying Helm and operators is how the existing ecosystem keeps working. Those two steps are jointly necessary.
questions.good_to_know: Add Fargate profiles if the stem also forbids worker-node patching. ECS cannot run Helm operators.

questions.q: Amazon ECS tasks in private subnets must start from private, scanned, immutable image tags. The registry must integrate with IAM. Tasks must pull at launch without a password in the task definition, and the registry must not be treated as compute. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Make the repository public so tasks can pull without IAM.
B. Store images in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive and restore at each start.
C. Push immutable image tags to Amazon ECR.
D. Invoke Amazon ECR directly as the application compute engine.
E. Grant the ECS task execution role permission to pull from the repository.

questions.explain: ECR holds the private versioned images; the execution role is how ECS pulls them. Public access and treating ECR as compute both violate the stem.
questions.good_to_know: Image scanning on the repository is the usual next control when the stem also names vulnerability findings. S3 Glacier is archive object storage, not a registry.

questions.q: A research group submits finite rendering jobs that must wait in a queue until capacity exists. Jobs should run on Fargate or Amazon EC2 according to cost. The group will not keep a 24-hour Amazon ECS service at peak desired count and does not need Kubernetes. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an AWS Batch job queue and job definitions.
B. Set an Amazon ECS service desired count equal to the lifetime job total.
C. Use Amazon EKS only to store job YAML in Amazon S3.
D. Use Elastic Beanstalk to replace the batch scheduler.
E. Attach a Fargate or Amazon EC2 compute environment to the queue.

questions.explain: Batch is the scheduler for queued jobs; a compute environment is where those jobs actually run. An always-on ECS desired count fights the idle-capacity constraint.
questions.good_to_know: ECS services remain the answer for long-running APIs with a load balancer. EKS Jobs would appear only if Kubernetes were required.

questions.q: A plant-floor controller must run on AWS-designed hardware next to the line because Regional round-trip time is too high and process data must stay on site. The company does not want to rewrite the controller as a short function in the Region. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Move the controller to AWS Fargate in a distant Region.
B. Install AWS Outposts at the plant.
C. Run the latency-sensitive workload on the Outpost.
D. Use Amazon CloudFront to satisfy factory-floor residency.
E. Store the process data only in Amazon ECR.

questions.explain: Outposts places AWS infrastructure on premises; the workload must actually run there to meet latency and residency. Regional Fargate still leaves the plant.
questions.good_to_know: ECS Anywhere would be the pair if the stem required ECS on servers the plant already owns. CloudFront is an edge cache, not a residency control plane.

questions.q: A public HTTPS API will run as containers in private subnets in one Region. The platform must keep a stated number of healthy copies, replace failed copies, and register those copies with an Application Load Balancer that already sits in public subnets. Kubernetes is not required. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use Amazon ECR lifecycle rules to listen for HTTPS.
B. Use AWS Batch job attempts as the load balancer.
C. Place an Amazon EKS control plane in a public subnet as the only entry point.
D. Create an Amazon ECS service and set the desired task count.
E. Integrate the service with an Application Load Balancer.

questions.explain: ECS services maintain desired count and integrate with load balancers. Those two controls match the stem. ECR and Batch are not HTTPS listeners.
questions.good_to_know: ALB host and path rules belong to Lesson 03. Fargate would be the launch-type add-on if the stem also forbade worker-node patching.

questions.q: A product team wants to deploy a conventional, uncontainerized web application in one AWS Region and let AWS provision the environment, including underlying load balancing and compute. They do not need Kubernetes, AWS Batch, or on-premises racks, and they will not assemble every resource by hand. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Elastic Beanstalk environment for the web application.
B. Upload the application bundle and let Beanstalk provision the underlying AWS resources.
C. Create an Amazon EKS cluster for an application that is not containerized.
