D. Use AWS Outposts as the only way to obtain a load balancer.
E. Use AWS Batch to serve interactive HTTPS clients.

questions.explain: Beanstalk is the environment-provisioning abstraction; uploading the bundle is how the app gets onto the resources Beanstalk creates.
questions.good_to_know: ECS on Fargate would be the pair after the app is containerized and Kubernetes is still not required. Outposts is latency or residency, not simpler PaaS.

questions.q: An order API on Amazon EC2 must accept requests in milliseconds and must not wait while a downstream fulfillment worker on Amazon ECS runs for minutes. Traffic bursts several times a day. Workers must scale independently of the API. Messages must still exist if every worker is down. An event bus must not be the only backlog. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Send work to an Amazon SQS queue that the workers poll.
B. Have the API call each worker with a synchronous HTTP request.
C. Publish only to Amazon SNS email subscriptions.
D. Put each order on Amazon EventBridge as the only durable backlog.

questions.explain: A durable queue buffers bursts and decouples the producer from slow consumers. EventBridge routes events; it is not the durable work queue in this lesson.
questions.good_to_know: SNS would be correct if the same event had to fan out to many independent subscribers. Synchronous HTTP couples API availability to worker runtime.

questions.q: A media site collects clicks on Amazon EC2 and must ingest them at very high throughput from many producers. Occasional duplicate deliveries are acceptable if consumers handle them safely. Strict ordering across all clicks is not required. Workers will scale independently of the collectors. The team wants a durable queue, not an event bus or a workflow engine. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with one message group for the entire site.
B. Use Amazon MQ because standard queues cannot scale.
C. Use an Amazon SQS standard queue and make consumers idempotent.
D. Use AWS Step Functions as the click buffer.

questions.explain: Standard queues prioritize scale and at-least-once delivery, so consumers must be idempotent. A single FIFO group would serialize the whole site for an ordering need the stem does not have.
questions.good_to_know: FIFO is the answer when per-group order and deduplication are required. Amazon MQ is for legacy broker protocols, not extra SQS scale.

questions.q: A payments platform on Amazon ECS workers already polls Amazon SQS. It must process each customer's transactions in order and must suppress duplicate submissions of the same payment. Different customers may be processed in parallel. Throughput can be lower than a standard queue. The team will not switch to an event bus for this backlog. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use an Amazon SQS standard queue and sort messages in each consumer.
B. Use an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with a message group ID per customer.
C. Use the Amazon EventBridge default bus as a globally ordered log.
D. Use an Amazon SNS standard topic as the only ordered payment log.

questions.explain: FIFO provides ordering and deduplication; message group IDs keep order per customer while allowing other groups to run in parallel. Standard queues do not give that contract.
questions.good_to_know: A standard queue remains correct when scale and at-least-once delivery matter more than order. EventBridge is pattern routing, not a per-customer FIFO log.

questions.q: Amazon SQS workers sometimes take four minutes to finish a message. A second worker must not receive that same message while the first is still working. If a worker crashes, the message should become visible again so another worker can retry. The team will not replace the queue with an event bus. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Set the visibility timeout to zero so every worker shares in-flight work.
B. Disable the dead-letter queue so messages never retry after a crash.
C. Replace the queue with Amazon EventBridge so in-flight state is implicit.
D. Set the visibility timeout longer than typical processing time.

questions.explain: Visibility timeout hides an in-flight message from other consumers until it is deleted or the timeout expires. Zero timeout would cause overlapping processing.
questions.good_to_know: A DLQ isolates poison messages after failed retries; it does not replace visibility for healthy in-flight work. Heartbeat-style timeout extension is the follow-on when processing time varies widely.

questions.q: An Amazon SQS consumer on Amazon ECS repeatedly fails a malformed message and retries it. After a bounded number of receives, that message must leave the main queue so other work continues. Operators must inspect it later for replay. Increasing retention alone is not enough, and CloudWatch must not be the redrive mechanism. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Configure a dead-letter queue and a maxReceiveCount on the source queue.
B. Increase message retention only and leave poison messages in the main queue.
C. Subscribe Amazon CloudWatch to delete failed messages automatically.
D. Enable Amazon SNS message filtering on the SQS queue.

questions.explain: A redrive policy moves a message to a DLQ after it exceeds maxReceiveCount. Retention only keeps the poison message blocking useful retries on the source queue.
questions.good_to_know: SNS filter policies reduce deliveries to a subscription; they do not isolate failed SQS receives. CloudWatch is observability, not a queue redrive.

questions.q: An ecommerce API on Amazon EC2 places an order record and then must notify billing, a mobile push notifier, and an HTTP webhook. Each of those three systems must receive a copy of the same event. The producer must not call them synchronously. Strict per-customer queue order is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Send each order to one Amazon SQS queue that all three services compete on.
B. Store orders only in Amazon ECR until each system polls S3.
C. Publish each order to an Amazon SNS topic with those three subscriptions.
D. Use Amazon MQ only because the webhook already speaks HTTPS.

questions.explain: SNS is pub/sub fanout to multiple subscribers. One shared SQS queue load-balances messages instead of copying them to every consumer.
questions.good_to_know: SNS to a dedicated SQS queue per consumer is the next step when each subscriber needs its own durable backlog. Amazon MQ is for existing broker protocols.

questions.q: A retailer API publishes one order event per checkout. Billing, fulfillment, and analytics must each process every order, survive independent outages, and retry at their own rates. The producer must publish once. A single shared queue would give each message to only one consumer. Direct synchronous calls from the API are not acceptable. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use one shared Amazon SQS queue for all three services.
B. Publish to Amazon SNS and subscribe a dedicated Amazon SQS queue per service.
C. Invoke the three services synchronously from the API in one request.
D. Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler as the order database.

questions.explain: SNS copies the event; a separate SQS subscription per service gives each team an independent durable backlog and retry loop.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge would be the router if the constraint were content-based matching across many sources rather than simple topic fanout. A shared queue is competing consumers, not fanout.

questions.q: Many microservices already subscribe to an Amazon SNS topic that carries several event types. The inventory service should receive only messages whose attribute type is Restock. The company wants to avoid delivering every message to inventory and does not want inventory workers to discard most payloads in application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue with no filter and drop messages in code.
B. Use AWS Step Functions to broadcast every message to every service.
C. Use Amazon MQ to replace SNS filters with unfiltered public topics.
D. Apply an SNS subscription filter policy on the inventory subscription.

questions.explain: SNS filtering reduces unnecessary deliveries on a subscription. Dropping in consumer code still incurs the delivery the stem wants to avoid.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge rules would be the answer if routing were by event source and detail-type on a bus rather than SNS subscription attributes.

questions.q: Internal applications and a supported SaaS partner emit JSON events into AWS. Only events with a given source and detail-type should reach a fulfillment AWS Lambda function. Producers must not hard-code every target. The team wants an event bus with pattern routing, not a durable work queue for a multi-hour backlog. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Put events on Amazon EventBridge and use rules that match source and detail-type.
B. Use a single Amazon SQS queue as the account event bus.
C. Use Amazon SNS without filter policies so every subscriber receives all SaaS events.
D. Use Amazon MQ brokers as the only way to match JSON fields.

questions.explain: EventBridge routes by rule patterns on source and detail-type and decouples producers from targets. SQS is a queue, not a pattern-matching bus.
questions.good_to_know: SNS subscription filters would fit attribute-based fanout on a topic. AppFlow is managed SaaS data transfer, not per-event routing.

questions.q: A plant control API produces work items that workers on Amazon ECS must drain after a multi-hour outage. Delivery can be at-least-once, and workers must scale independently of the API. Other applications already consume domain events from a bus, but the plant backlog itself must be a durable work queue rather than that bus. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon EventBridge as the only store for the multi-hour backlog.
B. Use AWS Step Functions Express as the durable plant queue.
C. Buffer plant work in Amazon SQS for the workers.
D. Use Amazon CloudWatch alarm history as the work queue.

questions.explain: SQS is the durable buffer for work that must wait through an outage. EventBridge routes events; this lesson distinguishes that bus from a work queue.
questions.good_to_know: Keep EventBridge for pattern routing of the same business events to other targets. Step Functions orchestrates workflows; it is not a replacement queue.

questions.q: A lending process in AWS waits days for a human approval, then branches on risk score, retries a credit check, and must show operators a visible execution history. AWS Lambda cannot stay running for the wait. A queue alone cannot model those branches and waits as a single coordinated process. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Keep one Amazon SQS message in flight for the entire week.
B. Orchestrate the process with AWS Step Functions.
C. Chain Amazon SNS topics as the approval state machine.
D. Use Amazon EventBridge as a workflow engine with built-in human waits.

questions.explain: Step Functions is the state-machine orchestrator for long workflows with waits, branches, retries, and visible history. SQS does not record that business process state.
questions.good_to_know: Event-driven choreography on EventBridge would fit if services coordinated through events without a central workflow. Standard Workflows are the long-run shape taught for day-scale waits.

questions.q: A company wants a central state machine to coordinate inventory reserve, payment, and shipping with explicit retries and a single execution history. Teams do not want each service's events to be the source of truth for progress. The process can run longer than a function timeout. Choreography through events alone is not the desired control model. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon EventBridge choreography only, with no central workflow.
B. Use Amazon SQS as the only record of business-process state.
C. Use Amazon SNS fanout as the approval wait.
D. Use AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the steps.

questions.explain: A visible, coordinated process is orchestration with Step Functions. Choreography lets services react to events without a central state machine.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge remains the right bus when the stem prefers choreography and pattern routing. SQS still buffers work inside a step; it is not the workflow engine.

questions.q: A Java application uses JMS against on-premises ActiveMQ and publishes from existing clients. The migration to AWS must keep the broker protocol so those producers are not rewritten to Amazon SQS APIs. The team wants a managed broker in AWS rather than operating ActiveMQ on Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon MQ with ActiveMQ.
B. Use Amazon SQS standard queues as a drop-in JMS broker.
C. Use Amazon EventBridge to speak AMQP to the existing clients.
D. Use AWS Step Functions as the JMS provider.

questions.explain: Amazon MQ is the managed traditional broker for ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ when the constraint is existing JMS or AMQP clients. SQS is not a drop-in JMS broker.
questions.good_to_know: Native SQS or SNS would be preferred once protocol compatibility is no longer required. RabbitMQ on Amazon MQ is the other engine when that protocol is named.

questions.q: A Salesforce operations team must run managed, scheduled transfers of records into Amazon S3 without writing a custom connector. They need SaaS-to-AWS data transfer, not an application event bus and not a worker queue. The records are bulk extracts rather than individual JSON events that must be pattern-routed. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon EventBridge partner events as the bulk extract of every record.
B. Use Amazon SQS to pull the Salesforce database over HTTP.
C. Use Amazon AppFlow to transfer the Salesforce data to Amazon S3.
D. Use Amazon MQ to batch Salesforce objects into Amazon S3.

questions.explain: AppFlow is managed data transfer between supported SaaS and AWS services. EventBridge routes events; it is not a bulk Salesforce extract.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge partner integrations would be correct for routing individual SaaS events by pattern. SQS would buffer work after a transfer, not perform it.

questions.q: An image pipeline on Amazon ECS has many identical workers that should share a backlog so each image is processed once. Fan-out to every worker would duplicate work. The producer API must not wait on a worker. Messages must persist if workers are scaled to zero overnight. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Publish each image to Amazon SNS with a subscription per worker.
B. Place images on one Amazon SQS queue that the workers poll.
C. Use Amazon EventBridge to deliver each image to every worker.
D. Use AWS Step Functions to copy the image to every worker.

questions.explain: Competing consumers on one SQS queue share work so each message is processed once (at-least-once). SNS fanout would copy the image to every worker.
questions.good_to_know: SNS plus a queue per distinct service is the fanout pattern when every team must see every event. Identical workers should compete on one queue.

questions.q: Security findings from AWS services, a custom fraud application, and a supported SaaS product must all route by pattern to different targets in one account. Each producer must not list every destination. The team wants an event bus, not a durable worker queue and not CloudWatch as the router. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon SQS as the account-wide event bus.
B. Use Amazon CloudWatch Logs as the event router.
C. Use Amazon AppFlow to route individual security findings in real time.
D. Use Amazon EventBridge with rules on a shared event bus.

questions.explain: EventBridge is built for AWS, custom, and SaaS events with pattern rules. SQS and CloudWatch Logs are not that bus.
questions.good_to_know: AppFlow would be correct for scheduled SaaS-to-AWS data movement. Put a queue behind a rule when a target needs its own backlog.

questions.q: A finance team needs a nightly report to start at 02:00 and then run a multi-step workflow with branches and retries. That start time is a schedule, not a multi-day plant backlog. Operators still need visible workflow history after the schedule fires. Amazon SQS delay seconds are not the daily clock. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon EventBridge scheduling to start an AWS Step Functions workflow.
B. Use Amazon SQS delay queues as the only daily cron at 02:00.
C. Use Amazon MQ to fire a broker alarm at 02:00.
D. Use Amazon AppFlow as the cron scheduler for the state machine.

questions.explain: EventBridge provides scheduling; Step Functions then orchestrates the report. SQS delay is not a daily cron, and AppFlow is SaaS data transfer.
questions.good_to_know: SQS would still buffer individual report tasks inside a state if workers need a backlog. Do not treat EventBridge as the durable queue for plant outages.

questions.q: Producers on an ecommerce API publish order events to a topic. Inventory should not receive marketing events, and marketing should not receive restock events. Each team already has its own Amazon SQS queue. The company wants filtering at the subscription rather than in every worker, and CloudWatch must not rewrite attributes. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Share one unfiltered Amazon SQS queue between inventory and marketing.
B. Use AWS Step Functions to drop events after they reach every worker.
C. Attach SNS filter policies on each queue subscription.
D. Use Amazon CloudWatch to rewrite message attributes on the topic.

questions.explain: SNS filtering on each subscription delivers only matching events to that team's queue. A shared unfiltered queue mixes both streams.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge rules would be the equivalent control on a bus using source and detail-type. CloudWatch is not a message filter.

questions.q: An ecommerce API must notify billing, fulfillment, and analytics for every order. Each team must keep an independent backlog during outages and retry at its own rate. The producer will publish once and must not call the three systems synchronously. Competing consumers on one queue would split orders instead of copying them. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon SNS topic for order events.
B. Use one Amazon SQS queue and have all consumers compete for the same messages.
C. Subscribe a dedicated Amazon SQS queue for each consumer service.
D. Call billing, fulfillment, and analytics synchronously from the API.
E. Store orders only in AWS Step Functions execution input without a topic.

questions.explain: SNS fans the event out; a queue per consumer is the durable, independently retried backlog. Competing on one queue would split orders, not copy them.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge plus targets would be the pair if routing were by event pattern across many sources. Step Functions would orchestrate a single ordered process instead of independent consumers.

questions.q: A brokerage platform already has workers that consume Amazon SQS. It must process each account's trades in order and suppress duplicate submissions of the same trade. Trades for different accounts may run in parallel. A standard queue would not provide that per-account contract. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use an Amazon SQS standard queue for strict per-account order.
B. Create an Amazon SQS FIFO queue.
C. Use Amazon EventBridge to guarantee global FIFO across all accounts.
D. Set the message group ID to the account identifier.
E. Use an Amazon SNS standard topic as the ordered trade log.

questions.explain: FIFO supplies order and deduplication; the message group ID is the per-account ordering key that still allows other accounts to proceed.
questions.good_to_know: A standard queue plus idempotent consumers is the high-scale path when order is not required. EventBridge does not replace FIFO message groups.

questions.q: Workers on Amazon ECS poll an Amazon SQS queue. Malformed messages keep failing the consumer and delaying healthy work. After a bounded number of failed receives, those messages must move aside for inspection and possible replay. Raising visibility timeout alone must not be the isolation design. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Raise visibility timeout to the maximum and never use a DLQ.
B. Use Amazon CloudWatch to rewrite failed payloads in place.
C. Attach a dead-letter queue to the source queue.
D. Replace the queue with Amazon AppFlow.
E. Set maxReceiveCount so poison messages move after failed retries.

questions.explain: The DLQ is the isolation destination; maxReceiveCount is how many failed receives occur before the move. Visibility timeout alone does not drain poison messages.
questions.good_to_know: Tune visibility timeout so healthy messages are not copied to the DLQ while still in flight. CloudWatch does not redrive SQS.

questions.q: Custom application events and a supported SaaS integration must reach different Lambda and queue targets according to source and detail-type. Producers must not maintain a list of destinations. The bus is not a substitute for a worker backlog, and CloudWatch dashboards must not route events. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Put events on Amazon EventBridge.
B. Use Amazon SQS as the pattern-matching event bus.
C. Use Amazon CloudWatch dashboards to route JSON events.
D. Use Amazon MQ as the only SaaS event integration.
E. Create rules that match source and detail-type and route to targets.

questions.explain: EventBridge is the bus; rules are the pattern/source routing. SQS and CloudWatch are not that router.
questions.good_to_know: Subscribe an SQS queue as a rule target when a consumer needs a durable backlog. Amazon MQ remains the legacy-protocol answer.

questions.q: An insurance claim process in AWS waits days for an adjuster, then branches on fraud score and retries a document check. Operators need a visible execution history. Keeping a function running for the wait is not allowed, and a queue visibility timeout must not be the workflow engine. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Keep an AWS Lambda function running for days to remember the approval.
B. Create an AWS Step Functions state machine for the claim flow.
C. Use wait and choice states for the human delay and fraud branch.
D. Use Amazon SQS visibility timeout as the multi-day workflow engine.
E. Use Amazon SNS filtering as the audit history.

questions.explain: Step Functions is the orchestrator; wait and choice states are how long delays and branches are modeled with visible history.
questions.good_to_know: Choreography on EventBridge would be the alternative if services coordinated through events without a central machine. SQS still buffers work inside a state.

questions.q: Existing clients speak JMS or AMQP to a self-managed broker in a data center. The move to AWS must keep those protocols. The team will not rewrite producers to Amazon SQS or Amazon SNS in this change, and it will not operate the broker on unmanaged Amazon EC2. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Rewrite all clients to Amazon SQS APIs in the same change.
B. Use Amazon EventBridge as a JMS provider.
C. Use Amazon AppFlow as the message broker.
D. Provision Amazon MQ using ActiveMQ or RabbitMQ.
E. Point the existing JMS or AMQP clients at the broker.

questions.explain: Amazon MQ is the managed traditional broker; keeping client protocols is the second required step. SQS and EventBridge are not JMS providers.
questions.good_to_know: After a later rewrite, native SQS or SNS would usually be simpler. AppFlow transfers SaaS data; it is not a broker.

questions.q: A company must copy supported SaaS records into Amazon S3 on a schedule without custom connector code. The need is managed data transfer, not an event bus and not a worker queue. Individual JSON events do not need pattern routing for this bulk extract. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use Amazon AppFlow for the SaaS-to-S3 transfer.
B. Choose a supported SaaS source and Amazon S3 as the destination.
C. Use Amazon SQS to extract the full SaaS database.
D. Use Amazon EventBridge rules as a bulk nightly dump of all records.
E. Use Amazon MQ to copy SaaS tables into Amazon S3.

questions.explain: AppFlow is the managed transfer service; picking a supported source and S3 as destination is how that transfer is configured.
questions.good_to_know: EventBridge would route individual SaaS events by pattern. SQS would buffer downstream processing after the files land in S3.

questions.q: A retail company runs an order API on Amazon EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer in a single AWS Region. The database is Amazon RDS with Multi-AZ enabled, and an Availability Zone outage last year caused no customer impact. Compliance now requires the workload to recover if the entire Region fails, with at most one hour of data loss. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Replicate data to a second Region and keep a regional failover runbook.
B. Add Auto Scaling across more Availability Zones in the same Region only.
C. Move the RDS instance to a larger class in the same Region.
D. Replace the Application Load Balancer with a Gateway Load Balancer.

questions.explain: The new failure domain is a whole Region. Multi-AZ high availability stays inside one Region, so recovery needs a second-Region copy and a failover plan.
questions.good_to_know: More AZs, a larger RDS class, or a different load-balancer type would still be in-Region high availability. They would be right if the stem only required surviving an Availability Zone failure.

questions.q: A payments team says that after a regional disaster the application may lose at most 5 minutes of committed transactions. Operators may take several hours to restore compute. The company wants the MOST cost-effective design that still meets that data-loss limit and will not run a second production fleet. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run a full-capacity active-active stack that already serves users in two Regions.
B. Keep a scaled-down but fully functional application fleet running in the second Region.
C. Copy data to a second Region at least every 5 minutes and rebuild compute from templates.
D. Take weekly Amazon EBS snapshots in the primary Region only.

questions.explain: Five minutes of acceptable data loss is the recovery point objective. Frequent cross-Region copies satisfy RPO while hours of restore time allow backup/restore compute instead of a standing second fleet.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby or active-active would be correct if the stem also demanded minutes-level restore time or near-zero downtime. Weekly same-Region snapshots miss both the RPO and the regional failure domain.

questions.q: A hospital portal can lose up to 24 hours of nonclinical analytics data. After a regional outage the portal must be usable again within 15 minutes. Finance will not pay for two full-capacity production Regions. A smaller copy of the application must already pass health checks, then scale out. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Store daily backups in the primary Region and rebuild the VPC after a disaster.
B. Run a warm standby in a second Region and scale it out at failover.
C. Use Multi-AZ Auto Scaling in the primary Region as the only recovery plan.
D. Run multi-site active-active at full capacity in two Regions.

questions.explain: A 15-minute restore time needs a stack that is already running, which is warm standby. A 24-hour data-loss window does not justify paying for a second full production site.
questions.good_to_know: Backup and restore would fit if RTO were measured in hours or a day. Active-active would fit if both sites had to serve users already and cost were secondary. In-Region Multi-AZ does not recover a failed Region.

questions.q: A monthly reporting job runs on Amazon EC2 and writes results to Amazon EBS. The company can lose up to 24 hours of reports and can wait a day to restore the job after a Region failure. Leadership wants the LOWEST ongoing disaster recovery cost and will not keep spare instances running. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Keep a warm standby of the reporting fleet running in a second Region.
B. Run the reporting job as active-active in two Regions at all times.
C. Place the instances in three Availability Zones in the primary Region only.
D. Copy AWS Backup recovery points to a second Region and restore them after a disaster.

questions.explain: Long recovery point and restore times plus minimum standby cost select backup and restore. Warm standby and active-active pay for running capacity the RTO does not require.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby would be the answer if the job had to resume in minutes. Multi-AZ placement is high availability in one Region, not a regional recovery site.

questions.q: A SaaS vendor must recover from a Region failure with a low recovery point objective. It will pay for replicated data and a small core of always-on services in a second Region, but it will not run a full application stack there until failover. Application instances will launch from templates after the disaster is declared. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use a pilot-light design: keep core data ready and scale remaining compute at failover.
B. Use backup and restore with weekly snapshots and no standing replica.
C. Use warm standby with a fully functional scaled-down application stack always running.
D. Use multi-site active-active with both Regions serving production users.

questions.explain: Core data and essential services kept ready, with the rest of compute launched at disaster time, is pilot light. That is warmer than backup-only and cooler than a working scaled-down fleet.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby would be correct if a smaller full application stack already had to pass health checks. Weekly backups would miss a low RPO. Active-active would be correct if both sites already served users.

questions.q: A business service needs a minutes-level recovery time and a very low recovery point in a second AWS Region. The company cannot fund a duplicate full-capacity production fleet. A smaller copy of the application must already be running and able to pass health checks, then grow after failover. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Keep only database replication and launch every application instance after the disaster.
B. Copy nightly backups to the second Region and create the VPC when needed.
C. Deploy a warm standby stack in the second Region and scale it on failover.
D. Serve all users from both Regions at full production capacity.

questions.explain: A smaller but fully functional environment that is already running is warm standby. Pilot light keeps only the core, so provisioning the rest can miss a minutes-level RTO.
questions.good_to_know: Pilot light would be correct if only core data services had to run until failover and a longer scale-out were acceptable. Active-active would be correct if both Regions already had to serve production traffic.

questions.q: A payments company runs a revenue platform on Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS in one AWS Region. The platform requires near-zero recovery time and data loss if that Region fails. Both sites must already serve production users. The company accepts the highest operating cost. Backups and standby scale-out would violate those objectives. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use backup and restore with infrastructure as code in a second Region.
B. Run multi-site active-active with replicated data and health-based traffic steering.
C. Keep a pilot light of the database only and launch the API after failover.
D. Run a warm standby at reduced size that is not in DNS until a disaster.

questions.explain: Near-zero RTO and RPO with both sites already serving users is active-active. Backup, pilot light, and warm standby all require startup or scaling that breaks that objective.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby would be correct if a minutes-level RTO and a scaled-down idle stack were enough. Pilot light and backup/restore fit longer RTOs at lower cost.

questions.q: A company uses AWS Backup for Amazon EBS volumes and Amazon EFS file systems in the US East (N. Virginia) Region. A regional disaster requirement says recovery must still be possible if that Region is unavailable. The recovery point may be measured in hours. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Increase snapshot frequency in US East (N. Virginia) only.
B. Enable Amazon EBS Multi-Attach on every volume.
C. Store extra copies of each volume on instance store of the same instances.
D. Copy recovery points on a schedule to a backup vault in a second Region.

questions.explain: A Region failure makes in-Region snapshots unreachable. Cross-Region copies of AWS Backup recovery points provide a restore source in another Region.
questions.good_to_know: More frequent same-Region snapshots would tighten RPO only while that Region still works. Multi-Attach and instance store do not create a second-Region recovery copy.

questions.q: Compliance requires that backups of production Amazon EBS volumes and Amazon RDS databases remain restorable if the workload AWS account is compromised and resources are deleted. Copies must not exist only in that account. The company already uses AWS Backup in the production account. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy recovery points to a backup vault in a separate AWS account.
B. Keep additional snapshots in the same account in a second Availability Zone.
C. Enable RDS Multi-AZ in the production account.
D. Store snapshot identifiers in Amazon DynamoDB in the same account.

questions.explain: Cross-account backup copies reduce blast radius when credentials in the workload account can delete local snapshots. Same-account Multi-AZ or extra AZs still sit inside the compromised account.
questions.good_to_know: Cross-Region copies in the same account help a regional outage but not an account wipe. Pair cross-account with cross-Region when the stem demands both failure domains.

questions.q: A company copies Amazon EBS snapshots of its application volumes to a second Region every night. Auditors found that nobody has ever launched an instance from those snapshots. The disaster recovery plan must prove that restores work before the next audit, not only that snapshot jobs completed. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Increase snapshot retention from 7 days to 35 days.
B. Enable Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling in the primary Region.
C. Restore a snapshot in the standby Region and boot the application.
D. Add a DisasterRecovery tag to every snapshot copy.

questions.explain: Untested backups are not a recovery plan. A scheduled restore that boots the application is the proof auditors asked for.
questions.good_to_know: Longer retention helps how long you can go back, not whether a restore works. Tags and in-Region Auto Scaling do not exercise the standby Region.

questions.q: An application has a primary Application Load Balancer in us-east-1 and a recovery load balancer in us-west-2. When the primary Region is unhealthy, DNS must answer with the recovery endpoint only. Weighted experiments, latency-based Region choice, and splitting traffic in normal operation are not the goal. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create a Route 53 weighted policy that sends half of answers to each Region.
B. Create a Route 53 failover pair with a health check on the primary endpoint.
C. Create a Route 53 latency policy for both load balancers.
D. Create an Auto Scaling group that spans both Regions.

questions.explain: Active/passive DNS with a health check is Route 53 failover. Weighted and latency policies steer for split or nearest Region, not primary-then-secondary.
questions.good_to_know: Weighted routing would be correct for a 90/10 release. Latency routing would be correct if users should land in the lowest-latency healthy Region. Auto Scaling groups do not span Regions.

questions.q: A web fleet runs on Amazon EC2 in three Availability Zones behind an Application Load Balancer in one AWS Region. Instances sometimes fail target-group health checks. The company needs replacement capacity automatically in the same Region and does not have a second-Region disaster requirement. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy nightly AMI backups to a second Region and wait for a disaster declaration.
B. Create a Route 53 failover record to a different AWS account.
C. Convert the fleet to a single instance that uses instance store.
D. Use an Auto Scaling group that replaces unhealthy instances behind the load balancer.

questions.explain: Instance-level failure in one Region is Auto Scaling replacement plus a load balancer that routes around unhealthy targets. That is high availability automation, not regional disaster recovery.
questions.good_to_know: Route 53 failover and cross-Region AMIs would appear if the stem required a second Region. A single instance store host is the opposite of automated replacement.

questions.q: A company uses backup and restore for a noncritical application on Amazon EC2. After a Region failure, operators previously rebuilt subnets, security groups, and Auto Scaling groups by clicking in the console, which missed the recovery time objective. Data backups already exist in the second Region. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Define the recovery stack in infrastructure as code and deploy it at failover.
B. Keep a full active-active production fleet in the second Region.
C. Increase RDS Multi-AZ capacity in the failed Region.
D. Store console screenshots of the architecture in Amazon S3.

questions.explain: Backup/restore RTO depends on how fast the empty Region can be rebuilt. Infrastructure as code makes that rebuild repeatable instead of console drift.
questions.good_to_know: Active-active would be correct if near-zero RTO required standing production in both Regions. Growing Multi-AZ in a Region that is already down does not help recovery.

questions.q: A company maintains a warm standby web fleet in the Europe (Ireland) Region. During a game-day test, Auto Scaling could not launch enough Amazon EC2 instances because the account was already at the On-Demand instance quota there. Production failover would have missed the recovery time objective. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use a cluster placement group in the primary Region only.
B. Disable Auto Scaling in the standby Region to conserve quota.
C. Request a quota increase in the standby Region before a real disaster.
D. Move the warm standby into the same Availability Zone as production.

questions.explain: Service quotas are per Region. A standby that cannot scale to production size fails RTO even if the architecture pattern is correct.
questions.good_to_know: Placement groups and disabling Auto Scaling do not raise the standby Region limit. Quotas must be requested and tested before a real disaster.

questions.q: A payments API on Amazon EC2 must keep processing authorizations if a single instance or a single Availability Zone fails, with no operator restore from backup. A full AWS Region failure is out of scope, and the company will not build a second Region for this workload. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy weekly backups to a second Region and restore them after every instance failure.
B. Run a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group behind a load balancer so remaining capacity keeps serving.
C. Keep a pilot-light database in another Region with no in-Region redundancy.
D. Use Route 53 failover to a static error page as the only availability control.

questions.explain: Surviving instance and AZ failure without a restore is in-Region high availability: redundant AZs, a load balancer, and Auto Scaling. Regional DR patterns are the wrong failure domain here.
questions.good_to_know: Pilot light, cross-Region backups, and DNS failover to an error page would appear if the stem required a regional disaster plan. They do not keep the API processing during an AZ outage.

questions.q: An Amazon RDS database already uses Multi-AZ and survived an Availability Zone outage with automatic failover. A new requirement is to recover if the entire Region becomes unavailable, with hours of acceptable restore time. The team wants a managed copy rather than a second writer in production. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add another Multi-AZ standby in a third Availability Zone of the same Region.
B. Convert the Multi-AZ deployment to Single-AZ to free quota.
C. Increase allocated storage on the primary instance.
D. Add a cross-Region backup or replica and a restore or promotion plan in a second Region.

questions.explain: Multi-AZ is high availability inside one Region. A Region-level disaster needs a copy outside that Region, which backups or a cross-Region replica provide.
questions.good_to_know: Extra in-Region Multi-AZ capacity would still fail with the Region. A cross-Region read replica promoted at failover is the warmer form of the same regional-DR idea.

questions.q: A compliance application on Amazon RDS may lose at most 15 minutes of data if a Region fails, but the application tier on Amazon EC2 may take 4 hours to rebuild. The company will not run application servers in the second Region until a disaster is declared. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy the database to the second Region at least every 15 minutes and rebuild compute later.
B. Run a full active-active application in both Regions at all times.
C. Keep application servers as a warm standby but back up the database only weekly.
D. Use Multi-AZ RDS only, with no second-Region copy of the data.

questions.explain: Recovery point and recovery time are independent. Tight RPO drives frequent cross-Region data copies; a 4-hour RTO allows compute to be rebuilt instead of kept warm.
questions.good_to_know: Warm application capacity would be correct if the 4-hour rebuild missed RTO. Weekly database backups would miss the 15-minute RPO. Multi-AZ alone is not regional DR.

questions.q: A company currently takes nightly AWS Backup jobs of Amazon EBS volumes to a second Region. A new product owner says the workload may lose at most 15 minutes of data. Restore time may still be several hours, and the company does not want a second live application fleet. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Switch to multi-site active-active at full capacity in two Regions.
B. Keep nightly backups and add a cluster placement group in the primary Region.
C. Take backups or replicas at least every 15 minutes into the second Region.
D. Disable backups and rely on Multi-AZ EC2 only.

questions.explain: Nightly copies imply up to a day of data loss. A 15-minute RPO requires more frequent backups or replication; hours of RTO still allow backup/restore compute.
questions.good_to_know: Active-active would be correct if restore time also had to be near zero. Placement groups and dropping backups do not tighten the recovery point.

questions.q: A noncritical batch application on Amazon EC2 can lose 24 hours of data and can be down for a day after a Region failure. The company wants the LOWEST standby cost and a tested path to rebuild the stack in another Region. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Copy AWS Backup recovery points to a second Region on a daily schedule.
B. Run a full-capacity active-active fleet in both Regions at all times.
C. Keep infrastructure as code templates and a restore runbook for the second Region.
D. Keep a warm standby Auto Scaling group at half of production size.
E. Disable all backups in both Regions to reduce ongoing cost.

questions.explain: Long RPO and RTO select backup/restore: cross-Region recovery points plus a repeatable rebuild. Standing warm or active-active capacity is extra cost.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby would be jointly correct if the stem required a minutes-level RTO. Turning backups off would remove the only recovery copy.

questions.q: Core databases must already exist in a second AWS Region so data loss stays in minutes. Application Auto Scaling groups should be created only after failover is declared. The company will not pay for a fully functional scaled-down web tier that runs all month. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Serve half of production users from the second Region continuously.
B. Replicate the database or keep a small replica running in the second Region.
C. Use only weekly full backups with no standing data store in the second Region.
D. Launch remaining application Auto Scaling groups from templates when disaster is declared.
E. Place all production instances in one Availability Zone to simplify failover.

questions.explain: Pilot light keeps core data ready and scales the rest of compute at disaster time. Those two steps are jointly necessary for this cost and RPO mix.
questions.good_to_know: Continuous user traffic from the second Region is active-active. Weekly backups alone would miss a minutes-level RPO. A single AZ weakens the primary site without building a pilot light.

questions.q: A customer-support portal on Amazon EC2 needs a minutes-level recovery time in a second Region and a very low recovery point. Finance will not fund a second full-capacity site. A smaller stack must already be healthy, then grow after DNS failover. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Leave the second Region empty except for AMI copies in Amazon S3.
B. Use Multi-AZ in the primary Region as the only recovery plan.
C. Deploy a scaled-down but fully functional stack in the second Region.
D. Delete the primary stack and run only in the standby Region.
E. Configure Route 53 failover to that stack and scale it out after failover.

questions.explain: Warm standby is a smaller live stack plus a health-aware cutover and scale-out. AMI copies with no running stack are backup/restore, which is too cold for minutes-level RTO.
questions.good_to_know: Multi-AZ in the primary Region still fails with that Region. Running only in the standby Region is a migration, not a dual-site recovery design.

questions.q: A trading portal on Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS requires near-zero recovery time and data loss if one AWS Region fails. Both sites must already serve production users, and the company accepts the highest cost. Scale-out after a disaster would be too slow. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Run production stacks in two Regions with continuous data replication.
B. Keep the second Region at zero compute until an incident ticket is filed.
C. Rely on daily snapshots in a single Region as the only copy.
D. Pin both stacks to one Availability Zone to reduce replication lag.
E. Use Route 53 latency or weighted routing with health checks for both Regions.

questions.explain: Active-active needs live capacity and data in two Regions plus health-aware DNS so clients already use both sites and drop an unhealthy one.
questions.good_to_know: Zero compute until a ticket is pilot light or backup/restore. Daily single-Region snapshots miss both RPO and the regional failure domain.

questions.q: Production Amazon EBS volumes and Amazon RDS instances must remain restorable after two events: the workload AWS account is compromised, and the primary Region is unavailable. A single AWS Backup plan already covers those resource types in the production account. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Store the only snapshots in the production account in the same Region.
B. Configure the plan to copy recovery points to a second AWS Region.
C. Copy those recovery points into a backup vault in a separate AWS account.
D. Enable RDS Multi-AZ as the sole blast-radius control.
E. Publish backups to a public Amazon S3 bucket.

questions.explain: Region failure needs a copy outside the primary Region. Account compromise needs a copy outside the workload account. AWS Backup can do both copies.
questions.good_to_know: RDS Multi-AZ is in-Region high availability, not an isolated backup vault. A public bucket would expose backup data rather than shrink blast radius.

questions.q: A company has a documented warm-standby design for an Amazon EC2 web app in a second Region. Game days have never restored a backup or scaled the standby to production size. The next audit requires proof that failover would meet the recovery time objective. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Skip restore tests if the backup job status shows completed.
B. Lower primary Region quotas so failover is forced every week.
C. Use instance store as the only backup target.
D. Restore a backup in the standby Region and verify the application starts.
E. Confirm standby Region quotas can support the recovered fleet size.

questions.explain: A recovery plan is reliable only if restores are tested and the standby Region can actually launch the scaled-out size. Completed backup jobs do not prove either.
questions.good_to_know: Quota cuts in the primary Region are not a test strategy. Instance store is ephemeral and is not a backup target.

questions.q: A web API must fail over from a primary Application Load Balancer in one Region to a recovery load balancer in a second Region when the primary endpoint is unhealthy. Operators must not split traffic 50/50 in normal operation. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create a Route 53 failover routing policy with primary and secondary records.
B. Associate a health check with the primary so DNS fails over when it is unhealthy.
C. Use geolocation routing as the active-passive mechanism.
D. Set a weighted 50/50 split with no health checks.
E. Point both records at load balancers in the same Availability Zone.

questions.explain: Active/passive DNS is failover records plus a health check on the primary. Weighted 50/50 is a split, not a standby. Geolocation steers by user location.
questions.good_to_know: Weighted routing with health checks would be correct for a canary or active-active share. Same-AZ endpoints would not be a regional recovery pair.

questions.q: A media company stores public product images in Amazon S3 in one AWS Region. Viewers on several continents report high download latency. The company wants HTTP caching at edge locations and does not want to turn the bucket into a static website endpoint or change the object keys. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin.
B. Create a Route 53 geolocation policy that points to the bucket website endpoint.
C. Create an AWS Global Accelerator accelerator in front of the S3 REST endpoint.
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and keep serving only from the bucket URL.

questions.explain: Global HTTP cache for static objects is CloudFront with an S3 origin. Route 53 only answers DNS. Global Accelerator is not a cache and does not take S3 as an endpoint.
questions.good_to_know: Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance transfers to S3; it is not the CDN caching pattern. Global Accelerator would appear if clients needed static anycast IPs for TCP or UDP, not object caching.

questions.q: A company serves media from Amazon S3 through Amazon CloudFront. The bucket must stay private. Users must not download objects by calling Amazon S3 directly, even if they guess an object key. Signed viewer URLs are not required because this catalog is public at the CloudFront URL. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable the S3 website endpoint and make every object public.
B. Create a Route 53 latency record that points to the S3 bucket.
C. Use origin access control and a bucket policy that allows only CloudFront.
D. Attach AWS Global Accelerator as the front door to the S3 bucket.

questions.explain: Origin access control lets CloudFront fetch from S3 while the bucket policy denies direct public access, so viewers cannot bypass the CDN.
questions.good_to_know: A public website endpoint would allow S3 bypass. Route 53 and Global Accelerator do not keep an S3 origin private. Signed URLs would appear if each viewer needed time-limited authorization.

questions.q: A training portal uses Amazon CloudFront in front of a private Amazon S3 bucket. Each learner may download one video file for 2 hours after purchase. The bucket must stay private. The company does not want IAM users for learners and will not make the object public. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Make the object public-read for 2 hours using a bucket ACL.
B. Issue a CloudFront signed URL that expires after 2 hours for that object.
C. Create an IAM user per learner with AWS Management Console access.
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and email the object key.

questions.explain: CloudFront signed URLs grant time-limited access to a private object through the CDN without IAM users or a public bucket.
questions.good_to_know: S3 presigned URLs (Lesson 04) would apply if there were no CloudFront distribution. Signed cookies would be better if the learner needed a whole path of files, not one object.

questions.q: A course platform streams many private HLS segments under one CloudFront path prefix from a private Amazon S3 bucket. Issuing a signed URL per segment is too operationally heavy. Viewers should access the whole path for a limited time after login. The origin must stay private. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Issue one S3 presigned URL for the first segment only.
B. Open the bucket with a wildcard principal for s3:GetObject.
C. Use Route 53 weighted routing to hide the origin.
D. Issue CloudFront signed cookies that grant access to the path prefix.

questions.explain: Signed cookies authorize many objects under a path through CloudFront. A single S3 presigned URL covers one object and is the wrong layer when the CDN is in front.
questions.good_to_know: Signed URLs would be correct for one file at a time. A public bucket policy would violate the private-origin constraint. DNS routing is not authorization.

questions.q: An Amazon CloudFront distribution caches product pages from an Application Load Balancer origin. The cache hit ratio is poor because a unique request header that the origin does not use is part of the cache key. Origin CPU is high, and the team does not want to lower TTL to 1 second. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Remove the unused header from the CloudFront cache policy.
B. Lower the maximum TTL to 1 second.
C. Add AWS Global Accelerator in front of CloudFront.
D. Switch the origin from the load balancer to an S3 website endpoint.

questions.explain: Values in the cache key create cache variants. An unused unique header prevents reuse; removing it from the cache policy lets requests share objects.
questions.good_to_know: A 1-second TTL would reduce hits further. Global Accelerator does not fix HTTP cache keys. Changing the origin type does not remove the extra key field.

questions.q: A marketing site uses Amazon CloudFront with an Amazon S3 origin. A CSS file was overwritten under the same object key. The cache TTL is 24 hours, but the broken style must disappear worldwide within minutes. Versioned file names are not in use yet. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Lower the Route 53 TTL on the alias record to the distribution.
B. Enable origin access control on the distribution.
C. Create a CloudFront invalidation for the CSS object path.
D. Change the origin from S3 to an Application Load Balancer.

questions.explain: Invalidation tells CloudFront to drop a cached object before TTL expiry so edges fetch the new CSS. DNS TTL does not control HTTP cache contents.
questions.good_to_know: Versioned object keys would avoid invalidation on the next deploy. Origin access control is a privacy control, not a freshness control. Route 53 TTL only affects how long resolvers cache the CloudFront domain name.

questions.q: An API on an Application Load Balancer sits behind Amazon CloudFront and returns JSON that may be reused for 60 seconds. The team wants fewer origin requests without serving day-old responses. Invalidating the distribution every minute is not acceptable, and DNS must not be the cache. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Set the TTL to 7 days and never invalidate.
B. Set the CloudFront cache TTL for those paths to 60 seconds.
C. Disable caching and use Route 53 latency routing only.
D. Replace CloudFront with AWS Global Accelerator so responses cache at the anycast layer.

questions.explain: TTL is how long CloudFront may reuse a response. Sixty seconds matches the freshness window without a 7-day stale cache or a no-cache design.
questions.good_to_know: Global Accelerator is not a content cache. Route 53 latency routing chooses a Region; it does not cache HTTP bodies. A long TTL would need invalidation or versioned URLs when content must change sooner.

questions.q: A company hosts a dynamic web application on Amazon EC2 behind an Application Load Balancer in one Region. Global users need HTTPS at the edge and optional caching of some paths. The origin must remain the load balancer, not a copy of HTML in Amazon S3. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create a CloudFront distribution that uses only an S3 bucket of HTML copies.
B. Point Route 53 geolocation records directly at each instance public IP.
C. Put AWS Global Accelerator in front of an Amazon S3 bucket.
D. Create a CloudFront distribution that uses the Application Load Balancer as origin.

questions.explain: CloudFront origins include Application Load Balancers. That keeps the dynamic app as origin while the edge handles HTTPS and optional caching.
questions.good_to_know: An S3-only origin would serve static copies, not the live ALB app. Global Accelerator in front of S3 is the wrong protocol and origin pairing. Geolocation to instance IPs skips both the load balancer and the CDN.

questions.q: A multiplayer game uses a custom TCP protocol on Amazon EC2 behind Network Load Balancers in two AWS Regions. Clients must be configured with two fixed IP addresses. Failover must not wait for DNS resolver caches. HTTP caching is not required for this protocol. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Place AWS Global Accelerator in front of the Regional Network Load Balancers.
B. Place Amazon CloudFront in front of the TCP game protocol.
C. Use Route 53 failover with a 300-second TTL as the only cutover.
D. Assign public IPv4 addresses from S3 Transfer Acceleration to the game servers.

questions.explain: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and shifts TCP traffic to healthy Regional endpoints over the AWS backbone without waiting on DNS TTL. CloudFront is an HTTP CDN, not a Layer 4 TCP proxy for a custom game protocol.
questions.good_to_know: Route 53 failover would work if DNS cache delay were acceptable and clients did not need fixed IPs. CloudFront would be correct for HTTP(S) content delivery, not this TCP game.

questions.q: A voice application uses UDP to Regional Network Load Balancers in two AWS Regions. The company wants traffic to enter AWS on static anycast IP addresses and ride the AWS global network to a healthy Regional endpoint. Content caching is not required for the voice packets. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon CloudFront with a long cache TTL for the UDP flows.
B. Use Route 53 geolocation without health checks on the endpoints.
C. Use AWS Global Accelerator with health checks on the NLB endpoints.
D. Use an S3 Multi-Region Access Point in front of the UDP listeners.

questions.explain: UDP plus static anycast IPs and health-based Regional failover is Global Accelerator. CloudFront caches HTTP; it is not a UDP anycast front door.
questions.good_to_know: Route 53 geolocation would steer DNS by country but would not give static anycast IPs or a UDP network-layer path. S3 Multi-Region Access Points are for object storage, not UDP sockets.

questions.q: A B2B API sits behind Application Load Balancers in two Regions. Corporate firewalls allowlist two IP addresses, and corporate DNS caches answers for many minutes. When a Region fails, clients must keep those same IPs and must not wait for DNS caches to expire. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Route 53 failover with a one-hour TTL as the only cutover.
B. Front the Regional load balancers with AWS Global Accelerator anycast IPs.
C. Use CloudFront signed cookies on the API responses.
D. Use Route 53 geoproximity routing with a large bias.

questions.explain: Allowlisted static IPs plus failover that DNS TTL must not delay is Global Accelerator. Route 53 failover still depends on resolver caches.
questions.good_to_know: A very short Route 53 TTL would reduce DNS delay but would not give two stable allowlisted anycast IPs. Signed cookies authorize CloudFront content; they are not a failover fabric.

questions.q: A company wants 10 percent of DNS answers to go to a new Regional Application Load Balancer and 90 percent to the existing load balancer during a canary. Active-passive failover and lowest-latency Region selection are not the goal. The records should target the two load balancers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create Route 53 failover records with the new load balancer as primary.
B. Create Route 53 latency records for both load balancers.
C. Create a CloudFront cache policy that samples 10 percent of requests.
D. Create Route 53 weighted records with weights 10 and 90.

questions.explain: Proportional DNS distribution is weighted routing. Failover is active/passive. Latency routing picks the lowest-latency Region, not a 10/90 split.
questions.good_to_know: Failover would be correct for primary-then-secondary. Latency would be correct if users should always reach the nearer healthy Region. CloudFront cache policies do not implement DNS percentages.

questions.q: A company hosts a public API on Application Load Balancers in two AWS Regions. Users should reach the Region that offers the lowest latency to them. DNS-based steering is acceptable, and the company does not need a fixed percentage split or an active-passive pair. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create Route 53 latency records for each Regional load balancer.
B. Create Route 53 failover records only.
C. Create Route 53 weighted 50/50 records.
D. Create Route 53 geolocation records that map every country by hand.

questions.explain: Latency-based routing selects the configured resource in the Region with the lowest latency measurement to the user. Weighted 50/50 is a split, not a latency choice.
questions.good_to_know: Geolocation would be correct if the rule were country or continent of the viewer rather than measured latency. Failover would be correct for active-passive priority.

questions.q: A web hostname should use the primary Region unless that Application Load Balancer is unhealthy, then it should use the secondary Region. Weighted splits and latency optimization are not required. The records should target the two load balancers with health evaluation in Route 53. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create Route 53 weighted records with equal weights for both Regions.
B. Create Route 53 latency records for both Regional load balancers.
C. Create Route 53 failover alias records with a health check on primary.
D. Create Route 53 geoproximity records with zero bias on both Regions.

questions.explain: Active/passive DNS with health evaluation is failover routing. Equal weights and latency policies do not express a primary-then-secondary priority.
questions.good_to_know: Weighted routing would be correct for a canary. Latency routing would be correct if the nearest healthy Region should win. Geoproximity would be correct if the team needed a geographic bias around resource locations.

questions.q: A company must serve a country-specific homepage from a Regional origin that holds that country's content. Routing must follow the viewer's geography, not the lowest-latency AWS Region and not a 50/50 DNS split. Both origins already sit behind Application Load Balancers. A default record is allowed. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create Route 53 latency records for each Regional load balancer.
B. Create Route 53 geolocation records that map countries to the right endpoints.
C. Create Route 53 weighted records with equal weights.
D. Create Route 53 failover records with a health check.

questions.explain: Geolocation routing answers based on the location of the DNS query, which is how you pin a country to a specific origin. Latency routing would ignore those content boundaries.
questions.good_to_know: Geoproximity would be closer if the team wanted to bias traffic around resource locations rather than map ISO countries. Failover is active/passive priority, not country mapping.

questions.q: A company wants DNS to prefer a nearby AWS Region for Application Load Balancers in two Regions, but will shift extra traffic toward a new Region that has spare capacity. Country-level content laws are not involved, and a fixed 90/10 weight is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Route 53 geolocation records for each ISO country code.
B. Use Route 53 failover records with a health check on primary.
C. Use CloudFront cache behaviors that vary only by country header.
D. Use Route 53 geoproximity routing with a positive bias on the new Region.

questions.explain: Geoproximity routes by the location of resources and a bias expands or shrinks how much of the map a Region wins. That is the spare-capacity shift without hand-mapping countries.
questions.good_to_know: Geolocation would be correct for country or continent content rules. Weighted routing would be correct for an explicit percentage split. Failover would be correct for active/passive.

questions.q: A company uses Amazon Route 53 to point www.example.com at an Application Load Balancer. Global users still wait on every image because nothing caches HTTP responses. DNS already resolves quickly. The team wants an HTTP delivery path at the edge while keeping the existing hostname. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add Amazon CloudFront as the HTTP path and alias the hostname to the distribution.
B. Change the Route 53 record from an alias to a multivalue answer policy.
C. Lower the Route 53 TTL to 1 second so images cache inside DNS.
D. Add more Route 53 latency records for the same load balancer.

questions.explain: Route 53 answers DNS; it does not cache HTTP bodies. CloudFront is the HTTP path that caches at edge locations. They commonly work together with an alias to the distribution.
questions.good_to_know: A 1-second DNS TTL only changes how long resolvers cache the name. Multivalue and extra latency records still return addresses; they do not become a CDN.

questions.q: A company wants Amazon Route 53 to return several healthy IP addresses for a small fleet and to omit unhealthy ones. It does not need weighted percentages or latency-based Region choice. The fleet is small enough that a full load balancer is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Route 53 failover with a single primary IP.
B. Use Route 53 geolocation with a default record only.
C. Use Route 53 multivalue answer routing with health checks.
D. Use Route 53 weighted routing with one record.

questions.explain: Multivalue answer routing returns multiple healthy records, like DNS round-robin with health checks. It is not a substitute for a load balancer on a large fleet, which this stem excludes.
questions.good_to_know: Failover returns one active endpoint. Weighted routing is for proportions. An Application Load Balancer would be the answer if the stem needed Layer 7 routing or a large fleet.

questions.q: Users worldwide need low-latency downloads from a private Amazon S3 bucket in one Region. The bucket must stay private, and users must not bypass the CDN by calling S3 directly even if they know the object key. Signed viewer URLs are not required. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin.
B. Enable the S3 website endpoint and allow s3:GetObject from 0.0.0.0/0.
C. Use origin access control and a bucket policy that denies direct public access.
D. Point Route 53 latency records at the bucket as the only global control.
E. Attach AWS Global Accelerator to the S3 bucket.

questions.explain: CloudFront caches at the edge. Origin access control plus a restrictive bucket policy keeps S3 private so clients cannot skip the distribution.
questions.good_to_know: S3 website endpoints cannot use origin access control and a public policy would allow bypass. Global Accelerator does not take S3 as an endpoint and does not cache objects.

questions.q: A media site uses Amazon CloudFront in front of Amazon S3. Authorized viewers must open private files for a limited time after login. The bucket must remain private, and the company will not create IAM users for those viewers. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Make the S3 bucket public-read for all objects.
B. Keep the S3 origin private with origin access control.
C. Share IAM access keys with each viewer account.
D. Issue CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies to authorized viewers.
E. Use Route 53 weighted routing as the authorization layer.

questions.explain: Private origin plus CloudFront signed URLs or cookies is the private-content pattern. A public bucket or IAM keys for each viewer would violate the constraints.
questions.good_to_know: Signed URLs fit one object; signed cookies fit a path of objects. Route 53 routing is not an authorization mechanism.

questions.q: An Amazon CloudFront distribution has a low cache hit ratio and a high origin load. A unique unused request header is in the cache key, and the default TTL is 7 days even though the API may be reused for only 2 minutes. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Add every viewer request header to the cache key.
B. Invalidate the entire distribution every second.
C. Remove the unused unique header from the cache policy.
D. Replace CloudFront with Route 53 failover routing.
E. Set cache TTLs near 2 minutes instead of 7 days.

questions.explain: Hit ratio improves when the cache key only includes values that actually change the response, and when TTL matches the freshness window.
questions.good_to_know: Adding more unique headers would worsen fragmentation. Per-second invalidations fight the cache instead of tuning it. Route 53 failover is DNS, not an HTTP cache.

questions.q: A custom TCP application behind Network Load Balancers in two AWS Regions must present two static anycast IP addresses to game clients. Failover must not depend on DNS resolver caches. HTTP caching is not in scope, and clients cannot change IP allowlists. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create AWS Global Accelerator with the Regional load balancers as endpoints.
B. Use Amazon CloudFront as the TCP Layer 4 proxy for the game sockets.
C. Use Route 53 failover with a 1-hour TTL as the only failover path.
D. Use S3 Transfer Acceleration for the custom TCP game sockets.
E. Enable accelerator health checks so traffic shifts without waiting on DNS TTL.

questions.explain: Global Accelerator supplies the anycast IPs and uses health checks to move new connections to a healthy Regional endpoint over the AWS global network.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront is HTTP(S). Route 53 failover still waits on DNS caches. Transfer Acceleration is for S3 transfers, not arbitrary TCP.

questions.q: A website name should use a primary Regional Application Load Balancer unless it is unhealthy, then a secondary load balancer in another Region. The company does not want a 50/50 DNS split during healthy operation. Both load balancers already exist. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use weighted 50/50 records with no health checks.
B. Create Route 53 failover records with primary and secondary targets.
C. Attach a Route 53 health check to the primary endpoint.
D. Use geolocation routing as the active-passive switch.
E. Use a CloudFront invalidation to fail over Regions.

questions.explain: Active/passive DNS is failover records plus a health check on the primary. Weighted 50/50 is a split. Invalidation refreshes cache, it does not fail over a Region.
questions.good_to_know: Latency routing would be correct if the nearest healthy Region should win. Geolocation would be correct for country-based content, not priority failover.

questions.q: Operations wants 90 percent of DNS answers to stay on the current Application Load Balancer and 10 percent to hit a new Regional load balancer during a gradual release. Failover and lowest-latency Region selection are not required. Both load balancers already exist. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use failover routing with the new endpoint as primary.
B. Use geoproximity with maximum bias instead of weights.
C. Use multivalue answer routing to pin 10 percent of users.
D. Create Route 53 weighted records for the old and new endpoints.
E. Assign weights such as 90 and 10 to match the desired DNS split.

questions.explain: Weighted records plus the actual 90 and 10 weights are the two steps that implement a DNS canary. Multivalue answer does not express percentages.
questions.good_to_know: Failover would make the new endpoint take all traffic when marked primary. Geoproximity bias shifts geographic share, not an explicit 90/10 split.

questions.q: A company hosts a public static website in Amazon S3 in one Region. Global users need low latency, and the hostname www.example.com must keep working. The team wants DNS to point at an HTTP cache, not at the bucket URL alone. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as the origin.
B. Create a Route 53 alias record that points the website name to the distribution.
C. Serve objects only from a public S3 website URL with no CDN in front.
D. Use AWS Global Accelerator as an HTTP cache in front of the bucket.
E. Use Route 53 to cache image bytes inside DNS answers for the hostname.

questions.explain: Static global content is S3 plus CloudFront. Route 53 alias records commonly point the hostname at the distribution. DNS does not cache HTTP bodies.
questions.good_to_know: Global Accelerator is anycast TCP/UDP acceleration, not an object cache. Serving the S3 website URL alone would skip edge caching.

questions.q: A logistics company collects device telemetry from thousands of trucks. Several analytics applications must read the same records independently, preserve per-device order, and replay history after a consumer failure. The team will write custom consumer code and does not want a managed delivery pipe into a data store. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with custom consumers.
B. Send the telemetry to Amazon Data Firehose for delivery to Amazon S3.
C. Query telemetry files in Amazon S3 with Amazon Athena only.
D. Load the telemetry into Amazon Redshift and poll warehouse tables.

questions.explain: Independent custom consumers, per-device ordering, and replay are Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Firehose is a managed delivery pipe, not a replayable consumer API.
questions.good_to_know: Firehose would be correct if the stem asked only to buffer, compress, and land files in S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch with almost no consumer code.

questions.q: A mobile studio publishes player events to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. Events for one player must stay in write order, but different players may be processed in parallel. A previous design used a single constant partition key and overloaded one shard. The studio must avoid that hot-partition pattern. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use one constant partition key so every event shares a shard.
B. Replace the stream with Amazon Data Firehose and ignore partition keys.
C. Use the player identifier as the partition key so order is per player.
D. Write the events to Amazon Redshift and rely on table sort keys for ingest order.

questions.explain: The partition key chooses the shard and the ordering scope. A high-cardinality player key keeps one player ordered while spreading load; a constant key creates a hot partition.
questions.good_to_know: Firehose still batches for delivery; it does not give the same shard-level consumer control. Warehouse sort keys are for query layout, not stream ingest order.

questions.q: A media company wants clickstream records delivered into Amazon S3 as compressed objects for later lake analytics. Operations wants AWS to buffer, optionally transform, and load the files with almost no consumer application to maintain. The company does not want to manage stream shards. Sub-second processing of each record is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams application for every file write.
B. Create an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to Amazon S3.
C. Run Amazon EMR Spark Streaming only to copy events into S3.
D. Insert each clickstream row into Amazon Redshift with a custom poller.

questions.explain: Managed buffering, compression, optional transform, and delivery to S3 is Amazon Data Firehose. It is near real-time delivery, not a custom shard consumer.
questions.good_to_know: Kinesis Data Streams would win if several applications needed to rewind and process the same records with their own code. EMR is the Spark/Hadoop cluster answer, not a low-ops delivery pipe.
