questions.q: An operations team must index application logs for search and near-real-time log analytics. Events arrive as a stream and should be delivered into the search service with buffering and little custom consumer code. The team does not need a general-purpose queue and will not query the logs with warehouse SQL as the primary interface. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Load the logs into Amazon Redshift and run nightly warehouse joins.
B. Catalog the logs in AWS Glue and query them only with Amazon Athena.
C. Store the logs in Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive for interactive search.
D. Deliver the logs with Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon OpenSearch Service.

questions.explain: OpenSearch is the search and log-analytics engine in this lesson. Firehose is the managed delivery path into OpenSearch when the goal is loading, not custom stream consumers.
questions.good_to_know: Athena on a partitioned S3 lake is the serverless SQL investigation pattern. Redshift is repeated warehouse analytics, not a search index.

questions.q: Producers emit order events that must land in Amazon S3 for a data lake. Developers asked for a general message queue so workers can delete each message after a job. Architects instead need a managed streaming delivery pipe that buffers and writes objects, not a queue and not custom shard consumers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Data Firehose as the delivery stream into Amazon S3.
B. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams with several rewindable consumers.
C. Use Amazon Athena to ingest the live events as a queue.
D. Use AWS Glue crawlers as the streaming transport into S3.

questions.explain: Firehose is a streaming delivery pipe to destinations such as S3, not a general-purpose queue and not a replayable consumer API.
questions.good_to_know: Kinesis Data Streams is the answer when the stem requires custom consumers and replay. Glue crawlers discover schemas; they do not replace ingest.

questions.q: Analysts must run SQL against years of objects in an Amazon S3 data lake. Several engines, including Amazon Athena, need a shared table and schema registry that crawlers can populate automatically. The company does not want to load a warehouse just to store metadata. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Redshift local tables as the only schema registry.
B. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service mappings as the lake catalog.
C. Use AWS Glue crawlers to populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
D. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams shards as table metadata.

questions.explain: Glue crawlers infer schemas and fill the Glue Data Catalog, which Athena and Redshift Spectrum use as lake table metadata.
questions.good_to_know: Lake Formation then layers lake permissions on those cataloged resources. Redshift still needs Spectrum or an external schema to see S3 through the catalog.

questions.q: A data lake in Amazon S3 holds raw JSON extracts that are slow and expensive for Amazon Athena to scan. Pipelines must rewrite the datasets into a query-friendly columnar layout with partitions that match common filters. The team wants managed ETL rather than operating a long-lived Hadoop cluster. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an Amazon EMR cluster as the only way to change file format.
B. Run AWS Glue ETL jobs to write partitioned columnar files in S3.
C. Stream the JSON through Amazon Data Firehose into Amazon OpenSearch Service.
D. Copy the JSON into Amazon Redshift and delete the S3 lake.

questions.explain: Glue ETL is the managed transform path that writes query-friendly formats and partitions in the S3 lake. EMR is for custom Spark or Hadoop when you need a cluster beyond Glue jobs.
questions.good_to_know: Firehose can convert incoming streams on the way to S3, but this stem is a lake rewrite of objects that are already stored, which is Glue ETL.

questions.q: Several business units share an Amazon S3 data lake registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Security wants a lake-focused permissions model on those cataloged databases and tables rather than relying only on individual bucket policies. Analysts will keep querying with Amazon Athena and will not move the lake into a warehouse just to control access. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon Redshift workload management as the lake permission system.
B. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service fine-grained access as the S3 catalog ACL.
C. Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams resource policies to authorize Athena.
D. Use AWS Lake Formation to govern permissions on the lake resources.

questions.explain: Lake Formation is the lesson’s data-lake governance and permissions layer on top of lake resources that the Glue Data Catalog already describes.
questions.good_to_know: Bucket policies still matter for the objects, but they are not the catalog-aware lake permission model this stem asks for. Redshift WLM controls warehouse concurrency, not S3 lake grants.

questions.q: Investigators sporadically query years of application logs that already live in Amazon S3. They need SQL without provisioning a warehouse cluster and without loading the logs into a database first. Queries are occasional, so paying for data scanned is acceptable if the lake stays in S3. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Query the S3 objects with Amazon Athena using the Glue Data Catalog.
B. Load every log into Amazon Redshift before any SQL is allowed.
C. Index every log in Amazon OpenSearch Service for SQL warehouse joins.
D. Run a persistent Amazon EMR cluster solely to answer ad-hoc SQL.

questions.explain: Athena is serverless SQL on S3. Cost follows data scanned, which fits sporadic investigation. Redshift is the provisioned warehouse for repeated heavy BI.
questions.good_to_know: OpenSearch is search and log analytics with an index model, not the serverless lake-SQL answer. EMR fits custom Spark or Hadoop processing beyond Glue jobs.

questions.q: Analysts already use Amazon Athena against JSON logs in Amazon S3. Queries filter on event date but still scan entire prefixes, and the bill tracks data scanned. The company will keep Athena, will not load a warehouse, and wants the same SQL to read less data. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: A. Replicate the JSON to a second Region so Athena scans less.
B. Increase Amazon Kinesis Data Streams shard count for the lake.
C. Convert the logs to Parquet and partition objects by event date.
D. Move the logs into Amazon OpenSearch Service and keep JSON in S3.

questions.explain: Athena charges by data scanned. Columnar Parquet reads needed columns, and date partitions let Athena skip files outside the filter.
questions.good_to_know: Redshift would appear if the stem demanded frequent high-concurrency warehouse joins. Extra Regions and extra Kinesis shards do not change Athena scan bytes.

questions.q: Many analysts run frequent complex joins and aggregations over terabytes of curated enterprise data throughout the day. The company needs a columnar massively parallel warehouse rather than ad-hoc scans of a raw S3 lake. Interactive search of application logs is not the requirement, and an OLTP database is not the analytics engine. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Query the raw lake only with Amazon Athena for every dashboard.
B. Load the curated model into Amazon Redshift for warehouse analytics.
C. Index the enterprise tables in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
D. Keep the only copy in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for SQL joins.

questions.explain: Repeated warehouse-style joins and aggregations are Amazon Redshift’s columnar MPP pattern. Athena is serverless SQL on S3 and is less the exam answer for heavy all-day BI.
questions.good_to_know: Athena remains the better fit when queries are sporadic and the data should stay in the lake. OpenSearch is search and log analytics, not a relational warehouse.

questions.q: A company already runs Amazon Redshift for dimensional analytics. Several large fact extracts remain in Amazon S3 and are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Analysts must join warehouse tables with those files without loading every object into Redshift local storage. Copying the entire lake into the cluster is too slow and costly. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Copy every S3 object into Amazon OpenSearch Service before joining.
B. Replace Redshift with Amazon Athena and abandon the warehouse.
C. Stream the S3 objects through Amazon Kinesis Data Streams into Redshift.
D. Query the S3 files with Amazon Redshift Spectrum through the catalog.

questions.explain: Redshift Spectrum queries data that lives outside warehouse storage, typically in S3, using catalog metadata Glue already holds.
questions.good_to_know: Athena would be the answer if there were no warehouse and the only need was serverless SQL on S3. Loading into Redshift is valid when the stem wants data inside the cluster.

questions.q: A genomics pipeline needs Apache Spark and Hadoop jobs with custom libraries that go beyond AWS Glue ETL. Input datasets already sit in an Amazon S3 data lake. The team wants a managed cluster for those frameworks rather than building Hadoop on unmanaged Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the jobs on Amazon EMR clusters that read the S3 lake.
B. Rewrite the Spark jobs as Amazon Athena SQL views only.
C. Deliver the datasets through Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon Redshift.
D. Index the genomes in Amazon OpenSearch Service instead of Spark.

questions.explain: EMR is the managed Spark and Hadoop service when processing goes beyond Glue jobs or Athena SQL. The S3 lake remains the durable store.
questions.good_to_know: Glue ETL is the lower-ops transform when Spark custom libraries are not required. Athena is serverless SQL, not a general Spark runtime.

questions.q: A support organization must search free-text ticket comments and run near-real-time log analytics on operational events. Users need an index and search model rather than serverless SQL over an S3 lake or a columnar warehouse. The company will not operate self-managed search clusters and rejected Amazon Athena as the primary search interface. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Query ticket objects only with Amazon Athena on Amazon S3.
B. Load the comments into Amazon Redshift as the search engine.
C. Index the comments and logs in Amazon OpenSearch Service.
D. Store the comments in AWS Glue Data Catalog as full-text documents.

questions.explain: OpenSearch is the lesson’s search and log-analytics service. Athena and Redshift are SQL over lakes or warehouses, not a search index.
questions.good_to_know: Firehose is a common managed path into OpenSearch when the source is a stream. Glue Data Catalog stores table schemas, not a full-text search corpus.

questions.q: A finance team already queries curated tables in Amazon Redshift. Business users need interactive dashboards and visuals without writing SQL for every request. The company wants a BI service rather than a search cluster, a Spark job, or another warehouse. The curated Redshift tables remain the source for the visuals. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Index the tables in Amazon OpenSearch Service for each visual.
B. Build the dashboards in Amazon QuickSight against the warehouse.
C. Run Amazon EMR Spark jobs to render every dashboard refresh.
D. Stream the tables through Amazon Data Firehose to create BI charts.

questions.explain: Amazon QuickSight is the BI service for dashboards and visuals. OpenSearch, EMR, and Firehose solve search, Spark processing, and stream delivery, not BI authoring.
questions.good_to_know: Athena can also feed QuickSight when the stem is lake SQL rather than a warehouse. Do not treat a lesson mention of Amazon Quick as a different product name.

questions.q: Batch extracts and streaming landings must be stored so Amazon Athena, Amazon Redshift Spectrum, and Amazon EMR can all read the same objects later. The company wants durable object storage as the system of record, not a provisioned warehouse and not a time-bounded stream. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Keep the only copy in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.
B. Keep the only copy inside Amazon Redshift local storage.
C. Keep the only copy in Amazon OpenSearch Service indexes.
D. Land the datasets in an Amazon S3 data lake.

questions.explain: S3 is the durable data-lake landing zone. Later engines query those objects after Glue catalogs them. Streams and warehouses are not the shared lake.
questions.good_to_know: Partition the lake and convert to columnar formats so Athena scan cost stays predictable. Redshift is for curated warehouse analytics on top of, not instead of, the lake when multiple engines must share files.

questions.q: Clickstream producers already write to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams. A new requirement is to land compressed files in Amazon S3 for the lake with minimal new consumer code. Existing custom consumers must keep reading the same stream for real-time processing. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead for the S3 path?

options.text: A. Add an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream from the existing stream to S3.
B. Rewrite every custom consumer to also multipart-upload files to S3.
C. Dump the stream into Amazon OpenSearch Service and export JSON nightly.
D. Load the stream into Amazon Redshift and UNLOAD to S3 each hour.

questions.explain: Firehose is the low-ops delivery path to S3. Kinesis Data Streams can still feed custom consumers; Firehose handles buffering and object writes.
questions.good_to_know: If no custom consumers existed, producers could send to Firehose directly. Warehouse UNLOAD is not the managed stream-to-lake pattern.

questions.q: A company already uses Amazon Redshift for BI. Streaming click events from producers must be buffered, compressed, and loaded into that warehouse. Operations will not write custom Kinesis consumers or manage shard capacity, and sub-second per-record analytics is not required. The warehouse remains the destination of record. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Have each producer issue SQL INSERT statements into Redshift.
B. Query the live events with Amazon Athena on the producer hosts.
C. Deliver the events with Amazon Data Firehose to Amazon Redshift.
D. Index the events in Amazon OpenSearch Service as the warehouse.

questions.explain: Firehose supports managed delivery into Redshift with buffering and compression. That is delivery, not custom stream processing.
questions.good_to_know: Kinesis Data Streams would be required if independent applications needed to replay the events. OpenSearch is not a columnar MPP warehouse.

questions.q: Amazon Athena queries against a JSON data lake in Amazon S3 scan too much data and cost too much. Analysts filter on date and a small set of columns. The company will keep Athena and the S3 lake and will not provision a warehouse for this workload. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Convert the datasets to columnar Parquet.
B. Increase Amazon Redshift node count for the Athena queries.
C. Partition the objects by the columns used in filters.
D. Copy the lake into Amazon OpenSearch Service to reduce Athena bytes.
E. Add Amazon Kinesis Data Streams shards in front of Athena.

questions.explain: Parquet lets Athena read needed columns, and partitions skip files outside common predicates. Those two layout changes are the direct scan-cost levers.
questions.good_to_know: Redshift nodes do not serve Athena. Extra Kinesis shards change ingest capacity, not lake scan bytes.

questions.q: IoT devices emit telemetry that several applications must consume in per-device order. After a consumer outage, each application must replay recent records independently. The team will write custom consumers and will not use a managed delivery stream as the only ingest path. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Replace the stream with Amazon Data Firehose only.
B. Ingest the telemetry into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams.
C. Store events only in Amazon Redshift and query them as a stream.
D. Set a device partition key and retain records for replay.
E. Catalog the live stream with AWS Lake Formation instead of shards.

questions.explain: Kinesis Data Streams plus a device partition key gives per-device order on a shard. Retention is what lets independent consumers rewind after failures.
questions.good_to_know: Firehose would be correct if the only goal were buffered delivery to S3, Redshift, or OpenSearch. Lake Formation governs lake permissions, not stream shards.

questions.q: Security analysts sporadically run SQL over years of logs in Amazon S3 and must not load a warehouse. Table schemas should be discovered and shared so Athena can query the objects. The company wants serverless SQL on the lake. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Load every object into Amazon Redshift before SQL is allowed.
B. Run Amazon EMR solely to host a permanent warehouse for this SQL.
C. Populate the AWS Glue Data Catalog with the lake table schemas.
D. Index the logs in Amazon OpenSearch Service as the SQL engine.
E. Query the S3 datasets with Amazon Athena.

questions.explain: Glue supplies the shared schema registry; Athena runs serverless SQL on S3. Together they are the sporadic lake-investigation pattern.
questions.good_to_know: Redshift is the answer when many users run frequent complex warehouse joins. OpenSearch is search and log analytics, not Athena’s lake SQL.

questions.q: A retailer must land streaming click events in Amazon S3 for a data lake with almost no consumer code. Records should be buffered, compressed, and optionally transformed before objects are written. The team does not need custom rewindable consumers for this path. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to Amazon S3.
B. Build custom Kinesis consumers on Amazon EC2 for every object write.
C. Use Amazon OpenSearch Service as the only store for the data lake.
D. Query the live stream with Amazon Redshift Spectrum.
E. Enable buffering, compression, and any required record transformation.

questions.explain: Firehose is the managed delivery stream to S3. Buffering, compression, and transform are the operational features that remove custom consumer work.
questions.good_to_know: Kinesis Data Streams is the custom-consumer and replay answer. Spectrum queries S3 from Redshift; it does not ingest a live Kinesis stream.

questions.q: Raw files already sit in an Amazon S3 data lake. Pipelines must rewrite them into partitioned columnar objects, and Amazon Athena must see the new tables. The team wants managed ETL and a catalog rather than a long-lived Hadoop cluster. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Move the lake into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams as the durable store.
B. Run AWS Glue ETL jobs to write partitioned columnar files in S3.
C. Update the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Athena can query the new tables.
D. Grant lake access only with Amazon OpenSearch Service index policies.
E. Replace Athena with Amazon Redshift by renaming the Glue database.

questions.explain: Glue ETL produces the query-friendly lake layout. The Glue Data Catalog is the schema registry Athena uses to find those tables.
questions.good_to_know: EMR would appear if the stem required custom Spark or Hadoop libraries beyond Glue jobs. Lake Formation would appear if the deciding constraint were lake permissions.

questions.q: A company already has curated tables in Amazon Redshift and a large Amazon S3 data lake registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Analysts must run frequent complex joins on the warehouse tables and must also join those results with lake files they do not want to load. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Delete the warehouse and run every join only with Amazon Athena.
B. Index the warehouse tables in Amazon OpenSearch Service for joins.
C. Copy the lake into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams before each query.
D. Run the frequent joins on Amazon Redshift.
E. Query the unloaded lake files with Amazon Redshift Spectrum.

questions.explain: Redshift is the columnar MPP warehouse for repeated joins. Spectrum reaches S3 data that stays outside local warehouse storage, using the catalog.
questions.good_to_know: Athena alone would be correct if there were no warehouse and queries were sporadic lake SQL. OpenSearch does not replace warehouse joins.

questions.q: A research team needs Apache Spark jobs with custom libraries that AWS Glue ETL does not cover. Input datasets already live in an Amazon S3 data lake. The team wants a managed Spark and Hadoop platform rather than self-managed clusters on Amazon EC2. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create an Amazon EMR cluster that runs Apache Spark.
B. Process the objects that already live in the Amazon S3 data lake.
C. Rewrite the Spark jobs as Amazon Athena SQL views only.
D. Ingest the lake into Amazon Kinesis Data Streams before Spark can run.
E. Store the only output in Amazon OpenSearch Service indexes.

questions.explain: EMR supplies managed Spark and Hadoop. The S3 lake is the durable input the lesson already treats as the landing zone for later engines.
questions.good_to_know: Glue ETL remains the answer when transform and partition jobs do not need a custom Spark cluster. Athena is serverless SQL, not a Spark runtime.

questions.q: A retailer must move 200 on-premises application servers to AWS with as little redesign as possible. Each server should be replicated continuously, then launched as Amazon EC2 instances at cutover. The company is not treating databases as a separate CDC project and does not need a file-transfer tool. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate servers onto EC2.
B. Use AWS Database Migration Service with change data capture.
C. Use AWS DataSync to copy each server image to Amazon S3 nightly.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family to expose SFTP for the server disks.

questions.explain: MGN is lift-and-shift server replication with test and cutover onto EC2. DMS moves database data, and DataSync and Transfer Family move files, not whole servers.
questions.good_to_know: Modernize after cutover if needed. DMS would be correct if the stem were a database full load plus CDC with a brief cutover.

questions.q: A company is using AWS Application Migration Service to move factory Windows and Linux servers. Before production cutover, operators must launch instances in AWS, validate the applications, and only then switch users. Architectural redesign can wait until after the move. The team is not using database CDC or a file-transfer tool as the server test path. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DMS change data capture to test the servers.
B. Use AWS DataSync to synchronize each server’s block devices.
C. Launch MGN test instances, then cut over to Amazon EC2.
D. Ship the servers with an AWS Snow Family device and skip test launches.

questions.explain: MGN continuously replicates source servers and supports launching test and cutover instances in EC2 so validation happens before users move.
questions.good_to_know: DMS is database CDC, not a server test path. Snow Family is physical dataset transport when the WAN cannot carry petabytes.

questions.q: A production PostgreSQL database on premises must move to Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL. Writes must continue on the source until a brief cutover. The team needs an initial copy plus ongoing replication of changes and is not moving file shares or whole servers. The engines already match, so schema conversion is not the deciding constraint. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to copy the PostgreSQL data directory over NFS.
B. Use AWS DMS with a full load and change data capture until cutover.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the database host only.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP to upload nightly database dumps.

questions.explain: DMS full load plus CDC keeps a supported database target synchronized until cutover. Homogeneous engine pairs still use DMS for the data movement.
questions.good_to_know: MGN would be correct if the constraint were lift-and-shift of the whole server. DataSync copies files and objects, not database CDC.

questions.q: An on-premises Oracle database must move to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with only a short outage. Table data must be copied and then kept current with source writes. The engines differ, so schema objects cannot be assumed to match without conversion. Copying data files with a NAS tool will not keep the target synchronized. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to copy Oracle data files onto an Aurora volume.
B. Use AWS Application Migration Service as the database CDC tool.
C. Use an S3 File Gateway to present Oracle redo logs as NFS to Aurora.
D. Convert the schema and use AWS DMS full load plus CDC.

questions.explain: Heterogeneous migrations may need schema conversion, then DMS full load plus CDC for low-downtime data movement. DMS is not a file copier.
questions.good_to_know: Homogeneous moves can skip conversion when the engines already match. MGN replicates servers, not database change streams.

questions.q: A factory keeps millions of files on an on-premises NFS NAS. The files must copy to Amazon S3 over the existing WAN on a nightly schedule, and each transfer must be verified. The company is not migrating servers or databases, and the network path is already working. Applications do not need a local NFS cache after the copy. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to schedule verified NFS copies to Amazon S3.
B. Use AWS DMS change data capture against the NAS file system.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the NAS controller.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family so the NAS initiates SFTP to itself.

questions.explain: DataSync is the online file and object transfer service with scheduling and integrity checks when a working network path exists.
questions.good_to_know: Storage Gateway File Gateway would be correct for ongoing local NFS access with S3 as the durable store, not a scheduled one-way migration. Snow Family is for when the WAN cannot finish the job.

questions.q: Linux applications in AWS must read a POSIX file system. The source is an on-premises NFS export that should be copied online, with validation, onto Amazon EFS. A working network path already exists, and the team does not want a physical appliance shipment. The team needs a managed file copy, not database CDC or server cutover. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DMS to replicate the file system as a database.
B. Use AWS Application Migration Service to cut the NAS over to EC2.
C. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the NFS export to Amazon EFS.
D. Use AWS Snow Family as the only path because EFS cannot be a DataSync target.

questions.explain: DataSync moves large file datasets between on-premises NAS, S3, EFS, and FSx when the network can carry the transfer.
questions.good_to_know: Snow Family is the offline answer when bandwidth would take too long. File Gateway would apply if the Linux apps still needed a local NFS cache instead of a copy onto EFS.

questions.q: A company must copy a large on-premises file share into an Amazon FSx file system in AWS. A reliable network path already exists, and operators want managed online transfer with integrity checking rather than a petabyte-scale physical shipment. Servers and databases are out of scope. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DMS full load to treat the share as a relational source.
B. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the share to Amazon FSx.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the file server VM only.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP as the only way to fill Amazon FSx.

questions.explain: DataSync supports online transfers to FSx-related targets when the network is usable. DMS and MGN address databases and servers, not this file copy.
questions.good_to_know: Transfer Family is the managed SFTP, FTPS, or FTP endpoint into S3 or EFS when partners must keep those protocols. Snow Family is the weak-WAN physical path.

questions.q: A media archive of several petabytes must reach Amazon S3. The data center WAN would take many months at the available bandwidth, and the company will not wait for that online copy. Files are cold objects, not a running database or a fleet of application servers. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync only and wait for the WAN to finish in months.
B. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP to create extra physical bandwidth.
C. Use AWS DMS change data capture to stream the archive files.
D. Use an AWS Snow Family device workflow to ship the encrypted dataset.

questions.explain: Snow Family is physical transfer for petabyte-scale datasets when the network is too slow or too constrained. Online tools stay bandwidth-bound.
questions.good_to_know: DataSync is correct when a working network can finish the copy on an acceptable schedule. Transfer Family does not add WAN capacity.

questions.q: External partners must keep using SFTP to upload files. AWS should operate the protocol endpoint, and objects must land in Amazon S3. The company already has private connectivity but does not want to run SFTP servers on Amazon EC2. Direct Connect and VPN are already available for network paths and must not be treated as the SFTP service. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint.
B. Use AWS DataSync agents on each partner laptop as the SFTP server.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate partner SFTP hosts.
D. Use AWS DMS to capture SFTP sessions into a database.

questions.explain: Transfer Family is the managed SFTP, FTPS, or FTP endpoint backed by S3 or EFS. Connectivity services do not replace that protocol endpoint.
questions.good_to_know: DataSync is scheduled NAS and object transfer with a working network, not a partner SFTP front door. File Gateway is local NFS or SMB cache in front of S3.

questions.q: A supplier still uses FTPS clients that cannot be rewritten this quarter. Files must land in Amazon EFS so Linux applications can mount them. The company wants AWS to manage the FTP-style endpoint rather than EC2 FTP daemons. Partners will not install DataSync agents, and SFTP is not the only client protocol in use. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync as a public FTP server for the supplier.
B. Use an S3 File Gateway as the internet FTP endpoint.
C. Use AWS Transfer Family FTPS into Amazon EFS.
D. Use AWS Snow Family to emulate FTP over the WAN.

questions.explain: Transfer Family provides managed FTP and FTPS as well as SFTP, and it can store files in S3 or EFS.
questions.good_to_know: File Gateway presents NFS (or SMB) on premises while objects live in S3; it is not the managed internet FTP service. DataSync is online sync, not an FTP endpoint.

questions.q: On-premises applications must keep using an NFS file share with local caching. New files should be stored durably as objects in Amazon S3. This is ongoing hybrid access, not a one-time migration of a NAS, and the applications cannot change protocols this year. A scheduled copy job is not an acceptable file interface for those applications. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync once and then disconnect the applications from storage.
B. Deploy an S3 File Gateway and present an NFS share that stores objects in S3.
C. Use AWS DMS to replicate the NFS share into Amazon RDS.
D. Use AWS Application Migration Service to convert the NAS into EC2.

questions.explain: S3 File Gateway exposes NFS with a local cache and keeps objects in S3, which is the hybrid interface the lesson teaches.
questions.good_to_know: DataSync is the scheduled online copy when you are moving files, not keeping a local NFS facade. Volume and tape gateways exist in the family but are not the NFS-plus-S3 pattern this lesson quizzes.

questions.q: Factory software must continue to mount NFS on the plant network while objects are retained in Amazon S3. Operators considered a nightly DataSync job, but the applications need a live local file interface rather than a batch copy. The software cannot switch to SFTP, and a Snow device is not a daily NFS server. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync on a schedule as the only application file interface.
B. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP and change the factory software to SFTP.
C. Use AWS Snow Family for each day’s files as the local NFS server.
D. Use S3 File Gateway for ongoing NFS access with S3 as the durable store.

questions.explain: File Gateway is ongoing hybrid access. DataSync is transfer and synchronization; it does not replace a local NFS mount for applications that cannot change.
questions.good_to_know: Transfer Family would win if partners had to keep SFTP into S3 or EFS. Snow Family is offline bulk movement, not a daily NFS server.

questions.q: Partners must upload over SFTP into Amazon S3. The company already has AWS Direct Connect for private IP connectivity to VPCs. Direct Connect does not terminate SFTP for those partners, and the team will not run SFTP on Amazon EC2. A Site-to-Site VPN is also not an SFTP application endpoint. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP into Amazon S3.
B. Use AWS Direct Connect alone as the SFTP protocol service.
C. Use an AWS Site-to-Site VPN as the SFTP server.
D. Use AWS DataSync as a public SFTP endpoint for partners.

questions.explain: Direct Connect and VPN provide connectivity. They do not migrate or replace the SFTP application protocol. Transfer Family is that managed endpoint.
questions.good_to_know: The same split applies to File Gateway: DX or VPN can carry NFS traffic, but the hybrid file interface is still Storage Gateway.

questions.q: A company must copy a 20 TB NFS dataset to Amazon S3. The WAN can finish the job in a few days, and operators want scheduled incremental runs with integrity verification. Petabyte-scale physical shipping is unnecessary. The source is a file system, not a database, and servers are not being lifted to Amazon EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Snow Family because any NFS copy requires a physical device.
B. Use AWS DMS to treat the NFS export as a source database.
C. Use AWS DataSync for scheduled verified copies over the WAN.
D. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the NAS as EC2.

questions.explain: When a working network can complete the file copy, DataSync is the online tool. Snow Family is for when bandwidth would take too long.
questions.good_to_know: Estimate transfer time from bandwidth before choosing online versus offline. MGN and DMS remain the wrong movers for a NAS file dataset.

questions.q: An on-premises NFS file server holds application documents that must move to Amazon S3. A colleague suggested AWS Database Migration Service because the documents are important. The source is a file system, not a database, and a working network path exists. Schema conversion and server replication are the wrong movers for this dataset. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS DMS full load and CDC against the NFS export.
B. Use AWS DataSync to copy the NFS files to Amazon S3.
C. Use AWS Schema Conversion Tool on the file names.
D. Use AWS Application Migration Service CDC for the documents.

questions.explain: DMS is for database data, not generic file-system migration. DataSync is the online file and object mover when the network exists.
questions.good_to_know: MGN is equally wrong here because it replicates servers, not document trees. File Gateway would apply if the apps still needed a local NFS cache.

questions.q: A production MySQL database must move to Amazon Aurora MySQL with ongoing replication until cutover. A colleague suggested AWS Application Migration Service because the database runs on a server. The requirement is database change capture, not lift-and-shift of the host. Copying table files with a NAS tool will not apply in-flight transactions. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Application Migration Service as the database CDC service.
B. Use AWS DataSync to copy MySQL table files into Aurora.
C. Use AWS Transfer Family to SFTP binlogs into Amazon S3 only.
D. Use AWS DMS with full load and change data capture to Aurora MySQL.

questions.explain: MGN replicates servers for lift-and-shift onto EC2. Database CDC and full load are DMS, including homogeneous MySQL-to-Aurora patterns.
questions.good_to_know: MGN can still move a database host if the exam asks to lift the whole server unchanged. This stem’s deciding constraint is database CDC.

questions.q: Hundreds of VMware virtual machines must be continuously replicated into AWS and launched as Amazon EC2 instances during a planned cutover. The company wants lift-and-shift with later modernization. File sync and database CDC tools are not the right mover for the VM fleet. Test launches should happen before users are switched. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate VMs onto EC2.
B. Use AWS DataSync to copy each VM disk file to Amazon EFS.
C. Use AWS DMS to migrate the hypervisor as a database.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family to SFTP the VM images into Amazon S3.

questions.explain: MGN is the server replication and cutover path onto EC2. DataSync, DMS, and Transfer Family match files, databases, and FTP-style protocols.
questions.good_to_know: Test launches in MGN come before production cutover. Do not use MGN when the stem is only CDC between database engines.

questions.q: A studio must move 8 PB of video masters to Amazon S3. Online tools were estimated to need many months on the current WAN. The company will accept physical logistics and encryption in transit to AWS. Partners do not need SFTP, and no database cutover is involved. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Transfer Family to add petabytes of WAN throughput.
B. Use AWS DMS CDC to replicate the video files as rows.
C. Use AWS Snow Family to ship the encrypted dataset.
D. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate each video file as a server.

questions.explain: Petabytes plus a weak or slow WAN select Snow Family physical transfer. Protocol and database services do not create that capacity.
questions.good_to_know: If the estimate showed days rather than months, DataSync over the existing path would be the online answer. Device generation follows capacity and edge needs, which this lesson does not pin to a quota number.

questions.q: A company will lift-and-shift 80 application servers to Amazon EC2 using AWS Application Migration Service. Operators must keep replicating the sources, launch instances to validate the applications, and then cut over users. Database CDC and file-transfer services are not the server mover. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Replicate the source servers continuously with AWS MGN.
B. Use AWS DMS change data capture as the server replication engine.
C. Launch test instances, then cut over to Amazon EC2 when validation succeeds.
D. Use AWS DataSync to copy each OS disk into Amazon EFS as the cutover method.
E. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP to move the running servers.

questions.explain: MGN’s pattern is continuous server replication plus test and cutover launches into EC2. Those two steps are jointly required for a controlled lift-and-shift.
questions.good_to_know: DMS remains the database full-load-plus-CDC answer. DataSync does not replace block-level server replication.

questions.q: A production SQL Server database must move to Amazon RDS for SQL Server with only a brief cutover. Source writes must continue until the switch. The move is homogeneous, so schema conversion is not the deciding problem. The team must not use a file copier or a server replication tool as the CDC path. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to copy SQL Server data files as the CDC mechanism.
B. Run an AWS DMS full load of the existing data onto the target.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service solely to capture database transactions.
D. Enable AWS DMS change data capture until the cutover window.
E. Use AWS Snow Family to replicate in-flight SQL transactions over the WAN.

questions.explain: Low-downtime database migration is full load plus CDC in DMS. Homogeneous engine pairs still need both steps when writes continue until cutover.
questions.good_to_know: Add schema conversion when the stem is heterogeneous. MGN would be correct for lifting the whole database host as a server.

questions.q: An on-premises Oracle database must move to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. Data must be copied and then kept current with source changes, and the engines differ so objects cannot be assumed to match. File copy and server replication will not convert schema or capture database changes. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to copy Oracle data files onto Aurora storage.
B. Use AWS Application Migration Service as the CDC path between engines.
C. Perform schema conversion for the heterogeneous engine change.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family to SFTP Oracle blocks into Aurora.
E. Use AWS DMS full load and change data capture to the Aurora target.

questions.explain: Heterogeneous migrations may require schema conversion. DMS then moves and replicates the data with full load plus CDC until cutover.
questions.good_to_know: Skip conversion when source and target engines already match. File and server tools do not perform database CDC.

questions.q: An on-premises NFS NAS must synchronize to Amazon S3 every night. Operators need incremental copies, integrity verification, and bandwidth-aware online transfer. The WAN is sufficient, and this is not a database or server move. Applications do not need a persistent local NFS cache after each copy. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync to transfer the NFS data to Amazon S3.
B. Use AWS DMS CDC against the NAS as if it were a database.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to cut the NAS over to EC2 nightly.
D. Use AWS Snow Family for each nightly increment because S3 requires a device.
E. Schedule the DataSync task and enable integrity verification.

questions.explain: DataSync is the online NAS-to-S3 mover. Scheduling and integrity checks are the operational controls the lesson pairs with that transfer.
questions.good_to_know: File Gateway would be the answer if applications still needed a local NFS cache in front of S3. Snow Family is offline bulk movement.

questions.q: Several petabytes of backups must reach Amazon S3. Bandwidth calculations show the current WAN would take months. The company will use a physical device workflow and track encrypted shipment. Online file transfer and SFTP endpoints cannot add that transport capacity. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use AWS DataSync only, because Snow Family cannot store backups.
B. Choose an AWS Snow Family device workflow sized for the dataset.
C. Ship the encrypted device to AWS instead of waiting on the WAN copy.
D. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP to multiply WAN capacity.
E. Use AWS DMS to replicate backup files as change data capture.

questions.explain: Snow Family bypasses a weak WAN with physical transport. Device choice follows capacity; logistics and encryption are part of the architecture.
questions.good_to_know: DataSync remains correct when the network can finish in an acceptable time. Transfer Family does not create physical transport capacity.

questions.q: External partners must keep SFTP clients and upload into Amazon S3. AWS must operate the protocol endpoint so the company does not manage SFTP on Amazon EC2. Direct Connect already exists for private VPC access but does not provide SFTP. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use AWS Direct Connect alone as the SFTP application protocol.
B. Use AWS DataSync agents on each partner workstation as SFTP.
C. Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate partner laptops.
D. Create an AWS Transfer Family SFTP endpoint.
E. Configure the endpoint to store uploaded files in Amazon S3.

questions.explain: Transfer Family is the managed SFTP service, and S3 is the taught durable backend (EFS is the other). DX is connectivity, not a protocol endpoint.
questions.good_to_know: FTPS and FTP are the same Transfer Family family of endpoints when clients are not SFTP. File Gateway is for on-premises NFS in front of S3.

questions.q: On-premises applications must keep an NFS mount with local caching while files are stored as objects in Amazon S3. This is ongoing hybrid access, not a one-time NAS copy, and the applications will not switch to SFTP. A scheduled DataSync job is not an acceptable live file interface. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Deploy Amazon S3 File Gateway in the on-premises environment.
B. Present an NFS share to the applications and store objects in Amazon S3.
C. Use AWS DataSync as the only live NFS server for those applications.
D. Use AWS DMS to replicate the NFS share into a database.
E. Use AWS Transfer Family SFTP and require the applications to change protocol.

questions.explain: File Gateway is the hybrid NFS interface with an S3 object store behind a local cache. Both the gateway and the NFS-plus-S3 mapping are required.
questions.good_to_know: DataSync would be correct for scheduled online migration of the share. Transfer Family is for partners that must keep SFTP, FTPS, or FTP.

questions.q: A retail company runs an Auto Scaling group of Amazon EC2 web servers behind an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. Operators need CPU utilization on a graph, a threshold that pages the on-call channel, and scale-out when the fleet is hot. They do not need API caller identity or configuration-history reports. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Amazon CloudWatch metrics and alarms to notify and scale.
B. Search AWS CloudTrail for RunInstances when CPU is high.
C. Evaluate AWS Config rules against the Auto Scaling group.
D. Open AWS Systems Manager Session Manager on each instance.

questions.explain: CPU, paging, and scale-out are CloudWatch metrics and alarms. CloudTrail is API audit; Config is configuration compliance, not live utilization.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would be correct if the stem asked which principal launched or terminated instances. Config would win for whether the group’s settings stayed compliant over time.

questions.q: A payments team stores application logs in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Security wants a numeric metric whenever a log line contains PAYMENT_FAIL, and an alarm when that count exceeds a limit in five minutes. The team must not parse logs on Amazon EC2 and does not need a record of which IAM principal called which API. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS CloudTrail data events on the log group.
B. Record the log group with AWS Config and a conformance pack.
C. Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter and alarm on that metric.
D. Run AWS Systems Manager Inventory against the log group.

questions.explain: Metric filters derive CloudWatch metrics from log events, and alarms fire on those metrics. CloudTrail records API callers, not application log patterns.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would be the answer if investigators needed who called FilterLogEvents. Config would apply if the question was whether the log group’s retention setting stayed compliant.

questions.q: A site-reliability team supports a three-tier application in one VPC across two Availability Zones. They want one screen that graphs Amazon EC2 CPU, Application Load Balancer 5xx count, and Amazon RDS connections. The services already emit CloudWatch metrics. The team does not need API audit tables or configuration timelines. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Search AWS CloudTrail Event history to draw the graphs.
B. Create an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard with those metric widgets.
C. Export AWS Config snapshots to a spreadsheet each hour.
D. Use Systems Manager Session Manager to watch top on hosts.

questions.explain: Operational health visualization across metrics is a CloudWatch dashboard. CloudTrail and Config do not replace metric graphs for CPU, 5xx, and connections.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would be correct for who changed the load balancer. Config would be correct for how the RDS instance’s configuration changed over weeks.

questions.q: A media company stores objects in a private Amazon S3 bucket in one Region. Security investigators need the IAM principal, source IP address, and time that called DeleteBucket on that bucket yesterday. The bucket’s current public-access block setting is already known. The team needs the API activity event, not a configuration snapshot. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Open AWS Config timeline for the bucket’s public-access block.
B. Graph Amazon CloudWatch BucketSizeBytes for yesterday.
C. Read Systems Manager Inventory on a nearby EC2 instance.
D. Query AWS CloudTrail event history for DeleteBucket.

questions.explain: Who called which API, from which IP, and when is CloudTrail. Config shows how the resource was configured, not the caller record.
questions.good_to_know: Config would be correct if the stem asked whether the bucket was public and how that setting changed. CloudWatch would win for storage size or request metrics.

questions.q: A company must record which IAM principal read a specific object in a private Amazon S3 bucket, including the source IP. An organization trail already logs management events. Object-level GetObject activity is not captured today. Configuration history of the bucket policy is out of scope. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable CloudTrail data events for that S3 bucket on the trail.
B. Turn on AWS Config recording for the bucket only.
C. Create a CloudWatch alarm on S3 BucketSizeBytes.
D. Store object keys in Systems Manager Parameter Store.

questions.explain: S3 object-level reads are data events, which a trail does not capture until you enable them. Management events cover control-plane calls such as CreateBucket, not GetObject.
questions.good_to_know: Management events alone would be enough if the stem asked who created or deleted the bucket. Config would win for whether the bucket policy was public, not who downloaded an object.

questions.q: A security team governs a growing AWS Organizations structure with many member accounts. They must collect API history from every account into one destination bucket. New member accounts must emit events without a per-account setup ticket. The team needs caller identity and source IP, not resource configuration snapshots. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS Config in the management account only.
B. Create a CloudWatch dashboard in each member account.
C. Create an organization trail in AWS CloudTrail for all accounts.
D. Use Systems Manager Automation as the organization audit log.

questions.explain: An organization trail centralizes API audit from current and future member accounts. Config snapshots are configuration state, not the caller-and-IP record.
questions.good_to_know: Control Tower would appear if the stem also required a landing zone, account vending, and guardrails rather than only a multi-account trail. Per-account trails would fail the no-ticket-for-new-accounts constraint.

questions.q: A healthcare company stores objects in Amazon S3 in one account. Compliance must prove whether a bucket was public last month and how its bucket policy and public-access block settings changed over that period. Investigators do not need the IAM user who called PutBucketPolicy and will not parse CloudWatch metrics for this proof. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Query CloudTrail only for the source IP of ListBuckets.
B. Use AWS Config configuration history for the bucket.
C. Graph CPU on an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard.
D. Open Session Manager to inspect the bucket.

questions.explain: Was the bucket public and how configuration changed is Config history. CloudTrail answers who called the API, which this stem explicitly does not need.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would be correct if the stem asked which principal and IP issued PutBucketPolicy. Use both when auditors want caller identity and configuration timeline.

questions.q: A bank runs Amazon EC2 in a VPC with many security groups. It requires continuous evaluation of whether those groups allow inbound 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22. Operations wants noncompliant groups listed over time against a desired condition. The question is configuration compliance, not which principal changed a rule yesterday. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Search AWS CloudTrail for AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress.
B. Create a CloudWatch alarm on NetworkIn.
C. Run Systems Manager Patch Manager on the security groups.
D. Deploy an AWS Config rule that flags SSH open to the world.

questions.explain: Config rules evaluate resource configuration against a desired condition and keep a compliance history. CloudTrail would identify who changed a rule, not whether the current config is compliant.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail is the answer when investigators need the identity and source IP for the API that opened port 22. Conformance packs group many such rules when the stem asks for a pack rather than one rule.

questions.q: A software company runs Amazon EC2 application instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. Administrators must open a shell on those instances. The security team forbids inbound SSH, bastion hosts, and distributing SSH keys. Instances already run the SSM Agent and can reach Systems Manager. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager for the shells.
B. Launch a bastion in a public subnet and allow port 22.
C. Allocate Elastic IPs and open SSH in the security group.
D. Use CloudFormation drift detection to open a console.

questions.explain: Session Manager brokers IAM-controlled shells without inbound SSH, bastions, or host keys. A bastion still needs inbound access, which the stem forbids.
questions.good_to_know: A bastion would appear if Session Manager were unavailable and inbound SSH from a locked CIDR were allowed. CloudFormation provisions infrastructure; it is not an interactive shell.

questions.q: A company runs a fleet of Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets behind an Application Load Balancer. It must apply OS patches on a schedule and report patch compliance. Operators will not log in to each host, will not open inbound SSH, and will not build a custom patch farm on EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable CloudTrail log file validation on the trail.
B. Create a CloudWatch alarm on StatusCheckFailed.
C. Use Systems Manager Patch Manager with a maintenance window.
D. Run Control Tower Account Factory every week.

questions.explain: Patch Manager plus a maintenance window is the managed fleet-patching path. CloudTrail validation protects log integrity; it does not patch operating systems.
questions.good_to_know: Session Manager would be correct if the stem asked for an interactive shell without SSH. Inventory would win if the need were installed-package lists rather than applying patches.

questions.q: Amazon EC2 application servers must retrieve a runtime configuration string and an API endpoint URL without baking them into the AMI. The operations team already uses AWS Systems Manager and does not want a custom configuration database. Rotation of database credentials is not in scope. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Put the strings in a CloudWatch dashboard widget.
B. Store the values in Systems Manager Parameter Store.
C. Record them as AWS Config custom resources only.
D. Write them into CloudTrail event history.

questions.explain: Parameter Store is the Systems Manager store for configuration strings the fleet can retrieve at runtime. Dashboards, Config, and CloudTrail are not a parameter database.
questions.good_to_know: AWS Secrets Manager would be the nearer answer if the stem required managed rotation of database credentials. Config would win for tracking whether an instance’s recorded configuration stayed compliant.

questions.q: A platform team manages Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets with the SSM Agent installed. Operators must run a documented multi-step runbook: stop a process, apply a patch document, then restart a service. They will not SSH to each host and will not write a custom orchestrator on EC2. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use a CloudWatch dashboard as the runbook engine.
B. Use CloudTrail log file validation to sequence steps.
C. Use Control Tower guardrails to reboot instances.
D. Use Systems Manager Automation documents for the runbook.

questions.explain: Systems Manager Automation runs multi-step operational documents against managed instances without inbound SSH. Dashboards and trails do not orchestrate a patch-and-restart runbook.
questions.good_to_know: Patch Manager alone would be enough if the stem only required scheduled OS patching. Session Manager would win for an interactive shell rather than an unattended runbook.

questions.q: An application team must provision the same VPC, subnets, and Auto Scaling group in three AWS accounts in one Region. Console clicking last quarter produced drift between accounts. The company wants declarative templates and repeatable updates rather than a runbook of console steps or a new landing zone. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Define the resources in AWS CloudFormation and deploy each stack.
B. Document the clicks in Systems Manager OpsCenter.
C. Track the VPCs with CloudWatch metrics only.
D. Enable Trusted Advisor and recreate resources by hand.

questions.explain: CloudFormation is infrastructure as code for repeatable stacks across accounts. Ops notes and Trusted Advisor checks do not provision the network as a template.
questions.good_to_know: Control Tower would be correct if the stem required a governed landing zone and account vending, not only identical application stacks. Drift detection then finds later console edits on those stacks.

questions.q: A platform team deployed an Application Load Balancer and security groups from an AWS CloudFormation stack in one account. An engineer later changed a listener in the console. Operators need to identify which stack resources no longer match the template before the next update and are not asking who made the API call. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable CloudTrail Insights on the organization trail.
B. Create a CloudWatch anomaly detection alarm on RequestCount.
C. Run CloudFormation drift detection on the stack.
D. Enroll the account in Control Tower again.

questions.explain: Drift detection compares supported resources’ actual configuration with the stack template. CloudTrail Insights looks for unusual API activity, not template divergence.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would tell you who changed the listener. AWS Config would show the security group’s configuration history even for resources not in a stack.

questions.q: A company is expanding from one AWS account to many member accounts in AWS Organizations. New accounts must receive a repeatable baseline, centralized logging, and preventive or detective controls without a custom landing-zone engineering project. Account vending must be self-service for approved application teams. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create CloudWatch dashboards in the existing account.
B. Use AWS Control Tower for the landing zone and Account Factory.
C. Use Systems Manager Session Manager as the landing zone.
D. Enable AWS Config in a single Region of one account.

questions.explain: Control Tower establishes a landing zone, guardrails, and Account Factory on Organizations. Config in one account does not vend accounts or install the baseline.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFormation alone would be correct for repeating one application stack, not a multi-account landing zone. Organizations without Control Tower would still leave landing-zone assembly to the customer.

questions.q: A solutions architect reviews a single AWS account that already runs production workloads. They need best-practice checks for idle load balancers, unassociated Elastic IP addresses, and MFA on the root user. The company does not need a new multi-account landing zone. Support already includes the relevant Trusted Advisor checks. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an organization CloudTrail trail only.
B. Deploy AWS Control Tower Account Factory.
C. Open AWS Health Dashboard for a Regional service event.
D. Review AWS Trusted Advisor recommendations in the account.

questions.explain: Trusted Advisor surfaces best-practice checks on the account, including cost and security findings when the support level includes them. Health Dashboard reports AWS service events, not idle-EIP checks.
questions.good_to_know: Health Dashboard would be correct if AWS had an incident affecting a service you use. Control Tower would win for landing-zone account vending rather than in-account best-practice checks.

questions.q: A company runs over-provisioned Amazon EC2 instances and Auto Scaling groups in one production Region. CloudWatch utilization metrics already exist. The team wants machine-learning recommendations to right-size those supported resources. They are not asking who called RunInstances and are not building a landing zone. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS Compute Optimizer and review the findings.
B. Search CloudTrail for instance-family changes.
C. Use AWS Config conformance packs for encryption.
D. Start AWS Control Tower in the management account.

questions.explain: Compute Optimizer recommends rightsizing for supported resources from utilization metrics. CloudTrail identifies API callers; it does not recommend instance sizes.
questions.good_to_know: Trusted Advisor also has some cost checks, but Compute Optimizer is the rightsizing-recommendation service the stem asked for. Cost Explorer (Lesson 16) analyzes spend; it does not output EC2 size findings.

questions.q: An application team runs Amazon RDS in one Region and must know when AWS has a service event that affects those databases. They do not need rightsizing advice, a new account factory, or an API caller list. On-call engineers should see AWS-side incidents, not only their own CloudWatch CPU alarms. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable AWS Compute Optimizer on the RDS instances.
B. Create a Control Tower landing zone.
C. Monitor the AWS Health Dashboard for events on those resources.
D. Run CloudFormation drift detection every hour.

questions.explain: Health Dashboard reports AWS events that affect services and resources. Compute Optimizer rightsizes; Control Tower vends accounts; drift compares templates.
questions.good_to_know: Trusted Advisor would be correct for best-practice findings about your configuration, such as idle resources. CloudWatch alarms would win for your RDS CPU, not an AWS Regional service event.

questions.q: A support team stores API error lines in Amazon CloudWatch Logs. They need a custom metric counted from matching log events and an alarm that pages when errors spike. They will not run a parser on EC2 and do not need configuration snapshots. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the error pattern.
B. Enable AWS Config recording on the log group.
C. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the metric the filter produces.
D. Use CloudTrail LookupEvents as the paging alarm.
E. Start Session Manager on the log group.

questions.explain: A metric filter turns matching log events into a metric, and an alarm on that metric pages the team. Both steps are required for log-derived alerting.
questions.good_to_know: Config would be correct if the need were log-group retention compliance. CloudTrail would win for who called PutLogEvents, not application error lines.

questions.q: Security must audit which principal called DeleteDBInstance in every member account of AWS Organizations, including source IP. New Organization accounts must be included automatically without a per-account trail ticket. Configuration compliance of the Amazon RDS databases is out of scope. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable an AWS Config rule for RDS public access only.
B. Create an organization CloudTrail trail in the management account.
C. Create a CloudWatch dashboard of FreeStorageSpace only.
D. Ensure management events are logged on that trail.
E. Use Systems Manager Inventory as the API audit log.

questions.explain: DeleteDBInstance is a management event. An organization trail with management events supplies caller and IP from every current and future member account.
questions.good_to_know: Config would be correct if the stem asked whether instances were publicly accessible. Data events would appear if the need were S3 object-level reads rather than control-plane deletes.

questions.q: Auditors review Amazon S3 buckets in one AWS account. They ask whether any bucket is public and how each bucket’s public-access block settings changed over the last 90 days. They are not asking which IAM user called PutBucketAcl and do not need CloudWatch object-count graphs. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Rely only on CloudTrail Insights for bucket size.
B. Graph S3 NumberOfObjects in CloudWatch.
C. Record the buckets with AWS Config.
D. Store the bucket names in Parameter Store.
E. Deploy a Config rule that flags public bucket access.

questions.explain: Config recording supplies configuration history; a Config rule evaluates whether buckets are public. Together they answer state-over-time and compliance, not API caller identity.
questions.good_to_know: CloudTrail would be the pair with a trail if the stem asked who made the bucket public. CloudWatch object-count graphs do not show public-access configuration.

questions.q: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. Operators need interactive shells on those instances. Security forbids inbound SSH, bastion hosts, and SSH key distribution. Instances already run the SSM Agent and can reach Systems Manager endpoints. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Attach an IAM instance profile that allows Session Manager.
B. Allocate a public IP and allow tcp/22 from 0.0.0.0/0.
C. Deploy a bastion Auto Scaling group in a public subnet.
D. Use CloudFormation drift detection to open SSH.
E. Connect with Session Manager instead of opening port 22.

questions.explain: Session Manager needs IAM permissions on the instance role and is the shell path that avoids inbound SSH. Bastions and public port 22 violate the security constraint.
questions.good_to_know: A VPC endpoint for Systems Manager would appear if the stem said instances had no NAT and still must not use the internet path. Patch Manager would win for scheduled OS patching rather than a shell.

questions.q: A platform team must deploy identical VPC networking stacks in two AWS accounts from one template and later detect console edits that diverged from that template. Click-ops is not acceptable for the initial build, and the company is not asking for a Control Tower landing zone. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Recreate the VPCs weekly from Trusted Advisor.
B. Deploy the network from an AWS CloudFormation template.
C. Run CloudFormation drift detection after the stacks exist.
D. Use CloudWatch alarms as the source of network state.
E. Capture the VPC with Systems Manager Inventory only.

questions.explain: CloudFormation provides the repeatable template; drift detection then finds resources that no longer match it. Both are required for the build-and-detect story.
questions.good_to_know: AWS Config would still track configuration if the resources were not in a stack. Control Tower would be the answer for a full landing zone rather than one network template.

questions.q: A company is moving from one AWS account to many. It needs a governed multi-account landing zone, self-service account vending, and guardrails on organizational units. A single AWS Config recorder in one account is not enough, and CloudWatch dashboards are not an account factory. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Replace Organizations with a CloudWatch dashboard.
B. Use Session Manager as the account factory.
C. Disable CloudTrail so Config can govern APIs.
D. Set up AWS Control Tower on AWS Organizations.
E. Use Account Factory to vend standardized accounts.

questions.explain: Control Tower on Organizations is the landing-zone service; Account Factory is how approved teams vend accounts with the baseline. Config alone does not provision accounts.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFormation would still deploy individual stacks inside those accounts. Organizations without Control Tower leaves landing-zone guardrails and vending as a custom project.

questions.q: A platform team in a shared AWS account must let projects launch only approved AMIs from a catalog and must track Windows Server license counts on Amazon EC2 against entitlements. Ad-hoc console stacks and untracked BYOL instances are forbidden. The team is not building a landing zone. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Publish the AMIs as AWS Service Catalog products.
B. Define AWS License Manager rules for the Windows entitlements.
C. Use CloudWatch dashboards as the launch catalog.
D. Rely on CloudTrail Insights to block extra licenses.
E. Open AWS Health Dashboard before each launch.

questions.explain: Service Catalog constrains teams to approved products. License Manager tracks and can enforce license entitlements. The two governance needs are independent and both required.
questions.good_to_know: Control Tower would appear if the stem required account vending and landing-zone guardrails. CloudTrail would win for who launched an instance, not for license counting or a product catalog.

questions.q: A company runs Amazon EC2 web servers behind an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones. CloudWatch shows 12 percent CPU and low memory. Finance wants a lower bill before any one-year commitment. The application must keep the same architecture and Multi-AZ placement. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST ongoing compute cost?

options.text: A. Right-size the instances to a smaller type that still meets performance.
B. Buy a Compute Savings Plan sized to the current oversized fleet.
C. Move the fleet to Dedicated Hosts in the same subnets.
D. Add read replicas of Amazon RDS that the web tier does not use.

questions.explain: Right-size from measured utilization before buying a commitment. A Savings Plan on oversized instances locks in waste. Dedicated Hosts and unused replicas raise cost.
questions.good_to_know: A Compute Savings Plan would be next after the fleet is sized to real load and the remaining baseline is predictable. Auto Scaling would win if the stem said idle peak capacity stayed provisioned all day.

questions.q: An ecommerce site provisions Amazon EC2 capacity for Black Friday all year because last year’s peak required that many instances. Daily traffic is far lower. The architecture already uses an Application Load Balancer. Finance wants idle peak capacity not to remain a permanent bill. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Buy Standard Reserved Instances for the Black Friday instance count.
B. Move the entire site to Dedicated Hosts for the year.
C. Put the instances in an Auto Scaling group that scales in after peaks.
D. Disable CloudWatch metrics so scaling cannot inflate cost.

questions.explain: Auto Scaling lets peak capacity exist only while load needs it. Committing to last year’s peak as Reserved Instances makes that idle cost permanent.
questions.good_to_know: Savings Plans would cover a measured steady baseline after scale-in is in place. Spot would appear if the extra peak work were interruptible batch rather than customer-facing web.

questions.q: A company has a predictable minimum compute spend for three years across Amazon EC2, but may change instance families, operating systems, and Regions. Some of the same spend also runs on AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. The team wants one commitment that still discounts those compute types and will not use Spot for this baseline. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances for one instance family.
B. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the baseline spend.
C. Purchase Dedicated Hosts in a single Availability Zone.
D. Run the entire baseline on Spot Instances only.

questions.explain: Compute Savings Plans apply across eligible EC2 families, sizes, OS, tenancy, and Regions, and also to Fargate and Lambda. Standard RIs and Dedicated Hosts do not follow those moves.
questions.good_to_know: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan would be correct if the stem locked the family in one Region and did not need Fargate or Lambda coverage. Spot would win only for interruption-tolerant capacity, not a noninterruptible baseline.

questions.q: FinOps already right-sized a steady Amazon EC2 fleet that runs 24 hours a day in one Region. Next year the same spend may move to a different instance family in another Region. The workload cannot tolerate Spot interruption and is not a Reserved Instance lock-in to one size. Which commitment gives the MOST flexibility while still discounting that predictable compute?

options.text: A. A Standard Reserved Instance for the current family and size
B. An On-Demand Capacity Reservation only
C. Spot Instances with a one-year duration
D. A Compute Savings Plan

questions.explain: Compute Savings Plans continue to apply when family and Region change. Standard RIs are tied to a specific family, size, OS, and Region. Capacity Reservations hold capacity; they are not the discount vehicle.
questions.good_to_know: EC2 Instance Savings Plans discount a family in a Region more deeply but fail the cross-family and cross-Region constraint. Convertible RIs are still EC2-only and less flexible than a Compute Savings Plan.

questions.q: A genomics lab runs fault-tolerant batch jobs on Amazon EC2 in one VPC. Workers checkpoint results to Amazon S3 and resume if a node is reclaimed. The scheduler can replace interrupted workers. Finance wants the deepest compute discount that still fits interruption and will not buy Dedicated Hosts for this fleet. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Run the workers on Spot Instances.
B. Buy Dedicated Hosts for the entire batch fleet.
C. Use On-Demand Capacity Reservations for every worker.
D. Purchase Standard Reserved Instances sized to peak batch.

questions.explain: Spot uses spare capacity at a steep discount and can be interrupted, which checkpointed, replaceable batch can accept. Reservations and Dedicated Hosts raise cost without matching that model.
questions.good_to_know: On-Demand or a Savings Plan would be correct for the noninterruptible scheduler. Lesson 03 owns mixed-instance interruption architecture; this item is the cost choice once the work is already fault-tolerant.

questions.q: Application logs land in Amazon S3 Standard. After 90 days they are almost never read, and legal still requires them for four years. Restores may take hours. Operations wants Amazon S3 to move objects automatically by age and does not want a nightly copy job. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Set the bucket to S3 Intelligent-Tiering and skip age-based rules.
B. Copy objects to Amazon EBS snapshots every 90 days.
C. Add a lifecycle rule that transitions objects to Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days.
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the log bucket.

questions.explain: Known age, rare access, and long retention are a lifecycle transition into an archive class. Intelligent-Tiering is for unknown access, not a fixed 90-day archive handoff.
questions.good_to_know: Intelligent-Tiering would win if access patterns were unknown or changing. Glacier Instant Retrieval would appear if rare reads still needed millisecond access.

questions.q: A media company stores millions of long-lived objects in Amazon S3. Access frequency varies by title and changes over months, so the team cannot pick a fixed lifecycle day. Objects must stay immediately available. Operations wants Amazon S3 to move objects between access tiers automatically. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use S3 One Zone-IA for every new object.
B. Use the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class.
C. Transition every object to Glacier Deep Archive on upload.
D. Keep every object in S3 Standard with no tiering.

questions.explain: Unknown or changing access plus immediate availability is Intelligent-Tiering. Deep Archive requires a restore. One Zone-IA is a single-AZ infrequent class, not automatic multi-tier movement.
questions.good_to_know: A lifecycle rule would be correct if age were known (for example, archive after 90 days). One Zone-IA would win if infrequent access and a single-AZ cost trade-off were explicit.

questions.q: A backup application writes large objects to Amazon S3. Objects are read only a few times a month but must remain immediately available.
