The company can accept storing them in a single Availability Zone to reduce cost. A zone failure may require rebuilding backups from the source. Which storage class will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. S3 Standard
B. S3 Glacier Deep Archive
C. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access
D. S3 One Zone-Infrequent Access

questions.explain: Infrequent access, immediate reads, and an explicit single-AZ cost trade-off select One Zone-IA. Standard-IA still stores across AZs; Deep Archive is not immediately available.
questions.good_to_know: Standard-IA is the answer when infrequent access must still survive an Availability Zone failure. Intelligent-Tiering would win if access were unknown rather than known-infrequent.

questions.q: Amazon EC2 workers in private subnets in one VPC download terabytes from Amazon S3 through a NAT gateway every night, and NAT data-processing charges dominate the bill. The buckets stay in the same Region. Instances must remain private and must not use public IP addresses. Which change most directly removes those NAT processing charges for the S3 traffic?

options.text: A. Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and route S3 traffic through it.
B. Scale the NAT gateway to a larger size.
C. Add a second internet gateway in another Availability Zone.
D. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the buckets.

questions.explain: An S3 gateway endpoint keeps that Regional S3 path off the NAT gateway and has no hourly endpoint charge. A larger NAT still bills per-GB processing.
questions.good_to_know: An interface endpoint would appear for services that lack a gateway endpoint, and it does have hourly charges. Transfer Acceleration is a long-distance transfer feature, not a NAT bypass.

questions.q: Application servers in private subnets send high request volumes to Amazon DynamoDB through a NAT gateway. NAT processing cost is rising. The table is in the same Region as the VPC. Servers must not use public IP addresses and must not move to public subnets. Which solution will meet these requirements MOST cost-effectively?

options.text: A. Place a NAT instance in front of the existing NAT gateway.
B. Move the servers to public subnets with Elastic IP addresses.
C. Add a DynamoDB gateway VPC endpoint and route table entries.
D. Enable DynamoDB Streams and read through the NAT gateway.

questions.explain: DynamoDB, like S3, supports a gateway VPC endpoint so private instances reach the service without NAT processing charges. Public IPs violate the private-server constraint.
questions.good_to_know: An S3 gateway endpoint is the same pattern when the heavy traffic is S3 instead of DynamoDB. Interface endpoints are the PrivateLink pattern for other AWS APIs and are not the zero-hourly-charge gateway path.

questions.q: Last month AWS spend in a multi-account organization rose sharply. Leadership wants to know which service, account, and usage type drove the increase. The team needs an interactive breakdown over time before they buy any commitment. Threshold email alerts are not the immediate need. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS budget that emails when cost exceeds last month.
B. Analyze the increase in AWS Cost Explorer by service, account, and usage type.
C. Open AWS Health Dashboard for Regional incidents.
D. Enable CloudTrail Insights on the organization trail.

questions.explain: Cost Explorer is the tool for why spend rose, sliced by service, account, tag, and usage type. Budgets notify at a threshold; they do not explain the driver.
questions.good_to_know: The Cost and Usage Report would be correct if the stem demanded the most detailed line-item export for analysis in Athena or a BI tool. Budgets would win if the ask were a threshold notification.

questions.q: Finance wants an email when actual or forecasted AWS cost in a linked account exceeds a monthly dollar threshold. The workloads already run in that account. The team does not need a full line-item export and is not yet investigating a past spike in Cost Explorer. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use Cost Explorer only, without a notification.
B. Enable AWS Compute Optimizer in the account.
C. Turn on AWS CloudTrail log file validation.
D. Create an AWS budget with email notifications at that threshold.

questions.explain: AWS Budgets exist to notify (and optionally act) when actual or forecasted cost or usage crosses a threshold. Cost Explorer analyzes history; it does not send that threshold email by itself.
questions.good_to_know: Cost Explorer would be correct for diagnosing why last month rose. CUR would win for a detailed export. Compute Optimizer recommends rightsizing, not budget emails.

questions.q: A FinOps analyst in a payer account needs the most detailed AWS billing and usage line items, including resource IDs where available, delivered on a schedule for custom analysis. Cost Explorer’s interactive view is not granular enough for this request. Threshold email is already configured. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Enable the AWS Cost and Usage Report to an Amazon S3 bucket.
B. Create an AWS budget with a 50 percent actual-cost alert.
C. Open Trusted Advisor cost checks only.
D. Graph Amazon CloudWatch Billing EstimatedCharges.

questions.explain: The Cost and Usage Report is the detailed billing and usage export. Budgets alert; they are not a line-item feed. CloudWatch estimated charges are a coarse metric.
questions.good_to_know: Cost Explorer would be enough if the stem only needed an interactive breakdown of why spend rose. Athena against CUR is a common next step; lake layout itself belongs to Lesson 13.

questions.q: After a traffic drop, several Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling groups and Amazon EBS volumes in one Region look oversized. The team wants service-generated rightsizing recommendations from utilization rather than guessing families. They are not asking for a spend-spike explanation in Cost Explorer and will not buy a Savings Plan on the current size. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create an AWS budget with a forecasted-cost alert.
B. Enable the Cost and Usage Report only.
C. Review AWS Compute Optimizer recommendations for those resources.
D. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan at the current oversized size.

questions.explain: Compute Optimizer produces rightsizing findings for supported EC2, ASG, and EBS resources from utilization. Buying a Savings Plan on oversized capacity freezes the waste.
questions.good_to_know: Cost Explorer would be correct for attributing a bill increase. Right-size first, then commit a Savings Plan to the remaining predictable baseline.

questions.q: Three product teams share one AWS account that runs Amazon EC2 and Amazon S3. Finance must allocate that cost to each team in Cost Explorer. Resource names are inconsistent. The company will not split into three accounts this quarter and will not rely on Health Dashboard for allocation. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Create one AWS budget with no team dimension.
B. Apply cost allocation tags and activate them for Cost Explorer.
C. Enable AWS Health Dashboard in each Region.
D. Move all objects to S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval.

questions.explain: Tags, once activated as cost allocation tags, let Cost Explorer and CUR break spend down by team without a multi-account split. A single budget with no dimension does not allocate.
questions.good_to_know: Separate accounts in Organizations would also isolate bills if the stem allowed an account-per-team move. Budgets can filter on tags after those tags exist.

questions.q: A web application has a steady year-round Amazon EC2 baseline plus unpredictable peaks behind an Application Load Balancer. Peaks are not interruptible. The company wants discounted baseline hours without paying a commitment for peak capacity that often sits idle, and will not put the baseline on Spot. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Buy Reserved Instances equal to last year’s highest peak.
B. Run the baseline and the peaks entirely on Spot Instances.
C. Place the baseline on Dedicated Hosts and the peaks on Spot.
D. Cover the measured baseline with a Compute Savings Plan and run peaks On-Demand.

questions.explain: Commit only the predictable baseline; On-Demand (or Auto Scaling) covers uncertain peaks. Committing to peak wastes money. Spot is unsafe for noninterruptible work.
questions.good_to_know: Spot would join the design if the stem marked the peaks as fault-tolerant batch. Right-size the baseline before choosing the Savings Plan amount.

questions.q: A storage review of a production AWS account finds years of unused Amazon EBS snapshots and unattached volumes left after instance replacements. Retention policy allows deletion of backups older than 35 days. The company wants that waste gone without changing the running application architecture or buying a compute commitment. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Delete obsolete snapshots and unattached volumes that policy allows.
B. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the idle volumes.
C. Move the unattached volumes to S3 Glacier Deep Archive.
D. Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on each EBS volume.

questions.explain: Idle snapshots and unattached volumes are a common bill leak; delete what retention allows. Savings Plans do not discount leftover EBS. Intelligent-Tiering is an S3 class, not an EBS setting.
questions.good_to_know: AWS Backup lifecycle would automate snapshot expiration if the stem asked for a managed retention plan going forward. S3 lifecycle would win for objects, not EBS volumes.

questions.q: An Amazon RDS for MySQL instance supports a three-tier application in one Region. CloudWatch CPU and connections stay low. Reads are not the bottleneck. The company wants a lower database bill without adding components that do not address a stated need, such as unused read replicas. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Add two read replicas to spread write traffic.
B. Place a NAT gateway in front of RDS.
C. Right-size the RDS instance class to measured utilization.
D. Buy Dedicated Hosts for the RDS instance.

questions.explain: Right-size the database to utilization. Read replicas solve read scale and add cost when reads are not the problem. A NAT gateway is not a database rightsizing tool.
questions.good_to_know: Read replicas would be correct if the stem required read scale-out. A serverless or autoscaling database option would appear if the load were highly variable rather than steadily oversized.

questions.q: A company wants to cut a predictable Amazon EC2 web-tier bill in one Region. CloudWatch shows the instances are oversized, and the remaining 24/7 load is steady for the next year. The team may later change instance family and will not move the web tier to Spot. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Right-size the instances to measured CPU and memory.
B. Buy Standard Reserved Instances for last year’s peak count.
C. Purchase a Compute Savings Plan for the remaining baseline.
D. Move the web tier to Spot Instances only.
E. Place every instance on a Dedicated Host.

questions.explain: Right-size first so the commitment is not bought on waste, then a Compute Savings Plan discounts the predictable leftover baseline and still allows family changes.
questions.good_to_know: Auto Scaling would be the extra step if idle peak capacity stayed up all year. Spot would be correct only if the web tier could tolerate interruption.

questions.q: Private Amazon EC2 jobs in one VPC pull large Amazon S3 datasets through a NAT gateway, driving processing charges. The buckets are in the same Region. Instances must stay in private subnets and must not receive Elastic IP addresses. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Resize the NAT gateway to process more gigabytes.
B. Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint in the VPC.
C. Attach Elastic IP addresses to the workers.
D. Update route tables so S3 prefixes use the endpoint, not NAT.
E. Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on every bucket.

questions.explain: A gateway endpoint plus routes that send S3 traffic to it removes that path from NAT processing. Both the endpoint and the routes are required.
questions.good_to_know: The same pair with a DynamoDB gateway endpoint would apply if the heavy private traffic were DynamoDB. A larger NAT does not remove per-byte processing.

questions.q: A media company stores millions of objects in Amazon S3 in one bucket. Access is changing and unpredictable. The company wants automatic cost-tier movement without guessing lifecycle dates, and objects in the frequent and infrequent tiers must remain immediately readable. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Transition every object to Glacier Deep Archive on day one.
B. Use S3 One Zone-IA for all objects regardless of AZ risk.
C. Store the objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering.
D. Keep all objects in S3 Standard with Transfer Acceleration.
E. Leave optional Intelligent-Tiering Archive Access tiers disabled.

questions.explain: Intelligent-Tiering monitors access and moves eligible objects among online tiers. Leaving optional Archive Access tiers disabled keeps millisecond reads. Deep Archive on upload would violate immediate availability.
questions.good_to_know: A lifecycle transition would be correct if age and rarity were known. One Zone-IA would win only with an explicit single-AZ cost trade-off.

questions.q: Leadership asks why last quarter’s AWS bill rose and which product team caused it in a shared account. Resources already have a Team tag, but Cost Explorer does not split on it yet. The team also wants an interactive view by service and is not asking for a budget email. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Activate the Team tag as a cost allocation tag.
B. Create only an AWS budget with no dimensions.
C. Open AWS Health Dashboard for the quarter.
D. Disable CloudWatch so metrics cannot increase cost.
E. Analyze spend in Cost Explorer by service and the Team tag.

questions.explain: Cost allocation tags must be activated before Cost Explorer can group on them. Explorer then answers why spend rose by service and team. Both steps are required.
questions.good_to_know: CUR would be the detailed export if Explorer were not enough. Budgets would add a threshold email after you already know how to slice the bill.

questions.q: Finance must receive email when a linked account’s actual monthly AWS cost exceeds a dollar threshold and again if the forecast is expected to exceed it. Workloads already run in that account. They do not need a line-item dump to Amazon S3 for this request. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Enable the Cost and Usage Report as the only control.
B. Create an AWS budget for that account and monthly amount.
C. Enable actual-cost and forecasted-cost notifications on the budget.
D. Use Compute Optimizer findings as the email system.
E. Graph CloudWatch EstimatedCharges without a threshold.

questions.explain: Budgets are the threshold tool; actual and forecasted notifications are the two alerts the stem asked for. CUR is a detailed export, not that email path.
questions.good_to_know: Cost Explorer would explain a past spike. A budget action could stop resources if the stem added an automated response, not only email.

questions.q: A company has a noninterruptible 24/7 Amazon EC2 control plane in one Region and a large fault-tolerant batch fleet that checkpoints to Amazon S3. Finance wants discounts on the steady control plane and the deepest discount on the batch workers. The control plane must not run on Spot. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Run the control plane on Spot Instances as well.
B. Buy Dedicated Hosts for every batch worker.
C. Purchase Reserved Instances equal to peak batch size.
D. Cover the control plane with a Compute Savings Plan.
E. Run the batch workers on Spot Instances.

questions.explain: Savings Plans fit predictable, noninterruptible baseline compute. Spot fits interruption-tolerant batch. Putting the control plane on Spot violates the noninterruptible constraint.
questions.good_to_know: On-Demand would cover control-plane hours if the baseline were still too uncertain to commit. Lesson 03 covers how to architect Spot interruption; this item is the purchasing split.

questions.q: A FinOps team in a payer account needs both an interactive view of why last month’s spend rose by service and a scheduled, highly detailed usage export for custom reports. Threshold email is already handled with AWS Budgets. They are not asking for rightsizing findings. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use Cost Explorer to break down the monthly increase by service.
B. Enable the AWS Cost and Usage Report to Amazon S3.
C. Create another AWS budget as the detailed export.
D. Use AWS Health Dashboard as the billing line-item source.
E. Turn on CloudTrail Insights to explain the bill.

questions.explain: Cost Explorer answers why spend rose in an interactive view. CUR is the detailed export for custom analysis. Budgets and Health do not replace either feed.
questions.good_to_know: Athena on CUR can query line items; do not treat lake file layout as the Lesson 16 answer. Compute Optimizer would appear if the need were EC2 rightsizing findings rather than billing detail.

questions.q: A company needs a public HTTPS website that stays available if one Availability Zone fails. Application instances must remain in private subnets behind a load balancer. The relational database must fail over automatically. The stem asks for the LEAST operational overhead among designs that meet those constraints. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Route 53 and an ALB to a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group, plus Multi-AZ RDS.
B. One public EC2 instance with MySQL on the same host.
C. Two EC2 instances in one AZ, each running self-managed MySQL.
D. Public EC2 instances in two AZs with a single-AZ RDS instance.

questions.explain: Underline private app, AZ failure, and least ops: ALB plus Multi-AZ compute and managed Multi-AZ RDS is the three-tier pattern. Public instances and self-managed MySQL violate private or operations constraints.
questions.good_to_know: Self-managed MySQL across AZs could meet availability if the stem allowed higher operational overhead. A serverless API would win if the stem forbade servers and did not require a relational engine on RDS.

questions.q: A new JSON API must handle unpredictable bursts of millions of requests and store items in a key-value model. The company wants the LEAST operational overhead and will not manage Amazon EC2 or container hosts. End users will authenticate with a hosted user pool. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. An ALB, an EC2 Auto Scaling group, and self-managed MySQL.
B. ECS on EC2 in one AZ and an RDS instance in that AZ.
C. API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, and Amazon Cognito.
D. A single public EC2 instance running the API process.

questions.explain: Unpredictable scale plus least ops and no servers selects the serverless API pattern. Cognito is the end-user identity piece of that pattern. EC2 and ECS-on-EC2 increase operations.
questions.good_to_know: ALB plus Auto Scaling would be correct if the stem required a long-running three-tier app on instances. RDS Proxy would appear if a relational database were mandatory behind high Lambda concurrency.

questions.q: A retailer runs an order API that must acknowledge accepted orders even when fulfillment is slow or temporarily down. Fulfillment workers already exist in private subnets and can poll for work. The company must not chain every fulfillment call on the user request path and will not keep orders only in instance memory. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Call each fulfillment microservice synchronously from the API.
B. Put an Amazon SQS queue between order acceptance and fulfillment.
C. Store pending orders only in instance memory on the API hosts.
D. Increase the Route 53 TTL on the API record.

questions.explain: Decouple and absorb downstream failure with a durable queue. Synchronous chaining and in-memory stores keep the user path coupled to fulfillment availability.
questions.good_to_know: SNS or EventBridge would join the design if the stem required fan-out to many independent consumers. A DLQ would appear if poison messages had to be isolated from the main queue.

questions.q: A business runs production in one AWS Region and can wait hours to recover a Regional outage and can lose up to a day’s data. Leadership wants the MOST cost-effective disaster recovery approach that still meets those objectives. Continuously running a second full environment is not required. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Multi-site active-active in two Regions at full production scale.
B. Warm standby sized equal to production in a second Region.
C. Synchronous writes to three Regions for every transaction.
D. Backup and restore, with recovery tested against the stated RTO and RPO.

questions.explain: Loose RTO and RPO make backup and restore the cost-effective starting point. Active-active and full warm standby overspend those objectives.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby or pilot light would be correct if RTO were minutes and RPO were small. Multi-site active-active would win only if near-zero RTO and RPO were hard requirements.

questions.q: Compliance states the database MUST stay in private subnets with no public IP. The application is a three-tier web app in one VPC. The question also asks for the LEAST operational overhead for a highly available relational engine. One option places Amazon RDS in public subnets. Which solution should a candidate select after eliminating constraint violators?

options.text: A. Amazon RDS Multi-AZ in private subnets.
B. Amazon RDS Multi-AZ in public subnets with a public IP.
C. Self-managed MySQL on a single EC2 instance in a private subnet.
D. Self-managed MySQL on two EC2 instances in public subnets.

questions.explain: Eliminate anything public first (MUST private), then among remaining valid designs pick managed Multi-AZ RDS for least ops. A single private EC2 database is a hidden single point of failure.
questions.good_to_know: Self-managed MySQL in two private AZs could survive an AZ failure if the stem allowed higher operational overhead. Public RDS would only appear if the private-subnet constraint were absent.

questions.q: A three-tier design already spreads Amazon EC2 behind an ALB across two Availability Zones in one VPC. The database is a single Amazon RDS instance in one AZ. The exam stem requires the application to remain available through an AZ failure. Operators will not solve this by moving all compute into the database AZ. Which change most directly removes the remaining single point of failure?

options.text: A. Add a second ALB in the same AZ as the database.
B. Increase EC2 instance size in the existing two AZs.
C. Convert the database to Amazon RDS Multi-AZ.
D. Move both EC2 groups into the database’s AZ.

questions.explain: Trace the full path: Multi-AZ compute does not help if the data tier is still one AZ. Multi-AZ RDS removes that hidden SPOF. Bigger instances and a second ALB in one AZ do not.
questions.good_to_know: A queue in front of workers would be the fix if the SPOF were a synchronous downstream dependency rather than the database AZ. Cross-Region replica would appear only if the stem were Regional DR, not AZ failure.

questions.q: On a practice item, two remaining answers both meet functional needs for a Multi-AZ workload. One is a self-managed cluster on Amazon EC2 that the team would patch and scale. The other is a managed AWS service with equivalent encryption and Multi-AZ controls. The stem says minimize operational overhead. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Choose the self-managed EC2 cluster.
B. Choose the managed AWS service.
C. Choose whichever written option is longer.
D. Choose the option that adds the most extra services.

questions.explain: When constraints are otherwise equal, least operational overhead selects the managed service. Length of the option text and extra services are not exam methods.
questions.good_to_know: The self-managed cluster would be correct if the stem required an OS-level agent or a feature the managed service does not offer. Always eliminate constraint violators before applying the ops superlative.

questions.q: A company must recover a production database in minutes with little data loss after a Regional event. Restoring last night’s backup from Amazon S3 would miss the recovery time. Leadership still wants to avoid running a second full-scale active-active environment in another Region. Which disaster recovery pattern should a solutions architect choose?

options.text: A. Backup and restore from Amazon S3 only.
B. Multi-site active-active at full production scale in both Regions.
C. A single-AZ RDS instance with no snapshots.
D. Warm standby in a second Region, sized to fail over within minutes.

questions.explain: Minutes of RTO with a small RPO need a running (or readily scaled) standby, not backup and restore. Full active-active overspends if the stem does not require it.
questions.good_to_know: Backup and restore would be correct if RTO were hours and RPO about a day. Pilot light sits between backup/restore and warm standby when a longer scale-out time is acceptable.

questions.q: A legacy HTTP application on Amazon EC2 in private subnets cannot be modified. Internet users must reach it over HTTPS. Instances must stay private across two Availability Zones behind a load balancer. The company will not assign public IP addresses to the application hosts. Which solution will meet these requirements without changing application code?

options.text: A. Terminate TLS on an Application Load Balancer with an ACM certificate.
B. Rewrite the application to terminate TLS in each process.
C. Assign public IP addresses and install certificates on every instance.
D. Replace the application with a new Lambda function this week.

questions.explain: No code changes plus HTTPS and private instances points to TLS termination on the load balancer. Rewriting the app or putting public IPs on hosts violates the constraints.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront with an ACM certificate would appear if the stem also required a global CDN in front of the origin. A Network Load Balancer would win for TLS passthrough of a non-HTTP protocol.

questions.q: A stem asks for the MOST cost-effective design that remains available if an Availability Zone fails. The current architecture is a three-tier web app with a relational database. One option uses a single AZ to save money. Another uses Multi-AZ compute and Multi-AZ RDS. Which option should a candidate choose?

options.text: A. The single-AZ design, because it is cheaper.
B. A single large instance to reduce the instance count.
C. The Multi-AZ compute and Multi-AZ database design.
D. A design that ignores the Availability Zone requirement.

questions.explain: Most cost-effective still has to meet every hard constraint. AZ failure is hard; a cheaper single-AZ answer is a violator, not a cost optimization.
questions.good_to_know: After Multi-AZ is satisfied, then compare remaining answers on cost (right size, avoid extra replicas, avoid active-active DR you do not need). Never drop a MUST for a lower bill.

questions.q: Several microservices in one AWS account must react independently to the same order-placed event. Each consumer needs its own durable buffer and scaling. A synchronous call chain from the order service is failing when one consumer is down. The publisher must not keep events only on local disk. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Have the order service call every consumer HTTP API in sequence.
B. Publish to Amazon SNS or EventBridge and give each consumer an SQS queue.
C. Store events only in the order service’s local disk.
D. Increase API Gateway throttling on the order service.

questions.explain: Event-driven fan-out is SNS or EventBridge plus a queue per consumer so each service scales and fails on its own. A synchronous chain couples availability.
questions.good_to_know: A single shared SQS queue would be enough if there were one consumer. A DLQ on each queue would appear if the stem required isolating poison messages.

questions.q: A company is connecting an on-premises data center to many AWS VPCs that must talk to each other and to the data center. The team wants a hub for routing rather than a full mesh of VPC peering. VPN or Direct Connect already reaches AWS. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Peer every VPC to every other VPC and to a VPN-only VPC.
B. Place all workloads in a single public subnet.
C. Use Amazon CloudFront as the east-west VPC router.
D. Attach the VPCs and the hybrid connection to AWS Transit Gateway.

questions.explain: The hybrid enterprise pattern is on-premises to VPN or Direct Connect into a Transit Gateway hub that attaches the VPCs. Peering does not transit and does not scale as a mesh.
questions.good_to_know: PrivateLink would be correct if a partner needed one service without broad network routing. VPC peering would win for a simple pair of VPCs with no transit requirement.

questions.q: A partner VPC must invoke one private application service that runs behind a Network Load Balancer in the company’s VPC. The company will not peer the VPCs, will not attach the partner to Transit Gateway, and will not expose the service on the internet. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Expose the service with AWS PrivateLink (an interface endpoint).
B. Create a VPC peering mesh that includes the partner CIDR.
C. Attach the partner VPC to the company’s Transit Gateway.
D. Put a public Network Load Balancer on the internet.

questions.explain: PrivateLink publishes a service without sharing the rest of the network. Peering, Transit Gateway, and a public NLB each violate a stated constraint.
questions.good_to_know: Transit Gateway would be correct if the partner needed many VPC routes and the company allowed a shared hub. A public ALB would win only if internet exposure were allowed.

questions.q: An Amazon SQS worker queue feeds fulfillment tasks from an order API. Some messages always fail and block retries for good work. The team wants failed messages isolated after a retry budget so operators can inspect them. Workers must keep polling the main queue. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Call the worker synchronously from API Gateway with no queue.
B. Store failed payloads only in the worker’s instance store.
C. Configure a dead-letter queue on the source SQS queue.
D. Disable the queue when any message fails once.

questions.explain: A DLQ isolates poison messages after maxReceiveCount so the main queue keeps moving. Removing the queue or using instance store couples failure and loses durability.
questions.good_to_know: Idempotent workers still matter because SQS can deliver a message more than once. EventBridge archive/replay would appear for bus-level recovery, not for an SQS poison-message path.

questions.q: A checkout path uses Multi-AZ Amazon EC2 behind an ALB but then calls a single Regional third-party HTTP API synchronously with no timeout or fallback. The exam requires high availability. Counting Availability Zones on the compute tier alone would miss this dependency. Which exam habit most directly reveals this hidden availability risk?

options.text: A. Count only how many Availability Zones the EC2 group uses.
B. Trace the full request and failure path, including external calls.
C. Select the newest AWS service in each option.
D. Ignore any dependency that is not an Amazon EC2 instance.

questions.explain: End-to-end tracing finds dependencies whose failure defeats otherwise redundant compute. Counting AZs alone misses a synchronous external SPOF.
questions.good_to_know: The architecture fix is often a queue, timeout, or graceful degradation once the hidden call is visible. Do not pick extra AWS services that do not sit on that failure path.

questions.q: A long scenario lists optional performance wishes and one MUST: application instances stay in private subnets. Two answers look similar; one assigns public IP addresses to the application tier. The item also asks for least LEAST operational overhead among otherwise valid designs. Which step should a candidate take first under time pressure?

options.text: A. Pick the public-IP design because it has fewer components.
B. Ignore the MUST and optimize only for latency.
C. Leave the question blank until after the exam.
D. Eliminate the public-IP design, then compare remaining answers on ops and cost.

questions.explain: Underline hard constraints and eliminate violators first. Fewer components does not rescue a MUST-private miss. Never leave an item blank.
questions.good_to_know: After elimination, use LEAST ops or MOST cost-effective among what remains. Flag a lengthy item and return if needed, but still submit an answer.

questions.q: Workforce users must sign in once to many AWS accounts in an Organization that is standing up a Control Tower landing zone. They need console and CLI access to those accounts. The company does not want a separate IAM user in every account and will not share the root password. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. Use IAM Identity Center with the Control Tower multi-account setup.
B. Create matching IAM users and access keys in each member account.
C. Share a single root password across accounts.
D. Disable AWS Organizations so each account is unmanaged.

questions.explain: The hybrid/enterprise pattern uses Organizations, Control Tower, and IAM Identity Center for workforce access across accounts. Per-account IAM users and shared root credentials violate that model.
questions.good_to_know: Amazon Cognito would be correct for application end users on a serverless API, not workforce access to the AWS Console. IAM users in one account would win only for a single-account shop.

questions.q: A public web application must stay up through an Availability Zone failure and absorb bursts of asynchronous report generation. Users hit HTTP on an ALB; reports may lag. The company wants Multi-AZ compute and does not want report work on the request path or on a single large instance. Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: A. One large EC2 instance that generates reports in the web request.
B. Synchronous HTTPS calls from the web tier to every report worker.
C. ALB to a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group, with SQS for report jobs.
D. A single-AZ RDS instance as the only HA control.

questions.explain: Multi-AZ plus Auto Scaling covers AZ failure; a queue isolates bursty report work from the user path. One instance and synchronous chaining are SPOFs.
questions.good_to_know: Multi-AZ RDS would still be required if the stem also demanded a highly available relational store. Lambda workers on the queue would appear if the stem asked for least ops on the report tier.

questions.q: A company needs a public website that survives an Availability Zone failure, keeps the application private, and uses a managed Multi-AZ relational database. Static assets should not live on the instances. The team will not place application Elastic IPs in public subnets. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Place an ALB in front of a Multi-AZ Auto Scaling group in private subnets.
B. Run MySQL on a single public EC2 instance with local disks.
C. Use Amazon RDS Multi-AZ and store static assets in Amazon S3.
D. Put application instances in public subnets with Elastic IPs.
E. Use a single-AZ RDS instance to reduce cost below the HA requirement.

questions.explain: The three-tier pattern is private Multi-AZ compute behind an ALB, Multi-AZ RDS, and S3 for static files. Public app IPs and a single-AZ database violate the constraints.
questions.good_to_know: CloudFront would sit in front if the stem required a global CDN. ElastiCache would appear if hot reads, not AZ failure, were the bottleneck.

questions.q: A mobile JSON API must scale with unpredictable traffic, avoid Amazon EC2 host management, and authenticate application end users rather than IAM users. Data is key-value and does not require SQL joins. The company wants the serverless API pattern. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Run the API on a single Amazon EC2 instance in a public subnet.
B. Front AWS Lambda with Amazon API Gateway.
C. Create IAM users for each mobile-app customer.
D. Store items in Amazon DynamoDB and authenticate users with Amazon Cognito.
E. Place a self-managed MySQL cluster on Dedicated Hosts.

questions.explain: The serverless API pattern is API Gateway to Lambda to DynamoDB, with Cognito for end users. IAM users and EC2 hosts fail least-ops and the end-user identity model.
questions.good_to_know: SQS or EventBridge would be the extra piece if the stem required asynchronous work off the API path. RDS Proxy would appear if a relational database were mandatory behind Lambda.

questions.q: Domain events from an order service must fan out to three independent consumers that each need their own backlog and retry behavior. A down consumer must not block the others. The publisher must not call each consumer HTTP API in one transaction. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Have the publisher call each consumer HTTP API in one transaction.
B. Share one SQS queue among all three consumers with competing logic.
C. Publish events to Amazon SNS or Amazon EventBridge.
D. Store events only in the publisher’s instance memory.
E. Subscribe each consumer through its own Amazon SQS queue.

questions.explain: Fan-out is the bus or topic; per-consumer queues give durable, independent scaling and failure domains. One shared queue or synchronous HTTP couples the consumers.
questions.good_to_know: Add a DLQ on each queue when the stem requires poison-message isolation. A single queue is enough when there is only one consumer to decouple.

questions.q: An enterprise must connect an on-premises data center to six AWS VPCs with centralized routing and must govern new accounts with a landing zone. A peering mesh and per-account IAM users are rejected. VPN or Direct Connect can reach AWS. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Use VPN or Direct Connect into AWS Transit Gateway for the VPCs.
B. Peer every VPC to every other VPC including the data center.
C. Create IAM users in each account for every employee.
D. Expose all six VPCs with public IP addresses instead of a hub.
E. Use AWS Organizations with Control Tower and IAM Identity Center.

questions.explain: Hybrid routing is Transit Gateway behind VPN or Direct Connect. Account and workforce governance is Organizations, Control Tower, and Identity Center. Both halves of the enterprise pattern are required.
questions.good_to_know: PrivateLink would replace broad routing if the need were one service to a partner. VPC peering would suffice for two VPCs with no transit.

questions.q: A company in one Region has recovery objectives of hours of downtime and up to a day of data loss. It wants the MOST cost-effective Regional DR that still meets those numbers and must prove restores work. A second full-scale production site is not required. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Run multi-site active-active at full scale in both Regions.
B. Use backup and restore rather than a full second production site.
C. Test restore procedures against the stated RTO and RPO.
D. Keep a warm standby equal to production at all times.
E. Disable snapshots to lower the storage bill.

questions.explain: Loose RTO and RPO select backup and restore; untested backups do not meet the objectives. Active-active and full warm standby overspend.
questions.good_to_know: Warm standby would be the pair with failover testing if RTO were minutes. Never disable backups to save money when an RPO still exists.

questions.q: An order API on AWS Lambda must stay responsive when fulfillment is down, and poison fulfillment messages must not block the queue. Workers already poll from private subnets. The API must not call fulfillment synchronously inside the user request. Which combination of steps should a solutions architect take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Call fulfillment synchronously inside the user request.
B. Store in-flight orders only in API instance memory.
C. Increase DNS TTL instead of buffering work.
D. Place Amazon SQS between the API and the fulfillment workers.
E. Attach a dead-letter queue after a limited retry count.

questions.explain: A queue decouples the user path; a DLQ isolates messages that always fail. Both are required for absorb-spikes plus poison isolation.
questions.good_to_know: SNS plus per-consumer queues would appear if several independent services consumed the same event. Idempotent processing still matters with at-least once delivery.

questions.q: A scenario says application hosts MUST remain private and asks for the LEAST operational overhead. After dropping a public-IP option, two private designs remain: a managed Multi-AZ database and a self-managed database on Amazon EC2. The candidate must not leave the item blank. Which combination of steps should a candidate take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A. Eliminate any answer that places the application on public IPs.
B. Choose the managed Multi-AZ database among the remaining private designs.
C. Choose the public-IP design because it uses fewer AWS services.
D. Choose the self-managed EC2 database to maximize operations work.
E. Leave the question unanswered if both private designs look plausible.

questions.explain: Exam method: drop constraint violators first, then apply least ops to what remains. Do not pick public-IP for simplicity, and do not leave the item blank.
questions.good_to_know: If the stem had required an OS agent the managed database cannot run, the self-managed pair could survive elimination. Flag long items and return, but still submit an answer.
